title: A CRISPR/Cas12a-based digital microfluidic platform for parallel detection of foodborne pathogens.
authors: Wang, Yinglin; Wu, Yafang; Huang, Xiaotian; Tian, Yachen; Liu, Qing
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rapid and automated on-chip detection of multiple foodborne bacterial pathogens remains challenging because conventional molecular assays require multistep liquid handling and are difficult to integrate for parallel analysis. Here, we developed an EWOD-based DMF platform integrating RPA with CRISPR/Cas12a for parallel detection of S. aureus, E. coli O157:H7, L. monocytogenes, and C. sakazakii. The 16-site DMF chip was organized into four pathogen-specific detection modules, each containing a positive control, a negative control, and two replicate sample sites, enabling programmable droplet manipulation and sequential on-chip amplification and fluorescence detection without external pumps or complex valves. RESULTS: Assay conditions were systematically optimized for fluidic compatibility and CRISPR/Cas12a performance. Following off-chip sample preparation and genomic DNA extraction, the automated on-chip RPA amplification and CRISPR/Cas12a detection workflow was completed within approximately 50 min. Under these conditions, the platform achieved detection limits of 10(3), 10(2), 10, and 10(2) CFU/mL for S. aureus, E. coli O157:H7, L. monocytogenes, and C. sakazakii, respectively. No apparent cross-reactivity was observed among 35 food-associated bacterial strains. In artificially contaminated milk, milk powder, and chicken samples, comparable detection limits were obtained after off-chip sample processing, despite matrix-dependent variations in fluorescence intensity. SIGNIFICANCE: These results demonstrate that integrating EWOD-based digital microfluidics with RPA and CRISPR/Cas12a enables rapid, parallelized, and programmable molecular detection of multiple foodborne bacterial pathogens on a compact platform. By integrating droplet manipulation, amplification, and fluorescence detection on-chip, the proposed system reduces reliance on external fluidic components and provides a promising basis for further development toward automated and integrated food-safety testing.

title: An extraction-free one-pot immunomagnetic-RPA-CRISPR/Cas13a platform for ultrasensitive detection of exosomal PD-L1.
authors: Shi, Hansen; Chen, Jiayi; Lin, Xiaocong; Zhang, Yaning; Wu, Haiqi; Zeng, Biyun; Zhang, Peijun; Luo, Qianying; Liu, Tiancai; Zeng, Tao
abstract: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expressed on the surface of exosomes (exo) is a promising liquid biopsy biomarker for monitoring response to immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, existing detection methods are limited by insufficient sensitivity and complicated operation. To address this, we developed an extraction-free immunomagnetic recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)-based one-pot high-sensitivity CRISPR/Cas13a platform (iMRO-HCRISPR) employing DNA-conjugated antibodies. Exosomes in blood were enriched with anti-CD63/CD81/CD9 antibody-conjugated magnetic beads and recognized by PD-L1-specific DNA-antibody probes; the probe DNA then underwent RPA amplification, in vitro transcription (IVT), and Cas13a trans-cleavage, achieving multi-level signal amplification with fluorescent readout. Toehold-mediated DNA affinity pull-down effectively reduced the detection background. The platform achieved a limit of detection (LOD) as low as 10(1) particles/mL (positive detection at the single-particle level), a limit of quantification (LOQ) of 10(3) particles/mL, and a quantitative range of 10(3)-10(11) particles/mL, with the entire process completed in a single closed tube without exosome isolation. Clinical validation demonstrated that the platform effectively distinguished HCC patients from healthy controls (P < 0.0001), with an area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) of 0.964. This study provides robust technical support for the ultrasensitive detection of exosomal PD-L1 in HCC and for dynamic monitoring of immunotherapy response.

title: Asymmetric V-shaped amplification-enhanced and PAM-relaxed one-tube dual-mode CRISPR/Cas12a platform for rapid and ultrasensitive detection of foodborne pathogens.
authors: Wen, Junping; Zhu, Zhi; Zhang, Jipei; Wang, Zhaoqin; Chen, Jidang; Chen, Yiping
abstract: Foodborne pathogen infections pose a serious threat to food safety and public health. As a low-cost method with strong potential for widespread use in most laboratories, conventional PCR and integrated PCR-CRISPR assays are still constrained by prolonged assay times, dedicated instrumentation, limited closed-tube naked-eye visualization, tube-opening-associated contamination risks, and PAM-dependent target recognition, thereby restricting their practical applicability. To address these challenges, we developed an asymmetric V-shaped (rapid thermal cycling) amplification-enhanced CRISPR/Cas12a one-tube dual-mode detection platform. Asymmetric amplification enabled rapid ssDNA enrichment by tuning primer concentrations, reducing amplification time from  approximately 1 h to <30 min while enhancing Cas12a cleavage efficiency and reducing dependence on canonical PAM sites. Moreover, one-tube dual-mode highly sensitive visual pathogen detection (naked-eye: 10 CFU/mL, fluorescence excitation: 1 CFU/mL) was achieved simply by adjusting the probe concentration in the reaction system. By eliminating post-amplification tube opening and reagent transfer while avoiding reliance on nanomaterials or lateral-flow strips, this platform provides a one-tube strategy for rapid, sensitive, and simplified visual detection of foodborne pathogens in resource-limited laboratories.

title: Metal-organic framework-assisted signal amplification in electrochemiluminescent microRNA biosensing: Current advances and barriers to clinical implementation.
authors: Ren, Jing; Cui, Huihui; Zhou, Xiaolong; Zhou, Xianshu; Zhu, Yawen; Wang, Jin
abstract: The rapid expansion of electrochemiluminescence (ECL) biosensing has created growing demand for efficient signal amplification strategies capable of meeting the sensitivity requirements of microRNA analysis. Among the available functional materials, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have evolved from simple signal carriers into multifunctional platforms that integrate probe loading, catalytic enhancement, programmable nucleic acid reactions, and emerging CRISPR-assisted amplification within a single sensing architecture. This review provides a mechanism-oriented perspective on MOF-assisted signal amplification strategies, highlighting how different amplification mechanisms govern analytical performance and practical applicability. Beyond summarizing representative biosensing systems, the advantages, limitations, and suitable application scenarios of different amplification strategies are critically compared to establish guidelines for rational biosensor design. Finally, the remaining obstacles to clinical translation are discussed, together with future opportunities for developing robust, integrated, and clinically deployable MOF-based ECL biosensing platforms.

title: Transcription factor-regulated rolling circle transcription cascaded with Cas12a for sensitive determination of tetracycline.
authors: Chen, Siyu; Wang, Rujia; Su, Yongguang; Zhang, Junjie; Li, Zhijie; Xie, Shiyi; Du, Zhonghui; Liu, Junjun
abstract: The ability to perform convenient and user-friendly quantitative analysis of antibiotic residues in water is critical for mitigating ecological risks, yet current methods often suffer from limited sensitivity, fixed detection ranges, or complex procedures. Here, we present a hierarchical cascade signal amplification platform integrating rolling circle transcription (RCT) with CRISPR-Cas12a for one-pot tetracycline (Tc) detection. A rationally designed circular DNA template containing a T7 promoter, a TetR-binding motif, and a crRNA-encoding sequence serves as the molecular switch. In the absence of Tc, TetR binds to the template and blocks transcription. Upon Tc addition, TetR detaches, triggering RCT to produce numerous crRNA copies, which activate Cas12a-mediated trans-cleavage of fluorescent reporters, generating amplified signals. By adjusting the TetR-to-template ratio from 10:1 to 15:1, the detection range can be tuned from 6.0-100 nM to 20-600 nM, with detection limits of 1.35 nM and 16.4 nM, respectively. The system exhibits excellent selectivity against common interferents and achieves satisfactory recoveries (90%-110%) in spiked aquaculture tailwater, with results consistent with HPLC analysis. This platform offers hierarchical signal amplification, one-pot operation, tunable dynamic range, and modular template design, providing a versatile strategy for environmental pollutant monitoring.

title: TRIM2 facilitates macrophage mediated anti-tumor immunity in renal cell carcinoma through enhancing SIRPA ubiquitination and degradation.
authors: He, Shuhua; Zhao, Chenxi; Wang, Feng; Li, Yunxuan; Liu, Ying; Jiang, Huimin; Yan, Yechao; Li, Ke; Zhang, Tingting
abstract: SIRPA delivers an anti-phagocytic "don't-eat-me" signal through its expression on macrophage membrane surface and promotes tumor progression via membrane-independent mechanism. However, current CD47- and SIRPA-targeting agents only disrupt cell-surface inhibitory signaling, highlighting the therapeutic potential of degrading SIRPA. Here, we identified that E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM2 interacted with SIRPA in vitro. Clinically, elevated TRIM2 expression is associated with prolonged overall and progression-free survival in renal-cell carcinoma (RCC) patients. Mechanistically, TRIM2 catalyzes K48-linked poly-ubiquitination of SIRPA, promoting its proteasomal degradation and reducing SIRPA protein levels. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of TRIM2 in macrophages upregulated SIRPA, significantly impairing phagocytosis of tumor cells. TRIM2 deficiency also promoted tumor growth by increasing intratumoral infiltration of M2-type macrophage, reducing accumulation of anti-tumor M1-like and antigen-presenting macrophages, and impairing effector CD8(+) T-cell recruitment. Importantly, combined TRIM2 overexpression and PD-L1 blockade synergistically enhance anti-tumor immunity. Together, these results suggest that targeting TRIM2 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy against RCC by degrading SIRPA in macrophage and provide a roadmap for clinical application.

title: Sonodynamic Therapy in Periodontitis: From Mechanisms to Biomaterial-Based Innovations.
authors: Li, Yijun; Xiong, Xin; Xu, Ziang; Zhong, Xinnan; Xu, Jingchen
abstract: Periodontitis is a common chronic inflammatory disease driven by pathogenic biofilms, leading to progressive periodontal tissue destruction and systemic health risks. Conventional therapies often fail to eradicate biofilms in deep periodontal pockets, promote antimicrobial resistance and offer limited regenerative potential. Although SDT has emerged as a promising alternative, its clinical efficacy is constrained by several material- and microenvironment-related barriers that have not been systematically addressed in previous reviews. Sonodynamic therapy (SDT) employs low-intensity ultrasound to activate sonosensitizers, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inducing mechanical disruption of biofilms, with advantages of deep tissue penetration, broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and low risk of resistance. Nevertheless, conventional sonosensitizers often exhibit poor water solubility, rapid clearance, limited specificity, and suboptimal ROS generation, while hypoxia, continuous fluid turnover, and mechanical disturbance within periodontal pockets further compromise local retention and therapeutic efficacy. Advances in biomaterials address these barriers by engineering high-performance sonosensitizers to enhance ROS efficiency, developing delivery systems to improve solubility and prolonged retention and integrating multimodal antibacterial and regenerative functions. This review summarizes the mechanistic basis of SDT with recent advances in sonosensitizer engineering, local delivery platforms, synergistic therapies, and multifunctional biomaterials, thereby linking antimicrobial performance to periodontal tissue regeneration. We further identify hypoxia, delivery efficiency, biosafety and the lack of standardized evaluation as key translational challenges, and propose future directions including AI-guided sonosensitizer design, precision delivery systems, and CRISPR-assisted antimicrobial combination strategies to accelerate the clinical translation of SDT for periodontitis management.

title: Integrated strategies for enhanced drought tolerance in tomato: from molecular mechanisms to field applications.
authors: Ma, Li; Wang, Huiru; Zhang, Bin; Guo, Yanan; Ou, Siying; Tian, Yue; Guo, Meng
abstract: Drought stress is a major abiotic constraint on agricultural production, and cultivated tomato varieties are generally sensitive to water deficit. This review systematically summarizes the physiological, biochemical, and molecular mechanisms underlying tomato drought responses. It also integrates recent high-impact insights to advance our understanding of this topic. It then surveys multidimensional improvement strategies. These include biostimulants, chemical regulators, nanomaterials, grafting, water management, and genetic engineering approaches such as transgenesis and CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing. Current research faces bottlenecks in translating laboratory findings to field applications, particularly due to the inherent trade-off between drought tolerance and fruit yield and quality. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that integrates several key components: precision editing tools (e.g. base editing and promoter editing), tissue-specific or stress-inducible expression systems, and parallel phenotyping of yield components and fruit quality traits under both well-watered and drought conditions. This framework is designed to balance stress resilience with productivity. Moving forward, a systematic multidisciplinary approach is required to overcome this trade-off, enabling water-efficient, stable-yielding, and high-quality sustainable tomato production. This review provides an integrative perspective and forward-looking guidance for future research and practical applications.

title: OVATE family protein 6 interacts with CONSTANS-LIKE 3 to regulate bolting by transcriptional control of FLOWERING LOCUS T/TERMINAL FLOWER 1 family genes in lettuce.
authors: An, Guanghui; Liu, Ruoqing; Zhao, Xinhui; Wang, Yueji; Li, Chenxi; Zhu, Lei; Yang, Luming; Sun, Peinan; Wang, Yong
abstract: As one of the most globally cultivated vegetables, lettuce's commercial yield is severely compromised by premature bolting, an undesirable agronomic trait that diminishes crop quality and market value. In this study, we genetically cloned the OVATE family protein 6 (LsOFP6) controlling bolting time in lettuce. LsOFP6 had a nonsense mutation in the late bolting parent. CRISPR/Cas9 knockout and complementary tests confirmed that LsOFP6 positively regulates bolting in lettuce. LsOFP6 physically interacts with the CONSTANS-LIKE 3 (LsCOL3). Genetic analyses suggest that LsOFP6 regulates bolting through an LsCOL3-dependent pathway in the Lsblh2 Lskn1 genotype background, where we have previously established that LsBLH2 and LsKN1, the positive and negative transcriptional regulators of bolting, respectively, both interact with LsOFP6 and exert their functions via the gibberellin pathway. LsCOL3 represses bolting development by directly binding to the promoters of TWIN SISTER OF FLOWERING LOCUS T (LsTSF1) and TERMINAL FLOWER 1 (LsTFL1), downregulating the former while upregulating the latter. These regulations are antagonized by LsOFP6, which promotes bolting by compromising the effects of LsCOL3 on LsTSF1 and LsTFL1. Therefore, loss of function of Lsofp6 decreases LsTSF1 and increases LsTFL1 expression, resulting in late bolting. In summary, the LsOFP6-LsCOL3 module regulates lettuce bolting development by controlling the transcript levels of LsTSF1 and LsTFL1 genes. This study deepens the molecular understanding of bolting development and provides valuable genetic resources and novel strategies for developing lettuce with improved resistance to premature bolting, highlighting the power of natural variation to address agricultural challenges.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-Mediated Mutagenesis of Two Alleles Encoding a Glutathione S-Transferase Confirms Their Identity as Fhb7 Conferring Fusarium Head Blight Resistance in Wheat.
authors: Safar, Shahed; Leng, Yueqiang; Poursafar, Alireza; Amusan, Olawumi; Riasat, Amna; Janga, Madhusudhana R; Yang, Shengming; Cai, Xiwen; Xu, Steven S; Shi, Gongjun; Jin, Zhao; Liu, Zhaohui; Zhong, Shaobin
abstract: Fhb7 is a gene derived from the homoeologous group-7 chromosomes of tall wheatgrass (Thinopyrum species), which confers resistance to Fusarium head blight (FHB) in wheat. Two resistance alleles at the Fhb7 locus (Fhb7Thp and Fhb7The2) were identified from Th. ponticum and Th. elongatum, respectively, and introgressed into the wheat genome by homoeologous recombination. Fhb7Thp was first cloned and reported to encode a glutathione S-transferase (GST), which detoxifies trichothecenes through de-epoxidation. However, a recent study has questioned the role of GST in Fhb7-mediated FHB resistance. To decipher the function of two GST-encoding alleles, Fhb7Thp and Fhb7The2, in FHB resistance, we generated haploid plants from three spring wheat lines (CS-Fhb7, WGC002, and FW23-009-80) carrying Fhb7Thp or Fhb7The2 through wide hybridizations with transgenic maize expressing Cas9 and guide RNA (gRNA) targeting GST. Of 57, 35, and 74 haploid plants derived from CS-Fhb7, WGC002, and FW23-009-80, respectively, 16, 5, and 9 had an insertion/deletion at the target sites of GST. Greenhouse evaluation of doubled haploid (DH) lines derived from the haploid plants for FHB resistance indicated that the GST-edited DH lines were significantly more susceptible and accumulated more deoxynivalenol (DON) than their corresponding wildtypes and non-edited DH lines, confirming GST as the causal gene for Fhb7-mediated FHB resistance. This study also demonstrated the power of wheat x maize hybridization coupled with genome editing in validating gene function in wheat.

title: IFT70 Facilitates Ciliary Hedgehog Signaling in Hindlimb Digit Patterning.
authors: Reynolds, Kurt; Vontell, Andrew; Stottmann, Rolf W
abstract: The function of IFT70A has been explored with a combination of loss of function in vitro experiments and Xenopus depletions. These data suggest that primary cilia require IFT70A for full function. Here we employed a mouse model to investigate the consequences of an IFT70A deletion. Using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing, we targeted the two mouse homologs Ift70a1 and Ift70a2 to generate deletion alleles of each individually (Ift70a1(null); Ift70a2(null)), and an allele in which both genes are removed (Ift70a1/a2(null)). Ift70a1(null/null) and Ift70a1/a2(null/null) double knockout mice exhibited partially penetrant hindlimb polydactyly, but no other phenotype was observed. Altered hedgehog signaling in the mutant hindlimb indicates the likely downstream mechanism by which IFT70A function contributes to digit patterning.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-directed engineering of Clostridium beijerinckii enhanced butanol production from whey permeate.
authors: Okereke, Omoaruemike; Duduyemi, Ademola; Ujor, Victor C
abstract: Whey permeate (WP), an abundant, lactose-rich byproduct of the dairy industry, constitutes an environmental and economic burden on the industry. Despite the high fermentable sugar content of WP, its bioconversion into biobutanol is limited by the poor lactose-utilization culminating in low solvent productivity by native solventogenic microorganisms. In this study, we report CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome engineering of Clostridium beijerinckii NCIMB 8052 (hereafter, C. beijerinckii) to improve butanol production from lactose-rich WP. A native putative lactose transporter encoded by Cbei_4545 and an aldehyde reductase (mgR) from Clostridium pasteurianum were integrated into the chromosome of C. beijerinckii at the acetoacetate decarboxylase gene locus to improve lactose utilization and solvent production. The resulting recombinant strain was evaluated alongside the wildtype using lactose, untreated WP, and ion exchange (Amberlite) resin-treated WP. Across all feedstocks tested, the recombinant strain consistently outperformed the wildtype, producing peak butanol titers of 7.9 g/L, 9.7 g/L, and 20.9 g/L on lactose, WP, and resin-treated WP, respectively, compared to 4.3 g/L, 7.1 g/L, and 11.3 g/L for the wildtype. These results demonstrate the utility of targeted CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering to substantially improve lactose utilization and butanol production in C. beijerinckii. In this work we constructed a strain of C. beijerinckii with strong potential for conversion of abundant and cost-effective WP to biobutanol.

title: The xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydrolase TaXTH16 enhances wheat drought tolerance and pre-harvest sprouting resistance via ABA-mediated pathways.
authors: Bi, Huihui; Wu, Peipei; Wang, Jiayi; Chen, Pandi; Zhang, Quan; Liu, Zeliang; Pang, Zijian; Yang, Xuewei; Wang, Yuqing; Qiao, Wenchen; Wang, Daowen; Zhang, Kunpu
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Drought and PHS are major constraints on wheat production worldwide. Cell wall remodeling plays a crucial role in plant adaptation to water deficit. Xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydrolases (XTHs) are key cell wall-modifying enzymes, yet how they integrate with ABA signaling, the central pathway controlling drought responses and seed dormancy, remains unknown in wheat. OBJECTIVES: The primary objective of this study is to functionally characterize TaXTH16 in drought tolerance and PHS resistance, with a focus on its transcriptional regulation by ABA responsive transcription factors and its natural haplotype variation for breeding applications. METHODS: We generated TaXTH16 overexpression and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout wheat lines for drought and PHS phenotyping. We performed biochemical assays for XET activity and subcellular localization, physiological measurements of water loss rate, stomatal aperture, ABA content, and ROS levels, transcriptomic analysis, and molecular assays including Y1H, EMSA, ChIP-qPCR, and dual-luciferase. Haplotype analyses were conducted across a wide range of wheat accessions. RESULTS: TaXTH16 encodes a functional XET enzyme localized to the plasma membrane and cell wall. Overexpression of TaXTH16 significantly enhanced drought tolerance, whereas knockout lines were more sensitive. TaXTH16 promoted xyloglucan and cellulose accumulation and enhanced ABA-mediated stomatal closure and ROS scavenging under drought. It also positively regulated PHS resistance, likely via ABA-mediated pathways. TaABF2 was identified as a direct transcriptional activator of TaXTH16. A natural variant, TaXTH16-2B-HapII, showed a higher promoter activity, significant association with greater drought resistance, and enrichment in modern cultivars. CONCLUSION: This study establishes TaXTH16 as a positive regulator of wheat drought tolerance and PHS resistance, linking ABA signaling and cell wall remodeling. TaXTH16 is directly activated by TaABF2, and TaXTH16-2B-HapII represents a promising allele for breeding. These findings provide mechanistic insights into ABA-cell wall crosstalk and a valuable resource for improving wheat stress resilience.

title: MANF promotes cell fitness and attenuates bortezomib sensitivity in multiple myeloma.
authors: Huang, Can; Yu, Wen-Jie; Rao, Yue-Xuan; Xu, Peng; Ji, Yun-Fei; Wang, Yan-Xia; Hu, Yong-Jun; Li, Zhen-Yu
abstract: BACKGROUND: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal plasma cell malignancy in which disease relapse and treatment resistance remain major clinical challenges. Identifying molecular dependencies that support myeloma cell fitness may reveal therapeutic vulnerabilities beyond recurrent genomic alterations. Mesencephalic astrocyte-derived neurotrophic factor (MANF) is an endoplasmic reticulum-resident, stress-responsive protein, but its clinical and biological significance in MM remains poorly defined. METHODS: Publicly available DepMap CRISPR dependency data were analyzed to identify candidate MM-preferential dependencies. MANF expression and prognostic associations were examined in the MMRF CoMMpass cohort. Single-cell RNA sequencing and in silico perturbation analyses characterized its cellular distribution and predicted functional associations. MANF knockdown and genetic rescue using an siRNA-resistant MANF construct were performed in RPMI-8226 and OPM-2 cells to assess proliferation, cell-cycle distribution, and bortezomib sensitivity. Transcriptomic profiling characterized gene expression changes following MANF knockdown, while measurements at multiple time points assessed the temporal patterns of IRE1alpha-XBP1s-associated readouts. RESULTS: MANF was identified as a candidate MM-preferential dependency. Higher MANF expression was associated with advanced ISS stage and inferior overall survival, with the survival association retained after adjustment for established clinical and cytogenetic risk factors. Single-cell analysis localized MANF expression predominantly to plasma cells, while virtual knockout predicted changes involving ER protein processing, proteasome function, and metabolism. MANF knockdown inhibited proliferation, increased G0/G1 accumulation, and reduced MYC/E2F-associated transcriptional programs and cell-cycle regulatory proteins. Time-course analyses revealed early enhancement followed by later attenuation in selected IRE1alpha-XBP1s-associated readouts. MANF knockdown also increased bortezomib-induced apoptosis and reduced its IC(5)(0). MANF re-expression partially reversed proliferation and cell-cycle phenotypes, restored IRE1alpha-XBP1s-associated protein abundance, and attenuated bortezomib sensitization. CONCLUSION: These findings identify MANF as a previously underexplored candidate myeloma-associated dependency that supports proliferative fitness and modulates bortezomib sensitivity in the tested MM models. MANF depletion is associated with dynamic changes in IRE1alpha-XBP1s-related readouts. These results support further investigation of MANF as a candidate therapeutic vulnerability in MM.

title: PSK2a is required for cambial development and xylem formation during secondary growth in poplar.
authors: Yue, Songqing; Tian, Dongdong; Ma, Xiao; Qi, Cheng; Wan, Mengjie; Qi, Juan; Cheng, Qian; Tian, Lidan; Shi, Xueping; Zheng, Bo
abstract: Phytosulfokines (PSKs) are sulfated peptide hormones involved in plant growth, development, and stress responses. However, direct genetic evidence for the involvement of PSK peptide in cambium development and secondary vascular development in woody plants remains largely lacking. Here, we identified nine PSK family members in Populus trichocarpa. Phylogenetic, gene structure, conserved motif, and local synteny analyses indicated that the poplar PSK family is evolutionarily conserved, and some members may have arisen from the whole-genome duplication (WGD) event. PSK2a is one of several PSK family genes that are highly expressed in poplar stem vascular tissues, but shows low expression in roots. Subsequently, we generated PtrPSK2a (cloned from P. trichocarpa) overexpression lines in hybrid poplar 717 and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout lines targeting its endogenous orthologs PtaPSK2a_HAP1 and HAP2hybrid poplar 717. Both gain-of-function and loss-of-function of PSK2a exhibited growth defects, characterized by reduced plant height and stem diameter, with more severe overall growth defects in OE lines. Consistently, histological analysis demonstrated that cambium activity and secondary xylem development were significantly inhibited in both transgenic lines, as reflected by fewer cambium cell layers, narrower xylem, and fewer vessels in young stems. In addition, genes associated with cambial development, vessel differentiation, and secondary cell wall formation were broadly downregulated, accompanied by altered expression of several hormone-related marker genes in transgenic lines. Together, these findings demonstrate that PSK2a is required for normal cambial activity and xylem development during secondary growth in poplar, providing the first direct genetic evidence for PSK function in woody plant vascular development.

title: Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma.
authors: Thakur, Shubham Kumar; Malviya, Rishabha; Chandra, Phool; Sridhar, Sathvik Belagodu; Shareef, Javedh; Wadhwa, Tarun
abstract: Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy, and effective gene therapy remains limited by ocular barriers, tumor heterogeneity, and inefficient nucleic acid delivery. This review critically analyses the molecular rationale, engineering principles, emerging nanoarchitectures, biological validation, and translational prospects of dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma. The manuscript also highlights key challenges and future strategies for clinical implementation. Current evidence indicates that dual-vector platforms enable independent optimization of mRNA and CRISPR cargos while maintaining coordinated spatiotemporal therapeutic activity. We conducted a literature search in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for relevant studies published from January 2015 to September 2026. Functional cargo partitioning, vector modularity, programmable intracellular trafficking, and ocular-targeted nanoengineering improve delivery precision and reduce biological compromise associated with co-encapsulation. Lipid, polymeric, hybrid, biomimetic, and viral-nonviral architectures each provide distinct engineering advantages depending on therapeutic objectives. Preclinical studies support enhanced genome editing, transient protein restoration, improved tumor suppression, and reduced off-target effects. Nevertheless, manufacturing scalability, regulatory standardization, long-term safety, and clinical validation remain major barriers to translation. Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR systems represent a promising next-generation platform for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma by enabling coordinated and programmable therapeutic delivery. Continued advances in modular nanoengineering, personalized cargo selection, and clinically scalable manufacturing will be essential for successful translation into precision ocular oncology.

title: Pangenomics as a framework for discovering structural variants underlying cold tolerance in chilli pepper.
authors: Ahmad, Syed Sohail; Nawaz, Muhammad Azher; Can, Wang; Zhao, Yue; Xin, Liu; Chen, Rugang
abstract: Pangenomics-based structural variant discovery offers a transformative framework to resolve missing cold-tolerance heritability in chilli pepper and accelerate climate-resilient cultivar development. Chilli pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) is a globally important crop severely restricted by cold sensitivity. SNP-based GWAS explain only 20-30% of the variance in cold tolerance, leaving a "missing heritability" gap. The GanZi/XianSheng paradox cultivars sharing >99% coding sequence identity yet exhibiting 5-10-fold differences in cold tolerance strongly implicates regulatory and dosage-based structural variants (SVs) as the primary drivers of phenotypic variation, a gap that pangenomics is positioned to address. This review synthesizes pangenomics, structural variant discovery, QTL mapping, and genome editing as an integrated framework for developing cold-tolerant chilli pepper cultivars. Based on cross-species evidence from rice, barley, and tomato pangenome studies, we propose four SV mechanisms predicted to underlie the GanZi cold-tolerance advantage: (1) regulatory SVs in promoters of CaMYB80, CBF/DREB (DREB, Dehydration-Responsive Element-Binding protein), and CaICE1; (2) copy number variations (CNVs) in antioxidant gene families (CaSOD (Superoxide Dismutase), CaCAT (Catalase), CaAPX (Ascorbate Peroxidase)) and the chlorophyll biosynthesis gene CaALAD (delta-Aminolevulinic Acid Dehydratase); (3) transposable element insertions creating novel regulatory elements in osmolyte biosynthesis genes (P5CS (Delta1-Pyrroline-5-Carboxylate Synthase), BADH (Betaine Aldehyde Dehydrogenase)); and (4) chromosomal inversions coordinating master cold-regulator gene clusters. A multi-SV haplotype in GanZi is predicted to explain 60-80% of phenotypic variance in cold tolerance, more than three times the explanatory power of SNP-based approaches. We outline a pangenome construction strategy (15-17 genomes, PacBio/Nanopore long-read sequencing, 18-24 months, $650K-$980K) followed by SV-GWAS on 200-500 accessions to identify 10-25 high-impact SVs. A four-phase breeding roadmap integrates QTL identification (1-2 years), candidate gene discovery via fine mapping and VIGS (1.5-2 years), CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing via TSWV/TRV viral vectors achieving 6.3-77.9% heritable editing efficiency (2-3 years), and multi-environment field validation across 4-6 locations (2-3 years).This integrated pangenomics-to-breeding strategy is projected to deliver climate-resilient chilli pepper cultivars with 2-5 degrees C improvements in freezing tolerance within 7-10 years, substantially outpacing the 10-12-year timeline of traditional breeding. The proposed structural variant mechanisms remain to be experimentally confirmed in pepper and represent a testable research agenda for the chilli pepper genomics community.

title: A homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the C-terminal of Tdrd5 causing early spermiogenesis arrest and azoospermia in mice.
authors: Xie, Meixuan; Zhang, Yutong; Zu, Chenwan; Ruan, Lewen; Li, Kuokuo; Guo, Rui; Tang, Dongdong
journal: Journal of assisted reproduction and genetics
abstract: BACKGROUND: TDRD5 is a germ cell-specific RNA granule component that plays a crucial role in chromatoid body organization, piRNA biogenesis, and spermiogenesis. We previously identified a homozygous C-terminal nonsense mutation in TDRD5 in an infertile patient. While in vitro studies suggested the production of a stable truncated protein, the physiological consequences of this specific C-terminal truncation in vivo remain unknown. PURPOSE: This study aimed to elucidate the in vivo pathogenicity of the TDRD5 C-terminal nonsense mutation and its underlying mechanism using a mouse model. METHODS: We generated a Tdrd5 knock-in mouse carrying a premature termination mutation (Q764X) at the corresponding C-terminal region of murine TDRD5 using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. The reproductive phenotype was assessed through fertility testing, histological analysis (H&E, PAS), and evaluation of apoptosis (TUNEL). The expression of TDRD5 protein was assessed by immunoblot analysis, and retrotransposon activity was examined by co-staining for LINE1 and the DNA damage marker gammaH2AX. RESULTS: Homozygous Tdrd5(Q764X/Q764X) male mice exhibited infertility, reduced testis size, and azoospermia. Histological examination revealed spermiogenic arrest at the round spermatid stage with defective acrosome biogenesis. Contrary to in vitro findings, immunoblot analysis demonstrated the complete absence of both full-length and truncated TDRD5 proteins in Tdrd5(Q764X/Q764X) testes. In addition, the mutant testes exhibited aberrant LINE1 upregulation, increased gammaH2AX signals in spermatocytes, and elevated germ cell apoptosis, thereby phenocopying the defects observed in Tdrd5(-/-) mice. CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrated that the C-terminal nonsense mutation causes a loss-of-function phenotype in vivo. This study highlighted the indispensable role of the TDRD5 C-terminus in maintaining protein stability and ensuring successful spermiogenesis in mice.

title: Scalable Arrayed T-cell CRISPR Screening in Autologous Tumor Co-cultures to Prioritize Combination Partners for T-cell Engagers.
authors: Ernste, Keenan; Zhang, Qiao; Cazares, Oscar; Lu, Kai; Palencia, Servando; Hatzi, Katerina; Eidenshenk, Celine; Tong, Zhixiang; Jiang, Yanwen; Jin, Hyun Yong
abstract: T-cell-engaging therapies (TCE) have shown clinical promise in hematologic malignancies, but the T-cell-intrinsic determinants of TCE-mediated cytotoxicity remain incompletely defined. This is in part because functional studies in patient-derived primary samples have been technically challenging. Here, we describe a flow cytometry-based arrayed CRISPR knockout screening platform to prioritize regulators of TCE-mediated cytotoxicity in suspension tumor cells using patient-derived, autologous chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) samples. The principal advantage of this system is the use of matched T cells and tumor cells from the same patient, retaining patient-matched effector-target pairings that are not captured in donor-mismatched or cell line-based assays. In this workflow, CD3+ T cells isolated from viably frozen CLL peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) are expanded and edited for 2 days using arrayed Cas9 ribonucleoprotein nucleofection. TCE-mediated cytotoxicity was assessed in a 72-hr, feeder-supported co-culture assay using patient-matched CLL tumor cells in the presence of CD20xCD3 TCE. In the current implementation, the workflow is organized into modules that accommodate up to 96 arrayed perturbations, with technical replicates evaluated under TCE and control conditions. Because perturbations remain physically indexed in an arrayed format, the workflow is amenable to parallelization and laboratory automation, providing a path toward substantially larger targeted screens. This platform therefore provides a scalable framework for mechanistic studies and combination-target discovery for TCE therapies. (c) 2026 The Author(s). Basic Protocol 1: CD3+ T cell isolation from CLL patient PBMC (Day 0) Alternate Protocol 1: Sequential label-free isolation of CD19+ and CD3+ T cells from healthy donor PBMC Alternate Protocol 2: Sequential label-free isolation of CD3+ T cells and B-CLL cells from CLL donor PBMC Basic Protocol 2: Transfer activated T cells to G-Rex for large-scale expansion (Day 4) Basic Protocol 3: Harvest and CRISPR Editing of Expanded T Cells (Day 11) Support Protocol 1: CRISPR knockout optimization and validation in T cells Basic Protocol 4: CLL co-culture with CRISPR-edited T cells (Day 13) Basic Protocol 5: Flow cytometry analysis of tumor viability and T cell phenotype (Day 16) Support Protocol 2: Selecting suitable co-culture conditions for E:T ratio and TCE concentration for large-scale screening.

title: CTRP3 disruption promotes a tendon-like matrix signature in tenogenically induced canine adipose-derived stem cells.
authors: Kim, Suhwan; Lee, Jeong-Hwa; Jang, Goo; Kang, Byung-Jae
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Tendon injuries heal through disorganized extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition rather than the restoration of native collagen architecture, thus resulting in suboptimal functional recovery. Although adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) are attractive for tendon regeneration because of their accessibility and expandability, their tenogenic differentiation efficiency is lower than that of tendon-derived stem cells (TDSCs). C1q/TNF-related protein 3 (CTRP3) is an adipokine implicated in ECM remodeling and fibrosis; however, its role in tendon lineage regulation is unknown. OBJECTIVE: CTRP3 (C1q/TNF-related protein 3) contributes to extracellular-matrix remodeling and, in tendon, is associated with a pathological fibrotic matrix signature; we therefore reasoned that reducing CTRP3 would favor a more mature tendon-like matrix. Using a loss-of-function approach based on clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), we investigated whether CTRP3 disruption alters tenogenic marker expression, at both the transcript and protein levels, and the tendon-associated ECM marker profile of canine ADSCs relative to wild-type ADSCs and native TDSCs. METHODS: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs were generated and validated using sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, and Western blotting. Wild-type ADSCs, CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs, and TDSCs were subjected to tenogenic induction for 0-3 weeks. Tenogenic transcriptional and ECM markers were analyzed at mRNA and protein levels. RESULTS: CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs showed increased collagen type I and tenomodulin (TNMD) expression during tenogenic induction compared with wild-type ADSCs. COL III expression showed a transient increase followed by a decline, with lower expression in CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs than in WT cADSCs at week 2. CTRP3 disruption increased early Mkx and Scx expression at the earliest time points but did not consistently alter the early transcriptional program, which rose comparably across all groups. CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs showed partial, marker- and time-point-dependent overlap with native cTDSCs, mainly for selected late ECM markers rather than across the overall transcript and protein profiles. CONCLUSION: CTRP3 disruption shifted the tendon-associated ECM marker profile during the tenogenic differentiation of ADSCs, with reduced COL III accumulation, rather than uniformly enhancing tenogenic differentiation. Although early transcriptional changes were observed, the more consistent differences were found in late tendon-associated ECM markers. The modulation of CTRP3 may represent a candidate strategy worth further investigation for stem cell-based tendon regeneration in veterinary medicine.

title: HNRNPH2-R114W remodels RNA splicing and neurodevelopmental gene programs in isogenic cerebral organoids.
authors: Caiaffa, Carlo Donato; Ghousifam, Neda; Watkins, Stephan Lloyd; Nakaya, Helder I; Bowling, Rodney A Jr; Finnell, Richard H; Cabrera, Robert M
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder has been linked to disrupted RNA processing during corticogenesis, yet variant-specific mechanisms remain difficult to resolve. Isogenic cerebral organoids derived from a patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) line carrying the HNRNPH2-R114W variant and its CRISPR-corrected counterpart serve as a human developmental model to investigate variant-associated RNA dysregulation. Imaging quantification and exploratory bulk RNA sequencing, performed at a single developmental time point on a pooled organoid RNA from each genotype, identify coordinated remodeling of neuronal and metabolic programs, along with junction-centered splicing dysregulation involving 6,310 differentially used junctions. Computational structural docking situates HNRNPH2 RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) 1-3 within a spliceosomal context and locates residue R114 near a predicted RNA-contact interface, indicating that the R114W substitution may alter RNA engagement. Integration of differential expression with event- and isoform-level analyses identifies regulatory hubs enriched for axon guidance and synaptic signaling pathways. Single-cell-reference-based deconvolution suggests modest compositional shifts that are unlikely to account for the extent of transcriptional and splicing alterations observed. Collectively, these findings imply HNRNPH2-R114W in widespread RNA rewiring and define candidate isoform-level endpoints for mechanistic and therapeutic investigation in human cortical organoids. These molecular signatures open new avenues to examine how HNRNPH2-associated RNA dysregulation evolves across developmental time and recurs across independent biological contexts, providing a foundation for further mechanistic studies of this rare neurodevelopmental disorder.

title: Botrytis cinerea uses effective detoxification mechanisms to overcome the plant RBOHD-dependent extracellular oxidative burst.
authors: Vielba-Fernandez, Alejandra; Sommer, Lea; Ross, Desiree; Ingelfinger, Julian; Wachtmeister, Thorsten; Hecht, Jochen; Safari, Nassim; Muller-Schussele, Stefanie J; Hahn, Matthias
abstract: The necrotrophic fungus Botrytis cinerea rapidly kills host tissue with its secreted proteins and metabolites. Necrotrophs can trigger the hypersensitive response, which is accompanied by reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, but it remains unclear whether this ROS burst promotes or restricts B. cinerea infection. We have combined Arabidopsis RESPIRATORY BURST OXIDASE HOMOLOG D (RBOHD) mutant analysis, luminol-based in vivo assays, and the use of CRISPR/Cas9-generated B. cinerea ROS detoxification mutants to analyze the toxic effect of the ROS burst. In addition, RNA-sequencing, transcript analyses and redox imaging were used to study RBOHD-dependent signaling and redox homeostasis. RBOHD mutants showed slightly increased susceptibility to B. cinerea infection, and the apoplastic ROS burst was found to be dependent on RBOHD. Fungal mutants confirmed the importance of SOD1 and AP1 for ROS detoxification and virulence. Unexpectedly, the transcriptomes of B. cinerea-infected Arabidopsis Col-0 and an activation-impaired RBOHD mutant were highly similar 48 hours after inoculation, providing no evidence for a connection of extracellular ROS production and intracellular ROS-induced transcriptional signaling. Nevertheless, RBOHD activity was found to be involved in the maintenance of cellular redox homeostasis under phytotoxic stress. Our results indicate a protective role of the RBOHD-dependent oxidative burst against B. cinerea, but this can be overcome by the fungus via different ROS detoxification mechanisms.

title: A novel FRET-force biosensor for nucleoporin gp210 reveals that the nuclear pore complex experiences mechanical tension.
authors: Wang, Peipei; Denis, Kevin; Luxton, G W Gant; Conway, Daniel E
abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is a large multi-protein structure that enables movement of macromolecules, such as mRNA and proteins, between the nucleoplasm and cytoplasm. There has been great interest in how the physical state of the NPC can influence nuclear-cytoplasmic transport. The hypothesis that the NPC may be mechanosensitive is supported by prior reports showing that the diameter of the NPC increases with nuclear envelope stretch as well as increased ECM stiffness. We therefore sought to develop a biosensor-based approach to determine if the NPC experiences mechanical tension. Using a previously developed FRET-force biosensor, known as TSMod, we developed a gp210 tension sensor. gp210 is a transmembrane nucleoporin, which may serve to anchor the NPC into the nuclear envelope. Using a CRISPR knock-in strategy, we developed a HeLa cell line which expresses the gp210 tension sensor at endogenous levels. The FRET-force responsiveness of the gp210 tension sensor was validated using hypo-osmotic and hyper-osmotic nuclear swelling experiments. Additionally, we observed that gp210 forces are sensitive to the ECM, nuclear LINC complex, chromatin condensation, and actomyosin contractility. Our results indicate that both nuclear strain and cytoskeletal forces contribute to mechanical tension across gp210. Our studies provide the first direct measurements of protein-level mechanical forces on the NPC. We anticipate that the gp210 force sensor will be of use for future studies of NPC mechanobiology.

title: A molecular rheostat of ABA signaling coordinates the trade-off between stem growth and drought adaptation.
authors: Lv, Chenfei; He, Yuling; Zhang, Donghai; Zhang, Mengjiao; Yuan, Mingjia; Zhong, Leishi; Tian, Chongde; Zhou, Jiaxuan; Huang, Rui; Jin, Zhuoying; Li, Peng; Lu, Wenjie; Xiao, Liang; Li, Jinlong; Quan, Mingyang; Li, Zhonghai; Zhao, Rui; Du, Liang; Liu, Li-Jun; Zhang, Deqiang; Du, Qingzhang
abstract: BACKGROUND: Plants balance vegetative growth and stress responses through antagonistic phytohormone crosstalk, notably between abscisic acid (ABA) and cytokinin. However, the genetic architecture and molecular mechanisms driving this adaptive trade-off, particularly in perennial trees, remain elusive. RESULTS: Integrating genome-environment and genome-wide association studies across 302 Populus tomentosa accessions, we identify PtoAG1 as a pleiotropic regulator of climate adaptation and stem growth. A naturally occurring frameshift mutation abolishes its repressor function, driving geographical niche differentiation by enhancing growth in humid habitats. Mechanistically, PtoAG1 acts as a molecular rheostat. Under drought, ABA-activated PtoSnRK2.2 phosphorylates PtoMYB84 to transactivate PtoAG1. PtoAG1 then represses the cytokinin-signaling regulator PtoRR12, consequently releasing its inhibition of PtoSnRK2.2. This positive feedback further suppresses vegetative growth under stress while amplifying ABA responses via PtoAREB3. Concurrently, PtoAG1 directly represses PtoAREB3 as a transcriptional brake to maintain signaling homeostasis. Evolutionary analyses reveal that PtoMYB84 and PtoAG1 constitute a tightly linked cis-regulatory module conserved across eudicots. Functional analysis on AG1 orthologs in poplar, Arabidopsis, rice, and tomato demonstrates conserved cross-species utility: loss-of-function increases vegetative biomass but overexpression significantly boosts drought resilience. CONCLUSIONS: Our study identifies a hierarchical crosstalk mechanism bridging ABA and cytokinin signaling to optimize environmental fitness. The evolutionarily conserved MYB84-AG1 cis-regulatory module establishes a versatile, translatable genetic target for precision breeding of climate-resilient and high-yielding crops.

title: GALE is a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint of Vgamma9Vdelta2 T cell-mediated killing.
authors: Shan, Zezhi; Wang, Dongdong; Zheng, Zening; Ye, Zilan; Mao, Shiyu; Xie, Longyan; Li, Yaxu; Guo, Yadong; Weng, Linjun; Wu, Qi; Wang, Yanjin; Ran, Qiao; Yang, Yanrong; Niu, Tingting; Li, Li; Luo, Dakui; Weng, Junyong; Yu, Lei; Wei, Liming; Ge, Xin; Li, Xinxiang; Wang, Ping
abstract: Vgamma9Vdelta2 T cells mediate HLA-independent targeting of tumor cells, offering unique opportunities for cancer immunotherapy, yet their therapeutic efficacy remains limited. Here, using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify UDP-galactose 4-epimerase (GALE) as a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint that restricts Vgamma9Vdelta2 T cell-mediated killing. GALE is a key nucleotide-sugar metabolic enzyme that controls the interconversion of UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose, thereby supporting protein glycosylation and cell-surface glycan remodeling. Mechanistically, GALE promotes complex N-glycosylation of CD155 and CEACAM1, favoring their engagement with the inhibitory receptors TIGIT and TIM3, respectively, while limiting CD155 binding to the activating receptor CD226. GALE loss potentiates Vgamma9Vdelta2 T cell-mediated tumor killing in multiple mouse models and colorectal cancer patient-derived organoids. Together, these findings reveal how nucleotide-sugar metabolism shapes tumor-immune communication through complex N-glycan remodeling and identify GALE and its downstream receptor-ligand interactions as potential therapeutic targets for enhancing Vgamma9Vdelta2 T cell antitumor activity.

title: BAZ2A-induced epigenetic states in cancer cells fuel palmitate accumulation in the tumor microenvironment driving CAR-T cell exhaustion.
authors: Wang, Hongye; Geng, Haigang; Zhao, Jingtong; Ge, Haodong; Shen, Yan; Wu, Zhaorong; Bian, Linke; Zuo, Jinlu; Sun, Zhen; Yang, Ying; Zhu, Jiufei; Shen, Weiming; Zheng, Jiaojiao; Cui, Dan; Ding, Jiawei; Yang, Shuxian; He, Hongchao; Huang, Hai; Gao, Yi; Gao, Keke; Huo, Mengfei; Liu, Hanqing; Liu, Yixun; Xiao, Jun; Xu, Dan-Feng; He, Qiang; Zhang, Yihao; Liu, Feng; Liu, Lianxin; Zheng, Minghua; Jin, Haojie; Zhai, Bo; Zhang, Chuanjie
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy shows limited efficacy in solid tumors, partly owing to poorly defined tumor-intrinsic resistance mechanisms. Here we show that the epigenetic regulator BAZ2A drives resistance to CD70-targeted CAR-T therapy by reprogramming tumor lipid metabolism. Using an in vivo CRISPR screen in a mouse renal cell carcinoma model, we identify BAZ2A as a key mediator that promotes the production and accumulation of palmitic acid, a saturated fatty acid in the tumor microenvironment. Excess palmitic acid is taken up by CAR-T cells and impairs mitochondrial fitness by inhibiting PGC-1alpha activity, thereby enforcing a dysfunctional state. Pharmacologic inhibition of BAZ2A reduces lipid accumulation and restores CAR-T cell activity in vivo. These findings reveal an epigenetic-metabolic mechanism of immune resistance and suggest that targeting tumor lipid remodeling represents a therapeutic strategy to overcome CAR-T resistance in solid tumors.

title: sox17 Mutagenesis Reveals Compounding Effects ofMaternal and Zygotic Contribution on Microglia Abundance.
authors: Spring, Camden A; Dennen, John; Gan, Dailin; Li, Jun; Smith, Cody J
abstract: Embryonic development is shaped by maternal and zygotic factors but how the interplay between these factors contributes to phenotypic variability and impacts specific populations of brain cells, and subsequently neurodevelopment, remains largely unknown. Here, we reveal a double hit phenomenon that impacts microglia and microglia precursors during development. Using zebrafish, we identified a mutation in sry-related HMG box gene-17 (sox17) that exhibits a maternal effect phenotype presenting as a reduction of microglia in the brain and precursors in the yolk sac. We demonstrate that microglia deficits are exacerbated in homozygous offspring from homozygous parents compared to homozygous offspring from heterozygous parents, suggesting a compounding effect of maternal and zygotic sox17 mutation on microglia abundance. We observe that sox17 is expressed in microglia and yolk sac precursors and is maternally contributed. Injections of sox17 RNA during embryogenesis are sufficient to rescue microglia and yolk sac cell abundance. To identify additional genes interacting with sox17, we perform a genetic screen using CRISPR mutagenesis and identify f11r.1, gas6, and mpp1 as microglia regulators, which we demonstrate are expressed in zebrafish microglia. Transcriptional and mutant analyses with these genes suggest sox17 positively regulates mpp1 transcription. These results demonstrate that microglia are susceptible to additive effects of maternal and zygotic sox17 mutation, and that offspring greatly differ in their susceptibility to microglia deficits depending on the mother's genotype. Our findings highlight that both the maternal and offspring genotype should be considered when examining neurodevelopmental disorders that could arise from microglia dysfunction.

title: Nucleic acid amplification-free, aptamer-gated Cas13a-Csm6 cascade for signal-on electrochemical detection of carcinoembryonic antigen in esophageal cancer.
authors: Song, Yuzhe; Zhao, Wan; Liu, Qiong; Yang, Huan; He, Yi; Jia, Suoyang
abstract: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a clinically relevant tumor-associated biomarker that has been investigated for auxiliary assessment and monitoring in the context of esophageal cancer. However, conventional CEA assays often require antibodies, complicated procedures, or nucleic acid amplification strategies to achieve high sensitivity. Herein, we developed a nucleic acid amplification-free, aptamer-gated Cas13a-Csm6 cascade electrochemical aptasensor for sensitive CEA analysis. In the proposed sensing model, the CEA aptamer serves as both a target recognition element and a Cas13a activator. In the absence of CEA, the free aptamer activates Cas13a, triggering cleavage of the Csm6 activator precursor and generation of secondary activators for Csm6. The activated Csm6 subsequently cleaves methylene blue (MB)-labeled single-stranded RNA reporters immobilized on the electrode surface, resulting in MB release and a decreased electrochemical signal. The increased signal observed in the presence of CEA is consistent with the proposed model that CEA binding may reduce the availability or accessibility of the aptamer for Cas13a activation, thereby attenuating the downstream Cas13a-Csm6 cascade. The proposed method achieved a detection limit of 1.12 pg/mL, which was approximately 21-fold lower than that of the Cas13a-only system (23.5 pg/mL). Without requiring PCR, RPA, RCA, or other nucleic acid amplification procedures, the platform exhibited excellent selectivity against interfering proteins and reliable performance in 1% fetal bovine serum. This work provides a sensitive nucleic acid amplification-free CRISPR-assisted electrochemical strategy for CEA quantification and highlights the potential of Cas13a-Csm6 cascades for tumor-associated biomarker analysis.

title: Integrated single-cell and bulk RNA-Seq analysis reveals a LCR-related prognostic signature for precision prognostication and therapeutic stratification in clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
authors: Zhong, Weimin; Rao, Rong; Zhang, Jinxiang; Cheng, Maoyang; Wu, Xiaohong
abstract: BACKGROUNDS: Lysine crotonylation (LCR) is an emerging post-translational modification, yet its clinical significance and therapeutic relevance in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) remain poorly understood. METHODS: Multi-omics data were collected from public repositories. Consensus clustering based on 18 LCR-related genes (LCRGs) was performed to define molecular subtypes. Co-expression modules identified via WGCNA were integrated into 101 machine-learning combinations to establish a LCR-related signature (LCRS). The signature was evaluated for survival prediction, immune microenvironment characteristics, and drug response across multiple cohorts, complemented by single-cell RNA sequencing. Candidate therapeutic targets and compounds were screened using DepMap CRISPR dependency data and pharmacogenomic databases (CTRP and PRISM). RESULTS: Two distinct molecular subtypes (C1 and C2) were identified, displaying significant differences in survival, immune infiltration, and signaling pathways. Integrating WGCNA hub genes with an optimal machine-learning framework yielded a robust 15-gene LCRS, which served as an independent prognostic factor in the TCGA cohorts. Single-cell analysis localized signature genes predominantly to endothelial cells. Pharmacogenomic profiling indicated higher sensitivity to sunitinib among high-risk patients, whereas low-risk patients displayed elevated sensitivity to axitinib and pazopanib. Furthermore, dependency screening prioritized CLCNKA as a key therapeutic target along with ten candidate compounds for high-risk patients. CONCLUSIONS: This study establishes a robust LCR-related prognostic signature and nominates CLCNKA as a novel therapeutic vulnerability, offering actionable insights for personalized stratification and treatment in ccRCC.

title: Manganese exposure activates the cGAS-STING-IL-17 axis and is associated with Tau and alpha-synuclein accumulation in mice.
authors: Yang, Jirui; Luo, Jinghao; Zhou, Qiongli; Chai, Xueting; Wang, Xuanfang; Li, Jierong; Wang, Mingfang; Gu, Xueyan; Chang, Xuhong; Li, Sheng; Yang, Manjun; Sun, Yingbiao; Wang, Hui
abstract: Excessive manganese (Mn) exposure is an environmental risk factor for neurodegeneration, yet the circuitry linking Mn‑induced innate immune activation to proteinopathy remains unclear. Here, by combining in vivo manganese chloride (MnCl(2)) exposure in mice with BV2 microglial models, we demonstrate that the cGAS-STING pathway promotes interleukin-17 (IL‑17)‑mediated neuroinflammation and neurotoxic protein accumulation. Mice administered MnCl(2) in drinking water for five weeks showed elevated levels of Tau, phosphorylated Tau (p-Tau), and alpha-synuclein (alpha-Syn), along with activation of the cGAS-STING pathway (upregulated cGAS, STING, p‑STING, p‑IRF3), increased IL‑17 A and IL‑1beta levels, and an increased proportion of differentially expressed genes from transcriptomic analysis annotated to the IL-17 pathway. In BV2 microglia, MnCl(2) similarly activated cGAS-STING and upregulated IL‑17 A and IL‑1beta. CRISPR‑mediated deletion of cGAS or STING abolished Mn‑induced STING-IRF3 phosphorylation, blunted IL‑17 pathway expression, and prevented the accumulation of Tau, p‑Tau, and alpha‑Syn. Neutralisation of IL‑17 A with a blocking antibody partially attenuated Mn‑induced Tau and alpha‑Syn upregulation. Molecular docking, co‑immunoprecipitation and molecular dynamics analyses suggested potential physical associations between IL‑17 A and both Tau and alpha‑Syn. Collectively, our findings implicate the cGAS-STING-IL-17 axis as a candidate pathway linking Mn-induced innate immune activation to neurodegeneration-related protein aggregation.

title: Functional dissection of conserved RNAi pathways in antiviral immunity of several hemipteran insects.
authors: Zhang, Yan; Ye, Zhuang-Xin; Ma, Qing-Lu; Wang, Bi-Yun; Zhuo, Ji-Chong; Huang, Hai-Jian; Zhang, Chuan-Xi; Chen, Jian-Ping; Li, Jun-Min
abstract: The small silencing RNA pathways are crucial post-transcriptional gene silencing mechanisms involved in antiviral defense, gene regulation, and transposon suppression. In insects, the three main pathways are the microRNA (miRNA), Piwi-interacting RNA (piRNA), and small interfering RNA (siRNA) pathways. While these pathways are well-studied in model insects like fruit flies and mosquitoes (Order: Diptera), their functions in non-model insects remain largely unexplored. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive functional screening of core RNAi-related genes in a hemipteran insect, the small brown planthopper (Laodelphax striatellus). Our results demonstrated that genes in the miRNA pathway (AGO1 and DCR1) and the piRNA pathway (Piwi and AGO3) are essential for the survival, development, and fecundity of L. striatellus, but they are not actively involved in the antiviral response. Unexpectedly, knocking down the key siRNA pathway gene DCR2 did not produce a detectable change in viral accumulation or the abundance of virus-derived small interfering RNAs. This finding suggests that substantial depletion of DCR2 does not detectably impair the measured antiviral siRNA responses in L. striatellus under our experimental conditions. A similar lack of detectable antiviral phenotypes following DCR2 knockdown was observed in three other representative hemipteran insects from different families/genera (Sogatella furcifera, Nilaparvata lugens, and Bemisia tabaci). Additionally, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of DCR2 resulted in embryonic lethality in homozygous mutant strains of L. striatellus, while heterozygous mutants showed significantly prolonged developmental duration. Functional RNAi-of-RNAi assays further demonstrated that DCR2 pre-knockdown did not detectably reduce silencing of a subsequently introduced dsRNA reporter in L. striatellus, and DCR2-heterozygous mutants with reduced DCR2 expression showed no change in viral accumulation. These results reveal an essential developmental role for DCR2 and indicate that partial DCR2 depletion does not measurably compromise antiviral immunity under the tested conditions. Collectively, our findings broaden our understanding of the organization and biological functions of small silencing RNA pathways in hemipteran insects.

title: Protocol to identify DNA methylation-sensitive enhancer sites.
authors: Taege, Natalie; Schriever, Sonja C; Kirchner, Henriette
abstract: Here, we present a protocol to identify DNA methylation-sensitive enhancer sites using the leptin-regulating enhancer RS1 in adipose tissue. We describe steps for validating RS1's endogenous function with a dCas9-KRAB repressor system and quantifying RS1 CpG methylation by pyrosequencing. We then detail procedures for assessing methylation sensitivity by luciferase reporter assay. This protocol is adaptable to other enhancers and tissues. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Taege et al.(1).

title: A High-Sensitivity RPA/Cas12a Assay for Rapid Detection of the Select Agent Ralstonia solanacearum R3b2.
authors: Ostlund, Sydney; Yang, Hsu; Newberry, Eric; Costanzo, Stefano; Yang, Yinong
abstract: Ralstonia solanacearum is a globally distributed, soil-borne species complex that causes bacterial wilt in many economically important crops. Race 3 biovar 2 (R3b2) is a cold-tolerant, highly aggressive subgroup within this complex that is responsible for an estimated $1 billion in annual global losses. Because R3b2 remains exotic to North America, it is classified as a USDA Select Agent due to its high potential to devastate U.S. solanaceous crops and ornamental industries. However, current diagnostic methods for this pathogen involve trade-offs among cost, sensitivity, specificity, and ease of use, particularly for point-of-care (POC) detection in field settings. CRISPR-based detection platforms have recently emerged as promising tools for high-sensitivity POC diagnostics. Here we developed an isothermal recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)/Cas12a assay for specific, sensitive and rapid detection of R3b2. By targeting a genomic region associated with the cool-virulence phenotype, the assay reliably differentiates R3b2 from plant hosts and other diverse R. solanacearum strains. Incorporation of a dual-guide RNA system and an 8-mer single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) fluorescent reporter further improved sensitivity and reduced detection time. Using dilution series of R3b2-spiked Pelargonium DNA extracts, the assay detected as few as 4 CFU per reaction. To facilitate POC applications, the system was adapted into a one-pot, contamination-resistan nott format compatible with portable fluorescence readers such as Genie III device and P51 viewer. By improving both sensitivity and portability, this assay enhances current diagnostic capabilities and, pending validation in real-world conditions, supports early surveillance efforts aimed at preventing the introduction of R3b2 into the United States.

title: Microfluidic-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Pathogen Detection in Urine Samples for Resource-Limited Settings: A Review.
authors: Tarim, E Alperay; Kumar, Natish; Mauk, Michael; El-Tholoth, Mohamed
abstract: Urine is a convenient, noninvasive specimen for molecular diagnostics, offering advantages in scalability, patient compliance, and suitability for decentralized testing. However, its clinical adoption for molecular pathogen detection remains limited by intrinsic physicochemical variability, low target abundance, and the presence of inhibitors of enzymatic nucleic acid amplification that may seriously compromise assay sensitivity and reproducibility. In this review, we introduce a urine-first design paradigm in which device architecture and assay chemistry are codesigned around the unique biochemical constraints of urine rather than adapted from conventional blood-based workflows. This paradigm is built on three interdependent principles: matrix-aware sample processing with efficient inhibitor removal and multifraction nucleic acid capture; amplification chemistry with built-in tolerance to pH fluctuations, ionic variability, and residual urinary inhibitors; and closed, integrated microfluidic architectures that minimize contamination risk. We compare on-chip amplification strategies, including PCR, isothermal amplification methods such as LAMP and RPA, digital PCR, and CRISPR-assisted detection, and evaluate trade-offs in sensitivity, inhibitor tolerance, and deployability. Detection modalities, including fluorescence, colorimetric, electrochemical, and lateral-flow readouts, are assessed for analytical performance and compatibility with resource-limited settings. By integrating biological insight with engineering design, this review provides a practical roadmap for developing accessible, field-ready urine-based diagnostic platforms.

title: Array Assembler: A Constraint-Aware Pipeline for Cas12 and Cas13 crRNA Array Design and Oligonucleotide Decomposition.
authors: Bryson, James William
abstract: Array-based CRISPR systems such as Cas12 and Cas13 enable compact multiplexed perturbations by encoding multiple spacers within a single precursor transcript that is autonomously processed into individual targeting crRNAs. In practice, however, crRNA arrays are difficult to synthesize directly because conserved direct repeats introduce extensive sequence repetitiveness, and reliable cloning requires that ligation junctions avoid repeated sequences while remaining compatible with a chosen plasmid context. Here, we describe Array Assembler, an interactive, browser-based computational workflow that formalizes crRNA array design as a constrained sequence construction and oligonucleotide decomposition problem. Given a CRISPR variant, an ordered list of spacer sequences, and basic cloning parameters (including direct-repeat context and overhang sequences), the pipeline constructs the full in silico array insert and algorithmically decomposes it into paired forward and reverse oligonucleotides that satisfy junction placement rules and practical synthesis limits. Output oligonucleotides are exported as a vendor-ready spreadsheet to enable rapid ordering and downstream assembly. The chapter provides step-by-step instructions for running the tool, outlines the underlying segmentation logic for developers, and includes a worked example illustrating design-to-assembly for a multiplexed Cas12 crRNA array.

title: Strain engineering of Aspergillus species for industrial enzymes bioproduction: a comprehensive review.
authors: Ullah, Irfan; Zhang, Zhihui; Geng, Dezhi; Zhou, Qiyang; Zou, Yahong; Xu, Bing; Zhang, Chong; Xing, Xin-Hui
abstract: Filamentous fungi of the genus Aspergillus, because of their exceptional secretory capacity and metabolic versatility have been extensively applied in traditional food fermentation and industrial biotechnology for production of diverse bioproducts. Their history of domestication and industrial application has enabled major progress in enzyme production; however, challenges associated with the filamentous growth and strain engineering for future biomanufacturing development still remain. This review summarizes the advances across the spectrum of strain-improvement methodologies, from classical mutagenesis, protoplast fusion, genome shuffling, and adaptive laboratory evolution to the modern era of CRISPR enabled genome editing, synthetic biology, and systems-level metabolic engineering. Previous reviews have primarily focused on individual Aspergillus species, specific industrial products or particular strain improvement approaches. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of classical and modern strain engineering technologies and industrial scale up across a wide range of Aspergillus species for industrial enzyme production. In particular, emerging non-GMO evolution tools such as atmospheric and room temperature plasma (ARTP) mutagenesis, and modern molecular biotechnology coupled with microdroplet-based ultrahigh-throughput screening, now allow the researchers to generate and screen a large number of Aspergillus species mutants with single-cell precision. The discovery of high-performance strains with enhanced secretion, stress tolerance, substrate utilization, and favorable enzymatic profiles for food and bioprocessing applications has been accelerated by the strain innovations. Collectively, these advances establish A. oryzae and the related species as increasingly reliable, scalable, and programmable hosts that can meet the biomanufacturing requirements of future circular and sustainable bioeconomies.

title: A comprehensive review of mixed-species biofilm infections and innovative therapeutic strategies.
authors: Nazari, Mohsen; Kardan, Romina; Ahmadi, Amjad; Abolhasani, Fatemeh Sadat; Hemmati, Jaber
abstract: Mixed-species biofilm infections are important causes of persistent and difficult-to-treat infections. Compared with monospecies biofilms, mixed-species communities contain microorganisms with different physiological and genetic characteristics that interact through metabolic cooperation, chemical signaling, competition, and modification of the local environment. These interactions, together with the EPS matrix, physiological heterogeneity, and HGT, can increase antimicrobial tolerance, contributing to treatment failure and infection recurrence. Polymicrobial biofilms are associated with chronic wounds, respiratory infections, catheter- and device-associated infections, and other persistent infections. However, treatment of polymicrobial biofilms remains challenging because their complex structure and interspecies interactions can reduce antimicrobial efficacy. This review summarizes the clinical significance, formation, and persistence of mixed-species biofilms and discusses recent therapeutic strategies for their control. We also discuss recent approaches for controlling polymicrobial biofilms, including natural compounds, QS inhibition, CRISPR-Cas-based approaches, biofilm matrix targeting, metabolic and nutrient disruption, nanotechnology, and phage therapy. Recent studies show that these approaches can inhibit biofilm formation, disrupt established biofilms, enhance antimicrobial activity, and selectively target specific microbial populations. However, their effectiveness varies with microbial composition, biofilm maturity, matrix characteristics, and treatment conditions. Overall, current evidence supports the development of targeted and combination-based strategies for mixed-species biofilms. Further studies using clinically relevant models are needed to exactly define treatment efficacy and support the translation of these approaches into clinical practice.

title: MIR2111a-mediated low-phosphate adaptation is linked to enhanced leaf phosphorus-use efficiency and growth maintenance in poplar.
authors: Wang, Jieyu; Chen, Ruibin; Jiang, Zhangqun; Yu, Shangyi; Huang, Zilong; Cheng, Jin; Wang, Yongjian; Zheng, Bo; Shi, Xueping
abstract: Inorganic phosphate (Pi) limitation constrains tree growth and necessitates coordinated physiological and developmental adjustments to maintain Pi homeostasis. However, the role of miRNA-mediated regulation in low-phosphate responses remains poorly understood in woody species. In this study, we investigated the role of MIR2111a in hybrid poplar (Populus tremula x P. alba; hereafter poplar 717). Overexpression (OE) and CRISPR/Cas9-generated mutant (CR) lines were generated to assess its function in low-phosphate adaptation. Among the MIR2111 family members, MIR2111a was more strongly induced under low-phosphate conditions, particularly in young leaves. Under phosphate limitation, the OE lines maintained higher biomass and showed increased root biomass allocation, whereas the CR lines exhibited enhanced root elongation but reduced overall biomass. Notably, the OE lines maintained lower leaf Pi content but significantly higher leaf phosphorus-use efficiency and ATP levels, indicating more efficient Pi utilization rather than increased Pi accumulation. In addition, under low-phosphate conditions, the OE lines exhibited reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) content and elevated superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity compared with poplar 717, suggesting decreased lipid peroxidation and enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity. Leaf transcriptome analysis further revealed that Pi-responsive genes involved in Pi signaling, transport, and energy metabolism were differentially regulated between OE and CR lines. Collectively, these results support an important role for MIR2111a in low-phosphate adaptation and biomass maintenance in poplar, providing new insights into miRNA-mediated phosphate responses in woody plants.

title: AND-gate CRISPR/Cas13a-assisted colorimetric assay for dual microRNA monitoring of cervical spondylosis prognosis and auricular point pressing therapy evaluation.
authors: Wang, Yizhuo; He, Wei; Yang, Xiaoyun; Zhang, Yang; Xu, Rong; Liu, Yinchun; Lin, Wenqian; Liu, Qingsong; Yang, Xiaoquan
journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
abstract: Simultaneous detection of dual microRNA biomarkers is crucial for accurate prognosis and treatment monitoring of cervical spondylosis, yet remains challenging due to the lack of stringent logic control and high-fidelity signal amplification. Herein, we report an AND-gate-controlled colorimetric assay that integrates target-recycling strand displacement amplification, CRISPR/Cas13a/crRNA-mediated trans-cleavage, and self-priming cyclic amplification for sensitive and specific analysis of two cervical spondylosis-associated miRNAs (miRNA-221 and miRNA-146a). Only when both targets are present does the cascade proceed, producing double-stranded amplicons that trigger SYBR Green I-catalyzed TMB oxidation, yielding a naked-eye-visible blue signal. The assay exhibits a broad linear range from 10 fM to 500 pM, a detection limit of 2.12 fM, excellent selectivity, and good repeatability. Importantly, we applied this method to clinically evaluate the therapeutic effect of auricular point pressing (ear acupressure), a traditional Chinese medicine intervention for cervical spondylosis. In a 4-week study of 20 patients, the treatment group receiving auricular point pressing showed significant downregulation of both miRNAs compared to baseline, while the control group showed no notable change. Results correlated well with RT-qPCR, confirming reliability. This logic-controlled CRISPR/Cas13a platform offers a robust, equipment-free strategy for early prognosis of cervical spondylosis and objective monitoring of auricular point pressing therapy.

title: Yeast-Based Platforms for Next-Generation Human Health Applications.
authors: Yook, Sangdo; Lee, Jae Won; Park, Myungseo; Koh, Hyun Gi; Shin, Jonghyeok
abstract: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

title: Paving the way for translational relevance in advanced therapies in Brazil: conference report from SBINT 2025.
