authors: da Silva, Artur Christian Garcia; Silva, Luis Antonio Dantas; Valadares, Marize Campos; Lima, Eliana Martins; Figueira, Ana Carolina Migliorini; de Freitas Souza, Bruno Solano; Guimaraes, Pedro Pires Goulart; Calvo, Thyago Leal; da Silva Junior, Joao Batista; Dos Santos Sena Brunel, Hilana; Silva, Hilda Petrs; Massaguer, Ana Luiza Garcia Millas; Stival, Ana Clara Silva; Meschiari, Cesar Arruda; de Sousa, Daniel Francisco; Ribeiro, Gabriel Brito; Do Nascimento, Gabriel Alves; Pires, Jader; Amorim, Julia Marinelli; Dias, Juliana Moraes; Neves, Lucianne Cardoso; da Silva, Ludimila Nascimento; de Paula, Luiza Gabriella Ferreira; de Lima E Silva, Maria Clara; Do Nascimento, Maria Eduarda Ribeiro; Mota, Pietra Soares; de Menezes, Rafaela Campos; Vasconcelos, Voltaire Vieira
abstract: The 2nd Symposium on Pharmaceutical Bioengineering and Nanobiotechnology Applied to Advanced Therapies (SBINT 2025) was held in Goiania, Brazil, under the theme "Challenges in preclinical evaluation: paving the way to translational relevance of advanced therapies." The meeting brought together approximately 150 participants from academia, industry, clinical institutions and regulatory agencies to discuss scientific, technological and regulatory barriers shaping advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs) in Brazil. Keynote lectures addressed human-relevant bioengineered platforms, organ-on-a-chip and microphysiological systems, regenerative biomaterials, extracellular vesicle-based therapies, nanobiotechnology-enabled nucleic acid delivery, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genome and epigenome editing, and the Brazilian regulatory framework for ATMPs. The discussions highlighted the need for predictive preclinical models capable of capturing human-specific mechanisms, as conventional animal models may have limited translational value for personalized cell, gene and tissue-engineered products. Regulatory and roundtable sessions emphasized risk-based assessment, Good Manufacturing Practice-compatible infrastructure, product characterization, traceability, and the development of national biotechnological raw materials, analytical services and vector production capacity. Overall, SBINT 2025 underscored Brazil's scientific maturity and structural bottlenecks in regenerative medicine, highlighting the importance of coordinated action among academia, industry, clinical centers, regulators and funding agencies to support ATMP translation in Latin America.

title: Biosynthetic Pathways and Regulation of Antibacterial Compounds From Endophytic Fungi: From Chemistry to Genomics and Biotechnology.
authors: Eshboev, Farkhod; Salihu, Abubakar Siddiq; Khayrullaeva, Lobar; Khamdamov, Doniyor; Gao, Alex X; Mardieva, Kamila; Salleh, Wan Mohd Nuzul Hakimi Wan; Azimova, Shakhnoz; Tsim, Karl W K
abstract: Endophytic fungi are non-pathogenic symbionts that represent a rich source of structurally diverse bioactive secondary metabolites. However, genome-mining studies reveal that most of their biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) remain transcriptionally silent under standard laboratory conditions, leaving much of their chemical diversity unexplored. This review examines antibacterial natural products from endophytic fungi by integrating three complementary aspects: metabolite chemistry, biosynthetic pathways, and strategies for activating cryptic BGCs. Endophytic fungi produce polyketides, non-ribosomal peptides, terpenoids, phenylpropanoid-derived compounds, and hybrid metabolites with antibacterial activities mediated through inhibition of ribosomes, cell wall and membrane biosynthesis, and bacterial resistance mechanisms. Their genomes encode diverse PKS, NRPS, TPS, and hybrid biosynthetic systems, many of which remain cryptic. Advances in chemical elicitation, co-cultivation, epigenetic modulation, CRISPR-based engineering, genome mining, and machine learning are accelerating the activation of silent clusters and the assignment of BGCs to their metabolites. Several fungal metabolites exhibit potent activity against multidrug-resistant pathogens, including MRSA, and some enhance the efficacy of existing antibiotics. This review highlights current progress, identifies remaining challenges in metabolite production and BGC annotation, and outlines future directions for translating endophytic fungi into a sustainable platform for next-generation antibacterial drug discovery.

title: The SlLRR-RLK94-SlPti1a Module Enhances Salt Tolerance by Modulating Reactive Oxygen Species and Hormone Homoeostasis in Tomato.
authors: Zhu, Jiaxuan; Yao, Yao; Li, Yan; Lv, Ruili; Yang, Ruirui; Luan, Yushi
abstract: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is a globally cultivated crop of high economic and nutritional importance, yet its growth and productivity are severely threatened by soil salinization. Although leucine-rich repeat receptor‑like kinases (LRR-RLKs) are key environmental sensors, the mechanisms governing tomato salt tolerance remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that the SlLRR‑RLK94 and its downstream interacting protein, the receptor‑like cytoplasmic kinase SlPti1a, form a functional plasma membrane complex that positively regulates salt tolerance in tomato. CRISPR/Cas9‑mediated knockout of SlLRR‑RLK94 or VIGS‑mediated silencing of SlPti1a markedly reduced salt tolerance, resulting in severe leaf chlorosis and restricted root growth under salinity. Disruption of this module severely compromised physiological defence systems, leading to excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation, altered antioxidant enzyme activities, and an elevated Na(+)/K(+) ratio caused by uncontrolled Na(+) buildup. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that loss of SlLRR‑RLK94 extensively reprogrammed metabolic networks under salt stress, impairing photosystem homoeostasis and suppressing the diterpenoid biosynthesis pathway. This transcriptional reprogramming led to an endogenous hormonal imbalance characterised by gibberellin deficiency and abscisic acid accumulation. Collectively, our findings elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which the SlLRR‑RLK94‑SlPti1a module coordinates ionic, oxidative, and hormonal homoeostasis, providing promising genetic targets for breeding salt‑tolerant tomato cultivars.

title: Sorghum grain biofortification by SbSTP20-mediated hexose influx and sub-aleurone thickening.
authors: Lu, Cheng; Wu, Xiaoyuan; Liu, Jinxin; Lou, Shumao; Pan, Long; Yao, Xuefeng; Hao, Dongyun; Xuan, Wei; Liu, Chun-Ming; Jing, Hai-Chun
abstract: Biofortification offers a sustainable solution to "hidden hunger, " yet the trade-off between grain yield and nutritional quality remains a persistent breeding bottleneck. Modern crop breeding emphasises the balance between high yield and nutritional values. Use of novel genes/alleles for grain quality lost during domestication and genetic improvement has been proven an efficient way to help achieve the dual goals. In sorghum, we report here the discovery of SbSTP20, encoding a sorghum monosaccharide transporter, as an essential component for biofortification by mediating the endosperm hexose influx and sub-aleurone (SA) thickness. SbSTP20 was ectopically expressed in sorghum developing grains and its expression levels were negatively associated with SA thickness. CRISPR edited Sbstp20 lines decreased the influx of hexoses, and exhibited thicker sub-aleurone layers and 6.6-7.5% higher grain protein and enriched micronutrients (Fe, Zn). SbSTP20thick natural variant increased sub-aleurone layer thickness and improved grain nutritional quality without altering grain size or thousand-grain weight. The SbSTP20thick allele was absent in 93% of modern improved lines, implying that the genomic region containing SbSTP20 showed a moderate selection signature. The metabolizable energy of SbSTP20thick containing sorghum lines was up to 6% higher than that of commercial corn standards in swine digestion and metabolism experiments. Reintroducing this haplotype via marker-assisted selection could provide a molecular strategy for nutritional enhancement.

title: Pyroptosis in cancer nanotherapy: Molecular mechanisms and advanced nanosystems (Review).
authors: Abdulaal, Wesam H; Aljarba, Nada H; Kim, Bonglee; Saadeldin, Islam M; Alenzi, Faris Q; Abdulkhaliq, Altaf A; Khan, Johra; Borai, Anwar; Tuomilehto, Jaakko; Lin, E; Ajoolabady, Amir; Al-Qahtani, Ahmed; Ren, Jun
abstract: Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death characterized by activation of inflammasome complexes and caspase signaling cascades, ultimately leading to the cleavage and activation of pore‑forming executioners such as gasdermin D (GSDMD), ‑E and ‑B. Accumulating evidence indicates that pyroptosis induction in cancer cells exerts potent antitumor effects. As a result, recent therapeutic strategies such as cancer nanotherapy have increasingly focused on harnessing pyroptotic cell death to improve cancer treatment outcomes. This review aimed to explore recent advances in nanotechnology‑based approaches designed to induce pyroptosis in cancer cells, with an emphasis on their potential to enhance antitumor immunity and overcome treatment resistance. It explored four distinct nanoplatforms: i) Chemo‑photodynamic systems that trigger GSDME‑mediated death by generating reactive oxygen species; ii) magneto‑plasmonic nanoparticles that use GSDME activation to modulate the tumor microenvironment, turning 'cold' tumors 'hot'; iii) bioorthogonal chemical delivery tools leveraging click chemistry for site‑specific gasdermin release; and iv) nano‑CRISPR activation scaffolds designed to boost GSDME expression and work alongside cisplatin. Beyond these platforms, the present review highlights how immune cell‑derived granzymes and interferon‑gamma drive vital downstream pyroptotic pathways via GSDME and GSDMB activation. Lastly, the review weighs clinical risks, such as chronic systemic inflammation and tumor‑promoting environments, providing a realistic perspective on how to safely progress these preclinical nanotherapies into selective, effective clinical immunotherapies.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-out of abnormal chemosensory jump 6 (acj6) gene impacts Helicoverpa armigera antennal lobe structure.
authors: Xie, Guiying; Chen, Shuting; Sun, Longlong; Chu, Xi; Lu, Jing; Khalid, Muhammad Lubaid; Lin, Rongmei; Chen, Wenbo; Zhao, Xincheng
abstract: The specificity of the olfactory system in the brain is determined not only by the expression of odorant receptor genes but also by the specific neural circuit assembly within the antennal lobe (AL). To investigate the developmental role of abnormal chemosensory jump 6 (acj6) in the moth Helicoverpa armigera, we generated Haacj6 mutants using CRISPR/Cas9 and examined the detailed structure of the AL based on immunostaining and three-dimensional reconstruction. The results showed that the AL in male Haacj6 mutants was markedly enlarged. In both sexes, the AL of Haacj6 mutants contained approximately 100 glomeruli, compared with about 75 glomeruli in wild-type. Glomerular volumes were also more heterogeneous in the mutants: the largest glomeruli were expanded, whereas the smallest were reduced, although the mean glomerular volume remained unchanged. These results demonstrate that the Haacj6 gene plays a critical role in normal AL development and that AL enlargement in the mutants arises primarily from the presence of additional glomeruli. These additional glomeruli likely reflect defects in olfactory receptor neuron axon wiring to AL projection neurons, or glial mediated glomerular boundary formation. These findings indicate that acj6 is an essential regulator of AL architecture and provide crucial insights into the molecular mechanisms governing neural circuits assembly in insects.

title: Genetic engineering of primary human mesenchymal stromal cells using the CRISPR/Cas9 synergistic activation mediator.
authors: Killer, M C; Zhang, X; Adhikary, T; Kasper, C; Neubauer, A; Frech, M; Brendel, C

title: Structure- and Exonuclease-Guided Engineering of Cas12o1 Enhances Genome Editing Efficiency and Deletion Outcomes.
authors: Wang, Linli; Wang, Yanlu; He, Xiaoya; Chen, Jian; Ai, Yue; Han, Hongbing
abstract: Small and efficient CRISPR nucleases hold great promise for genome engineering but often exhibit suboptimal activity and limited control over DNA repair outcomes. Here, we engineer Cas12o1 using a structure- and exonuclease-guided strategy to enhance both editing efficiency and deletion profiles in mammalian cells. Structure-guided arginine-scanning mutagenesis of 42 residues identifies a single substitution, D534R, that markedly improves editing efficiency across multiple genomic loci, outperforming combinatorial variants. In parallel, fusion of T5 exonuclease (T5 exo) profoundly remodels DNA repair outcomes, strongly enriching long-fragment deletions without compromising overall activity. Integrating the D534R mutation with T5 exo fusion increases Cas12o1 editing efficiency by 1.2-1.9-fold and yields a higher proportion of deletions exceeding 10 bp. Notably, at selected loci such as HBB, the enhanced Cas12o1-T5 exonuclease (enCas12o1-T5 exo) achieved comparable or higher editing efficiencies than canonical SpCas9 and LbCas12a. Together, these results establish a rational framework for simultaneously enhancing the efficiency and repair outcomes of compact CRISPR nucleases, expanding the genome-engineering potential of Cas12o1.

title: Design and artificial synthesis of gRNA library for genetic breeding of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
authors: Wang, Xinyi; Ma, Peiyan; Hanioui, Majda; Wang, Zhangnian; Yu, Qianqian; Waheed, Abdul; Liu, Kun; Liu, Yan; Xue, Zhenglian; Zhao, Ming
abstract: CRISPR mediated genome engineering strategies were developed and applied for genome-wide mutagenesis. However, high-throughput gRNA libraries require design and synthesis, which limits their economy and versatility. In this study, we designed in vitro transcription strategy for artificially synthesizing random gRNA libraries, which were transformed into cells to guide the diverse mutations generated through Cas protein induced double stranded DNA breaks. As a proof of concept, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain C0 with overexpression of tHMG1 and beta-carotene biosynthesis key genes was used as the original strain, and the beta-carotene synthesis ability of strain C0 was increased to that of 5.8 times after three rounds of iterative mutation. Furthermore, for the mutated S. cerevisiae strain C7-143 with high-level beta-carotene production, a mutant strain AgC8-174 with a 26% increase in beta-carotene yield was obtained through one round of mutation. This strategy completely avoided the limitations of plasmid library, significantly shortened the experimental cycle, and improved the versatility of gRNA library across different species. The results fully demonstrated the feasibility of the technology and lays a solid foundation for its application in the field of microbial genetics and breeding.

title: Breeding, genetics, and physiology of improving phosphorus use efficiency in food legumes.
authors: Lalchand; Venkataraja, Rajesh Ramasandra; Meghwal, Pramod Kumar; Sarkar, Ritabrata; Pal, Deblina; Lakshminarayanaraju, Bhavana Nagenahalli; Pandey, Avinash; Lal, Shambhu Krishan; Bhadana, Vijai Pal; Kumar, Jitendra; Gupta, Debjyoti Sen; Djalovic, Ivica; Kumar, Sudhir
abstract: Phosphorus (P) is a crucial plant macronutrient, but the non-renewable nature of P sources for plant growth in soils globally limits crop productivity, causing great concern for future sustainable agriculture and global food security. Thus, improving plant phosphorus use efficiency (PUE) by increasing P-utilization and P-acquisition efficiencies is immediately needed in various crops, including legumes, for intensive cropping systems. This review explores how to harness genetic variability in PUE traits across grain legume gene pools using various conventional breeding and emerging breeding approaches. The role of phytohormones in root architecture development, importance of root exudates secretion, and microbe-assisted breeding represent important strategies for improving PUE, considering the non-renewable nature of P resources and its essential role in plant growth. The genetic makeup of PUE is intricate, orchestrated by quantitative traits and significantly affected by environmental factors. Biparental quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping has been employed to decipher the genetic basis of PUE traits. Progress in legume genomics, particularly high-throughput single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotyping, has enabled genome-wide identification of regions associated with PUE. Concurrently, advancements in multi-omics approaches (functional genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics and proteomics) have facilitated the identification of key genes, transcription factors and pathways regulating PUE, P transport, recycling and low-P tolerance. This study also elucidated gene networks, signaling pathways, and molecular mechanisms governing P acquisition and utilization essential for improving PUE. We also evaluate the carbon and metabolic costs associated with P-acquisition traits and critically synthesize consistent findings, discrepancies and knowledge gaps across studies. Lastly, we summarize how to formulate innovative breeding strategies, including genomic selection, accelerated breeding, rhizosphere engineering and emerging clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9)-based genome editing technologies. This may aid in developing P-use-efficient cultivars and adapting grain legumes to low-P environments. Consequently, enhancing PUE by integrating various "omics" approaches could boost P-acquisition and P-utilization efficiencies in modern grain legume cultivars in intensive cropping systems, thereby mitigating P-fertilizer overuse and safeguarding the diminishing non-renewable global rock phosphate resources for ensuring a sustainable and economically viable agrarian future.

title: Nanoimaging, Spectroscopy, and Biosensor Assays for Alternatively Spliced RNA Isoforms in Disease Diagnostics.
authors: Kadam, Ulhas S; Zhou, Zhongwu; Irudayaraj, Joseph; Cho, Il-Hoon; Hong, Jong Chan
abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) generates distinct mRNA isoforms, and frequently distinct proteins, from single genes; its dysregulation is established in cancer, neurodegeneration, and immune disease. Sequencing now nominates candidate splice events at scale, but a nominated event does not become a usable measurement until an isoform-discriminating sequence has been converted into a physical signal. Existing AS reviews concentrate on sequencing workflows, computational event calling, or disease catalogs; the assay-engineering step that follows target nomination remains comparatively underserved, and it is where most translational failures occur. This review addresses that gap. We group postsequencing detection into five classes defined by the physical origin of the signal: (i) fixed-tissue in situ localization, (ii) live-cell RNA imaging, (iii) plasmonic and spectroscopic readouts, (iv) label-free nanophotonic biosensing combined with site-specific RNA processing, and (v) protein-level proteogenomic confirmation. These classes are compared on target definition, reported analytical performance, multiplexing, matrix compatibility, perturbation risk, and clinical readiness. The reported performance spans single-copy imaging of splice variants in living cells to label-free detection at 580 fM in under 30 min without cDNA synthesis or PCR. Three conclusions follow. First, assay selection should be governed by the class of claim being made rather than by platform novelty. Second, analytical sensitivity measured on synthetic targets systematically overstates readiness in clinical matrices; therefore, matrix-matched validation is not optional. Third, cross-laboratory comparison is currently obstructed by inconsistent reporting, which we address by proposing a minimum performance-reporting set and explicit platform-selection criteria. We close with emerging directions, including CRISPR-based isoform detection, biosensor integration with nanopore sequencing, AI-assisted probe design, and digital and microfluidic formats.

title: LNP-mediated CRISPR gene editing of human vascular endothelial cells in 2D and 3D microfluidic cell culture systems.
authors: Olsen, Amalie Lykke; Brandt, Camilla Blunk Vorso; Larsen, Rasmus Karred; Fonager, Sofie Vestergaard; Zubia-Aranburu, Judith; Hasko, Janos; Helmig, Rikke Bek; Degn, Soren Egedal; Dong, Mingdong; Jessen, Niels; Etzerodt, Anders; Rieben, Robert; Lin, Lin; Luo, Yonglun
abstract: Efficient and cell-type-specific delivery remains a major barrier to CRISPR-based genome editing in vascular endothelial cells. Here, we systematically evaluate lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mediated mRNA and CRISPR delivery in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). While a conventional SM-102-based LNP formulation enables highly efficient mRNA delivery to both HEK293T cells and HUVECs, CRISPR-SpCas9 gene editing is observed exclusively in HEK293T cells, revealing strong cell-dependent limitations. We identify reduced SpCas9 mRNA translation as a key bottleneck in endothelial cells and demonstrate that rational modification of LNP lipid composition dramatically enhances SpCas9 protein expression and restores robust genome editing in HUVECs. Using the optimized LNP formulation, we achieve efficient editing of VEGFA and HIF1A in both 2D cultures and physiologically relevant 3D microfluidic endothelial systems mimicking flow conditions in vivo. Together, our results establish lipid composition as a critical determinant of endothelial CRISPR editing efficiency and provide a scalable, non-viral strategy for genome engineering in the vascular endothelium.

title: Targeted insertion of partial CFTR cDNA replicates native CFTR expression with restored channel function in CF airway epithelium.
authors: Barilla, Cristina; Suzuki, Shingo; Park, So Hyun; Nalluri, Divyasri; Wen, Hui; Hanafy, Mohamed A; Betancourth, Daniel; Umrigar, Ayushi; Leir, Shih-Hsing; Lovrenert, Katreya; Sivachenko, Andrey; Tabak, Barbara; Liu, Zhong; Zhao, Rui; Valley, Hillary C; Rab, Andras; Sorscher, Eric J; Solomon, George M; Mense, Martin; Carulli, John P; Harris, Ann; Bao, Gang; Davis, Brian R
abstract: Our objective is to develop a universal gene editing therapeutic for individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). Due to the large number of CFTR variants, we sought to develop a correction methodology utilizing targeted integration of CFTR (2-27) sequence into CFTR intron 1 (TI-1). Following electroporation of CF primary airway basal stem cells with intron 1-targeted Cas9/gRNA, we delivered CFTR (2-27) donor, flanked by a splice acceptor and polyadenylation signal, via an integrase defective lentiviral vector. Molecular characterization revealed highly efficient integration of the CFTR (2-27) sequence into the native CFTR intron 1 with most insertion events reflecting the desired homology-directed repair. Fully differentiated airway epithelium, derived from TI-1 treated basal cells without enrichment for corrected cells, exhibited functional restoration of CFTR channel activity with significant improvement of mucus hydration and transport. ATAC-seq revealed that the native CFTR chromatin architecture was unaffected by the CFTR (2-27) sequence insertion, and importantly, scRNA-seq demonstrated that the cell-type-specific expression of the introduced transgene replicated that of the endogenous CFTR. In this report, we demonstrate an almost completely mutation-agnostic therapeutic approach that is capable of functional CFTR restoration. These results may also be relevant to CFTR (2-27) integration via other editing and delivery methodologies.

title: Oligonucleotide and RNA-targeted therapeutics for chronic hepatitis B: Antigen reduction, delivery, and functional cure strategies.
authors: Meng, Xingchen; Mahmood, Faisal; Li, Hui; Zhou, Taicheng
abstract: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains difficult to cure because nucleos(t)ide analogs suppress hepatitis B virus (HBV) replication but do not eliminate covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) or integrated HBV DNA, which sustain viral RNA and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) production. RNA-targeted therapeutics, including small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), and CRISPR-Cas13 platforms, offer sequence-directed approaches to suppress HBV transcripts and reduce antigen burden. Clinical evaluation of emerging HBV-directed therapies, including JNJ-3989, bepirovirsen, imdusiran, and related candidates, has demonstrated meaningful declines in circulating HBsAg levels. The recent phase III B-Well data further support the role of ASO-mediated antigen reduction as a potential therapeutic approach to increase the likelihood of functional cure within finite treatment regimens for selected patients. However, therapeutically induced HBsAg reduction alone rarely guarantees durable off-treatment control. This review summarizes HBV-directed RNA and oligonucleotide therapeutics from a translational pharmacology perspective, emphasizing transcript-silencing mechanisms, delivery constraints, pharmacodynamic endpoints, safety considerations, biomarker-guided patient selection, and integration with nucleos(t)ide analogs and immunomodulatory interventions. We propose that RNA-mediated antigen reduction may support finite therapy in biomarker-selected patients and may also serve as an antigen-conditioning component within staged functional cure strategies.

title: The minipig as a programmable translational platform for experimental oncofertility.
authors: Wedy, Rodrigo Albertho Almeida; Simoes, Lucas Dame; Pacheco, Bruna Silveira; de Leon, Priscila Marques Moura; Seixas, Fabiana Kommling; Leme, Ligiane; Brito, Luciano Abreu; Goulart, Ernesto; Dagli, Maria Lucia Zaidan; Collares, Tiago Veiras
abstract: Experimental oncofertility remains fragmented across models of cancer biology, treatment-associated gonadotoxicity, fertility preservation, and reproductive recovery. We propose extending the Oncopig concept into a translational platform that reconnects these states within one genetically defined, cancer-bearing host. The Oncopig provides the oncologic backbone, combining programmable cancer in an immunocompetent large-animal host with clinically scaled intervention and longitudinal sampling. High-resolution porcine genomics, CRISPR-based genome engineering, somatic-cell nuclear transfer for line generation, comparative experimental pathology, and mature reproductive biotechnology extend this architecture toward reproductive endpoints. Here, programmability refers to deliberate specification of the cancer state-genotype, cell lineage or induction strategy, and timing-whereas the reproductive phenotype is measured longitudinally rather than programmed. Distant-cancer modules can test whether cancer status modifies gonadotoxicity, while reproductive-organ modules require disease-specific alleles, appropriate cell-of-origin targeting, and pathology-led validation. Because porcine and human reproduction align in several endocrine and gonadal processes but differ in cycle organization, implantation, placentation, and pregnancy, translation should emphasize process-level endpoints rather than numerical equivalence. The platform is particularly suited to unresolved questions involving targeted therapies and immunotherapies, preservation timing, and pediatric or prepubertal patients. Porcine reproductive biotechnology provides functional endpoints from gonadal tissue and gametes to embryos and offspring. Rather than replacing rodent or human-based models, the Oncopig framework adds an integrated translational layer for questions requiring clinically scaled intervention, longitudinal physiology, and functional reproductive recovery.

title: Natural variation in the evolutionarily conserved F-box gene SDEF promotes seed dormancy in rice.
authors: Zhou, Yuliang; Wang, Yueping; Zhao, Guangmiao; Liu, Chunbao; Zeng, Ruizhen; Liang, Wenxuan; Han, Ru; Kong, Hui; Cao, Xiaofan; Li, Minshi; Chen, Huhui; Tan, Bin; Liu, Hong; Xu, Zhenjiang
journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology
abstract: Insufficient seed dormancy causes pre-harvest sprouting (PHS) and severe yield losses in rice; however, genetic resources with practical breeding value remain limited. Here, we isolated a major dormancy gene, SDEF, via map-based cloning using chromosomal single segment substitution lines (SSSLs), identifying a functional SNP (Arg-to-Trp) as the causal mutation. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of SDEF led to PHS susceptibility, while overexpression significantly enhanced dormancy. Importantly, SDEF enhanced seed dormancy without compromising grain yield in SSSLs, confirming it as a promising breeding target. Moreover, SDEF encodes an angiosperm-conserved, nuclear-localized F-box protein and is preferentially expressed in the embryo, with expression increasing during seed maturation and declining upon germination. Mechanistically, protein interaction assays confirmed that SDEF recruits OSK1, with the Trp-type SDEF(K) exhibiting a more stable interaction than the Arg-type SDEF(H). SDEF is induced by abscisic acid (ABA) and appears to promote seed dormancy through the ABA pathway by activating ABA signaling genes and repressing alpha-amylase genes, as evidenced by the reduced ABA sensitivity of sdef mutants. Additionally, haplotype analysis revealed that natural variation in SDEF is associated with divergent dormancy levels, and reduced nucleotide diversity in cultivated rice indicates that SDEF was selected during domestication. Collectively, our results provide insights into the molecular basis of SDEF-mediated dormancy, providing an ideal target for breeding PHS-resistant rice.

title: Two novel phosphodiesterases (PDEs) found from woody plant jujube exhibit diverse biological functions via regulating cAMP, cGMP and hormones.
authors: Zhao, Xin; Wang, Di; Deng, Xiaofeng; Mai, Junyan; Liu, Zhiguo; Liu, Mengjun
abstract: Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) are the key enzymes hydrolyzing cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) and cGMP (cyclic guanosine monophosphate), two important second messengers triggering many physiological responses, and regulating growth, development and defense in plants. As the identification of PDEs from plants is really puzzling, only very few herbaceous plant PDEs have been functionally verified, and the biological functions of plant PDEs are still unclear. Here, we identified two novel PDE genes (ZjPDE1 and ZjPDE2) of cAMP/cGMP dual-specificity from a woody plant jujube (Ziziphus jujuba Mill.) known for its fruit rich in cAMP and cGMP. The two PDE genes have very poor sequence similarity but quite similar secondary structure, motif, and binding mode to cAMP/cGMP. Their phosphodiesterase activities were verified via in vitro catalytic assays, in vivo transient overexpression, and stable genetic transformation. After knocking out the homologous sequences of ZjPDE1 and ZjPDE2 in model plant tomato via CRISPR/Cas9, the mutants, compared to WT, showed increased cAMP/cGMP accumulation, accelerated seed germination, promoted flowering, as well as advanced fruiting and coloration, which were largely consist with the effects of spraying cAMP/cGMP. These biological functions are the combined effects of cAMP and cGMP cross talking with phytohorones including GA and ABA. These results demonstrate that ZjPDE1 and ZjPDE2 are functional PDEs capable of hydrolyzing cAMP and cGMP, and PDE-mediated cAMP/cGMP signaling may crosstalk with phytohormone pathways such as IAA, GA and ABA, to regulate plant growth, flowering and fruiting.

title: CRAT-mediated acetylcarnitine shuttling sustains p65 acetylation and NF-kappaB-associated radioresistance in colorectal cancer.
authors: Liu, Yixuan; Xiao, Yu; Chen, Yiran; Huang, Chaoxiong; Lin, Feifei; Zhuang, Qingyang; Li, Hui; Lin, Peicheng; Tang, Lirui; Li, Jinluan
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy is a standard treatment for locally advanced rectal cancer, yet acquired resistance limits durable tumor control. Whether stress-adaptive acetyl-group metabolism contributes to this resistance remains unclear. METHODS: We performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screen under fractionated irradiation and integrated the results with transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of radioresistant colorectal cancer models established by stepwise irradiation. CRAT function was interrogated using genetic perturbation, catalytic-dead reconstitution, acetylation-mimetic p65 rescue, RELA depletion, stable-isotope tracing, free coenzyme A quantification, NF-kappaB reporter assays, chromatin immunoprecipitation-qPCR, and xenograft and syngeneic tumor models. RESULTS: CRAT was prioritized through cross-platform convergence of the CRISPR screen with transcriptomic and proteomic signatures of radioresistant cells, and post-treatment tumors with poorer pathological regression showed higher CRAT and nuclear p65 immunohistochemical scores. CRAT manipulation had limited, model-dependent effects on basal proliferation but more pronounced effects after irradiation, where CRAT loss reduced clonogenic survival and was associated with increased oxidative stress and persistent DNA damage. Stable-isotope tracing showed that irradiation increased acetate-to-acetylcarnitine flux and expanded the free coenzyme A pool in control cells, whereas CRAT loss disrupted this acetyl-group buffering. Mechanistically, CRAT catalytic activity helped maintain irradiation-induced p65 Lys310 acetylation, H3K27ac enrichment at NF-kappaB-responsive loci, and NF-kappaB-associated transcriptional output through a p300/CBP-sensitive acetylation axis. p65-K310Q rescue and RELA depletion supported p65 acetylation and RELA-dependent transcription as downstream contributors to, rather than sole mediators of, CRAT-dependent radioprotection. In syngeneic MC38 tumors, Crat deletion enhanced the response to fractionated radiotherapy. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support CRAT-dependent acetyl-group metabolism as a contributor to an NF-kappaB-associated radioprotective program and nominate this metabolic dependency as a candidate vulnerability for radiosensitization in colorectal cancer.

title: Alternative polyadenylation in cancer: mechanisms, functions, and therapeutic potential.
authors: Huang, Yu; Li, Zhihong; Yu, Fenglei; Wang, Lujuan
abstract: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) is a pervasive post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism that generates transcript isoforms with distinct 3' untranslated regions, terminal exons, or coding potential, thereby influencing mRNA stability, translation, localization, and protein output. Rather than representing a uniform 3'UTR-shortening process, APA comprises heterogeneous 3'-end regulatory events, including tandem 3'UTR APA and upstream APA events such as intronic polyadenylation (IPA), which differ in mechanisms, detection strategies, functional consequences, and clinical interpretation. Dysregulated APA is increasingly recognized as an important contributor to cancer initiation and progression. Tandem 3'UTR APA can remove miRNA- or RNA-binding protein-mediated repression and enhance oncogenic transcript output, whereas upstream APA events, including IPA, can generate prematurely terminated RNAs, truncated proteins, soluble isoforms, or neoantigenic products. In this review, we summarize the classification and biological consequences of major APA events, as well as experimental and computational approaches for APA analysis. We then discuss regulatory mechanisms involving core 3'-end processing factors, RNA-binding proteins, splicing-polyadenylation coupling in upstream APA/IPA, transcription-associated regulation, and promoter-terminator communication. Functionally, aberrant APA contributes to proliferation, invasion and metastasis, metabolic reprogramming, tumor microenvironment remodeling, antitumor immunity, and immune escape. Finally, we highlight APA events, APA regulators, 3'UTR-based signatures, and upstream APA/IPA-derived products as emerging biomarkers and discuss small-molecule, RNA-based, and CRISPR-based strategies for targeting APA or 3'-end processing in cancer.

title: Rapid visual detection technologies for Botrytis cinerea resistance to QoI and SDHI fungicides based on RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a.
authors: Yuan, Yafeng; Liu, Mei; Wang, Baoyu; Wang, Xuncheng; Xing, Qikai; Liang, Wenwen; Wang, Gan; Zhang, Wei; Yan, Jiye
abstract: Grape gray mold caused by Botrytis cinerea is one of the most important fungal diseases affecting grape production and postharvest quality. The extensive use of fungicides has led to the emergence of resistance in B. cinerea, particularly to quinone outside inhibitors (QoIs) and succinate dehydrogenase inhibitors (SDHI), which compromises the efficacy of disease control. Therefore, detection techniques for fungicide resistance in B. cinerea are needed to provide scientific guidance for disease management. Based on recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)-CRISPR/Cas12a technology, this study designed specific RPA primer pairs and crRNA targeting resistance-related mutation sites in fungicide target genes cytb and SdhB, incorporated single-stranded fluorescent reporter molecules, and optimized key reaction components. This study achieved rapid fluorescence-based resistance detection within 1 h, with detection sensitivities of 450 and 430 pg/microL for the two fungicide genes.

title: Research progress of gene correction for genetic diseases via in vivo prime editing.
authors: Shuran, Zhang; Yuzhen, Hu; Zili, Zhang; Wenming, Huang; Baosheng, Zhu; Ying, Chan
abstract: Curative therapies for genetic diseases caused by pathogenic mutations demand precise and safe genome editing technologies. Prime editing (PE), a CRISPR-Cas9-derived technology that enables precise base conversions without double-strand breaks (DSBs), has emerged as a transformative tool with the ability to correct 89% of human pathogenic mutations. However, transitioning PE from preclinical models to clinical applications faces critical challenges, particularly in the development of in vivo delivery systems and scalable manufacturing. This review systematically summarizes advances of in vivo PE therapeutics, focusing on the therapeutic outcomes across some retinal, metabolic, and hematologic genetic diseases. We further dissect barriers to clinical translation, including in the immunogenicity of viral vectors, off-target risks in nondividing cells, and large-scale production bottlenecks. By highlighting the unique advantages of in vivo PE and proposing actionable solutions for scalable manufacturing, the work provides a roadmap for accelerating in vivo PE-based therapies toward clinical reality.

title: TRAP complex is essential for coronavirus replication and glycoprotein biogeneses.
authors: Tian, Yihan; Shi, Junchao; Mu, Shaoqian; Wei, Hanlu; He, Wenqi; Li, Zi
abstract: Coronaviruses remodel the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to build replication organelles while producing heavily glycosylated membrane proteins, but the mechanisms coordinating these demands are unclear. Here, we describe the ER-resident translocon-associated protein (TRAP/SSR) complex as a conserved host dependency across diverse coronaviruses. Using porcine hemagglutinating encephalomyelitis virus (PHEV) as a model, we identify TRAPgamma in a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen as essential for productive viral infection. TRAPgamma depletion suppresses viral replication, disrupts canonical replication organelle formation, and amplifies innate immune signaling. Viral glycoproteins (nsp4, Spike, and hemagglutinin-esterase) selectively engage specific TRAP subunits (alpha, beta, gamma, and delta), and reducing their signal-sequence hydrophobicity compromises glycoprotein production and N-glycosylation, consistent with impaired co-translational ER targeting or translocation. Inhibition of the oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex recapitulates these defects, supporting a sequential signal recognition particle (SRP)-TRAP-OST axis. Thus, our findings reveal an essential role for the TRAP complex in viral subversion of ER proteostasis, highlighting ER co‑translational translocation machinery as a pivotal host-pathogen interface during the viral lifecycle.

title: DCST1 drives cisplatin resistance via non-canonical ubiquitination and stabilization of NFAT5 to suppress PANoptosis in bladder cancer.
authors: Cao, Chun; Lai, Yiqi; Ye, Wanteng; Wang, Zihuan; Chen, Yuwen; Fan, Qin; Deng, Fan; Hou, Lina; Wang, Zhizhang; Tan, Wanlong; Li, Fei
abstract: Cisplatin-based chemotherapy constitutes the cornerstone of first-line treatment for muscle-invasive and metastatic bladder cancer (BCa); however, the frequent emergence of chemoresistance presents a formidable clinical obstacle. In the present study, by combining a systematic CRISPR-Cas9 E3 ligase library screen with drug sensitivity data from the GDSC database, DCST1 (DC-STAMP Domain Containing 1) was identified as a pivotal driver of cisplatin resistance. DCST1 expression was found to be markedly upregulated in chemoresistant BCa tissues, and its elevated expression served as an independent predictor of poor patient prognosis. Functionally, DCST1 deficiency sensitizes BCa cells to cisplatin in vitro and in vivo by triggering PANoptosis (simultaneous apoptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis). Mechanistically, DCST1 functions as an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase to catalyze the K11/K27-linked polyubiquitination of NFAT5 at residue K450. This non-canonical ubiquitination stabilizes NFAT5 by preventing its lysosomal degradation and promotes its nuclear accumulation. Nuclear NFAT5 then transcriptionally activates SOD2, orchestrating an anti-PANoptotic program that ensures BCa cell survival under chemotherapeutic stress. Furthermore, through molecular docking and CETSA validation, digoxin was identified as a potent pharmacological inhibitor of NFAT5 that overcomes DCST1-mediated chemoresistance and synergistically restores cisplatin sensitivity. Collectively, these findings unveil a previously unrecognized ubiquitination-dependent mechanism of chemoresistance and establish the DCST1-NFAT5 signaling axis as a promising therapeutic target for overcoming drug resistance in BCa.

title: Planetary-scale metagenomic analysis reveals CRISPR targeting dynamics across ecosystems.
authors: Roux, Simon; Neri, Uri; Bushnell, Brian; Fremin, Brayon J; George, Nikhil A; Gophna, Uri; Hug, Laura A; Camargo, Antonio Pedro; Wu, Dongying; Ivanova, Natalia; Kyrpides, Nikos C; Eloe-Fadrosh, Emiley A
abstract: Interactions between microorganisms and their mobile genetic elements (MGEs), including viruses and plasmids, impact microbiome dynamics. CRISPR-Cas systems are important regulators of these host-MGE interactions, but a global understanding of the diversity, activity and roles of CRISPR spacers across Earth's biomes is still lacking. Here we develop a computational approach to search short-read data and collect 794 million CRISPR spacers across 367,609 public metagenomes, from which we identified 1.18 billion hits between 41 million spacers and 2.5 million viruses and plasmids. While spacers were highly variable across samples, those matching known viruses were more prevalent and conserved, consistent with a positive selection pressure associated with phage targeting. Among these, however, we find evidence suggestive of recurrent entry of phage genomes into non-host microbial cells, further blurring the line between CRISPR targeting and virus-host interactions. These results highlight key drivers of CRISPR targeting patterns likely to influence strain-level diversification and selection processes in microbiomes.

title: T cell engineering by targeted small extracellular vesicles delivering CRISPR/Cas9 system for PD-1 knock-out.
authors: Farahani, Mahboube Shahrabi; Shamsara, Mehdi; Moazzeni, Seyed Mohammad; Khalili, Saeed; Johnson, Ben; Darzi, Leila; Shoae, Mohammad; Ghavami, Mahlegha; Razi, Abdolah; Hosseini-Beheshti, Elham; Moghadam, Mehdi Forouzandeh
abstract: Among the emerging cancer therapies, immunotherapy using T cell engineering stands out as one of the most promising approaches. While the clustered regularly interspaced palindromic repeats (CRISPR/Cas) system is widely recognized as one of the most common gene-editing system tools, the main challenge for in vivo delivery applications remains the lack of an efficient and safe intracellular carrier. Small extracellular vesicles (s-EVs), as natural nanoparticles with low immunogenicity, emerge as a promising candidate for delivering the CRISPR/Cas system. Two guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting the programmed cell death (PD-1) gene were cloned into the PX-459 vector, and these CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids were loaded into targeted s-EVs by electroporation. Subsequently, T cells were exposed to these s-EVs, and the disruption to the PD-1 gene was examined using flow cytometry and sequencing. Flow cytometry results indicated that newly produced targeted s-EVs exhibited a higher uptake by T cells compared to non-targeted s-EVs. The successful loading of PX-459 plasmids into targeted s-EVs and their functional delivery to T cells were confirmed. Subsequent carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE) staining and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) analyses demonstrated that the knockout (KO) of the PD-1 gene in T cells significantly enhanced both their cytotoxicity and cytokine release compared to untreated T cells. Targeted s-EVs were used in the current study as a means to deliver the CRISPR/Cas9 system into T cells, enabling genetic modification of target cells. This approach holds the potential to improve and simplify immunotherapy. This study demonstrates a novel approach to genetic modification in T cells using targeted s-EVs containing the CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing system. KEY POINTS: *CRISPR/Cas9 is a kind of powerful gene editing system in cancer therapeutics. *s-EVs can be applied as a biological carrier for CRISPR/Cas9 system. * T cell engineering-based immunotherapy is a promising form of anticancer therapy.

title: Repurposing Cas12a2-mediated abortive infection for efficient and low-toxicity microbial genome editing.
authors: Wang, Hao-Da; Hu, Lan; Han, Jing; Cheng, Zhou-Hua; Yu, Han-Qing; Liu, Dong-Feng
abstract: CRISPR-Cas systems have revolutionized microbial genome engineering, yet counter-selection strategies typically rely on targeted DNA cleavage, where the severe cytotoxicity of double-strand breaks restricts transformation efficiency and clonal recovery. Here, we present an innovative strategy, SuCas12a2-Universal Recombination Editing (SURE), that circumvents these limitations by repurposing the RNA-targeting CRISPR-Cas12a2 system. Instead of directly attacking the genome, SURE utilizes Cas12a2's RNA-triggered collateral activity to induce an abortive infection-like state, providing a potent yet recoverable selective pressure. This strategy increases transformation efficiency by up to 1,000-fold compared to Cas9- or Cas12-based systems while achieving over 90% editing efficiency for gene knockout, insertion, and replacement in Escherichia coli MG1655. We validate the SURE platform's broad utility by extending it to diverse species, including Bacillus subtilis BSZR and Shewanella oneidensis MR-1. Mechanistically, we identify collateral double-stranded DNA degradation as the decisive factor for driving efficient selection. Finally, we apply this system to engineer E. coli MG1655 for efficient assimilation of the plastic monomer ethylene glycol, demonstrating its practical utility. Collectively, this work establishes a universal and robust RNA-guided editing framework that resolves the toxicity-efficiency trade-off inherent to the conventional DNA-targeting methods.

title: Metabolization of human milk oligosaccharides by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
authors: Bacher, Katharina; Martysiuk, Ustina; Bonifacio-Pereira, Greicy K; Mignolet, Johann; de Bakker, Vincent; Ghazaghi, Melika; Troxler, Lukas; Bommer, Tabea N; Gjuroski, Ilche; Furrer, Julien; Muller, Loretta; Burgaya, Judit; Mostacci, Nadja; Neill, Daniel R; Veening, Jan-Willem; Hilty, Markus
abstract: It is unclear whether human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) can be used as a nutrient source by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Here, we investigate whether and how S. pneumoniae metabolizes HMOs and whether these compounds inhibit pneumococcal adherence. We find that S. pneumoniae can metabolize several HMOs, except for 2'-fucosyllactose (2'FL). The process is regulated by the carbon catabolite repression system. Transcriptome analyses showed reduced expression of the lac operon I (lacABCD) in bacteria grown with two tested HMOs when compared to lactose (Lac). Genes for the Leloir pathway and exoglycosidases were upregulated. A genome-wide CRISPR interference screen showed that the lac operons I and II (lacEFG-2) are essential for metabolizing HMOs. Lac and non-metabolizable 2'FL were found to inhibit pneumococcal adherence to host cells in vitro. Importantly, 2'FL showed a stronger inhibitory effect compared to Lac in vivo. Further research is warranted to investigate whether the non-metabolizable 2'FL can be used to inhibit pneumococcal adherence.

title: Decoding proteomic complexity of transcript variants and homologous isoforms for precision therapeutics.
authors: Kum, Seo A; Ha, Hong Koo; Bae, Sun Sik
journal: The Korean journal of physiology & pharmacology : official journal of the Korean Physiological Society and the Korean Society of Pharmacology
abstract: The traditional "one gene, one protein" paradigm is insufficient to capture the vast phenotypic and physiological complexity of eukaryotes. This review aims to comprehensively elucidate the molecular mechanisms of transcriptomic diversification, namely, alternative splicing, alternative usage of promoter, and alternative polyadenylation, and their profound impacts on cellular homeostasis and human disease. By synthesizing recent breakthroughs in targeted long-read RNA sequencing, single-cell isoform-specific multiomics, and AI-driven 3D structural modeling, we systematically examine how transcript variants are generated and functionally annotated. Our analysis highlights that multiple transcript variants originating from a single genetic locus are not merely redundant copies; rather, subtle sequence alterations dynamically rewire protein-protein interaction networks and dictate precise subcellular localization. The exquisite spatiotemporal regulation of these variants controls critical cell fate decisions and organ development. Consequently, the pathological dysregulation of these processes, frequently termed spliceopathies, acts as a primary driver in severe pathologies, including cancer multidrug resistance, metabolic reprogramming, and neurodegenerative disorders. In conclusion, understanding the eukaryotic proteome requires a fundamental shift from conventional gene-level to isoform-level perspectives. Decoding the complex regulatory syntax of transcript variants paves the way for next-generation precision medicine, highlighting the therapeutic potential of RNA-targeted interventions, such as antisense oligonucleotides and CRISPR-based RNA editing, to correct pathogenic isoforms.

title: Muco-obstructive lung disease exhibits distinct hypoxic and inflammatory airway epithelial gene pathways.
authors: Mikami, Yu; Burns, Ella; Dang, Hong; van Heusden, Catharina; Caldwell, Ray A; Reidel, Boris; Furusho, Minako; Murano, Hiroaki; Asakura, Takanori; Gentzsch, Martina; Kesimer, Mehmet; Okuda, Kenichi; Ribeiro, Carla M P; Randell, Scott H; O'Neal, Wanda K; Boucher, Richard C
abstract: BACKGROUND: Intraluminal obstruction produces chronic airway epithelial hypoxia. We investigated how chronic airway epithelial hypoxia and inflammatory stimuli interact in human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cultures and resected human bronchiectatic lungs to produce an airway epithelial environment characteristic of muco-obstructive disease. MATERIALS AND METHODS: HBE cultures were exposed to normoxia or hypoxia (1% O(2)) for 5 days, followed by administration of supernatants from cystic fibrosis (CF) lung-derived mucopurulent material (SMM) or PBS for 24 h. A reverse order protocol with SMM followed by hypoxia was also performed. Bulk RNA-sequencing and functional (Na(+) transport) studies were performed. HIF1A and EPAS1-mediated transcriptional responses were characterised in CRISPR knockdown HBE cells. RNA in situ hybridisation studies of excised bronchiectatic lungs and bioinformatic analyses of published datasets tested for relevance of in vitro findings to in vivo conditions. RESULTS: Hypoxia and SMM regulated largely separate airway epithelial transcriptional programmes regardless of treatment order. PTGS2 (COX-2), CCL20, MUC5B, and CXCL8 (IL-8) represented a small number of genes upregulated by both hypoxia and SMM. HIF1A knockdown and EPAS1 knockdown produced distinct, often opposing, effects on hypoxia-responsive pathways. HIF1A dominated upregulation of glycolytic pathway signalling. EPAS1 regulated genes that increase mucus concentration under hypoxia (e.g., SCNN1G). An EPAS1 inhibitor blocked hypoxia-induced upregulation of Na(+) transport. CONCLUSION: Chronic hypoxia and inflammation regulated distinct genes/pathways that combine to produce a complex diseased environment in muco-obstructed airway epithelia. HIF1A and EPAS1 regulated distinct hypoxia-induced transcriptional responses. EPAS1 inhibition may exhibit a favourable therapeutic ratio for treatment of muco-obstructive lung diseases.

title: Seed Morphogenesis: Genetic Architecture, Regulatory Mechanisms, and Breeding Opportunities.
authors: Waqas, Muhammad; Nadeem, Muhammad; Shahid, Muhammad Qasim; Daowu, Hu; Shopu, He; Xiongming, Du
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
abstract: Seed morphogenesis determines seed size, shape, tissue organization, and developmental patterning, which influence crop yield and quality. This review compiles the genetic architecture, regulatory mechanisms, and breeding strategies for seed morphogenesis in major crops. Functionally validated genes and QTLs are cataloged with clear inclusion criteria to distinguish direct evidence for the causal gene from candidate genes identified by GWAS and linkage mapping. Developmental and environmental signals converge through hormonal crosstalk and epigenetic control, including Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) mediated histone modifications, DNA methylation, chromatin remodeling, and non-coding RNAs to shape seed morphogenesis. Six central regulatory modules govern seed morphogenesis: endosperm proliferation and cellularization, seed coat development, embryo patterning, hormonal integration, cell cycle and expansion control, and ncRNAs. Conserved and species-specific pathways are compared across Arabidopsis, cereals, and legumes, demonstrating that embryo patterning (LAFL, WOX, HD-ZIP III) is highly conserved, while endosperm development (MINI3/IKU2, AGL62) and seed coat development (SHP1/SHP2, STK, MYB5) are divergent, highlighting the need for species-specific frameworks. Modern technological advances such as high-throughput phenotyping, multi-omics, and CRISPR/Cas9 enable module-level functional validation. Breeding programs can deploy validated module genes through MAS, GS, and genome editing. Despite these advances, phenotyping, G x E interactions, pleiotropy, and the functional validation gap in underutilized crops remain unresolved. These gaps can be overcome by shifting from single-gene level manipulation to network-level engineering, integrating multi-omics and systems biology to translate module-level discoveries into improved seed morphogenesis.

title: Next-generation analytical platforms for neurochemical sensing: from conventional biosensors to intelligent brain interfaces.
authors: Ardah, Mustafa T; Kubaev, Aziz; Patel, Jalpa R; Saxena, Rahul; Mutee, Ahmed Faisal; Al-Hussein, Maryam Abdul; Sharma, Chandan; Shayesteh, Omid Heydari
abstract: Neurochemical sensing is central to understanding brain function, neurological disorders, and precision neurotherapeutics. Despite advances in electrochemical, optical, implantable, wearable, and genetically encoded technologies, current platforms remain limited by molecular selectivity, long-term stability, biofouling, complex data interpretation, and clinical translation. This review critically examines 83 representative studies encompassing nanomaterial-enabled electrochemical sensors, implantable and wearable devices, genetically encoded and CRISPR-engineered systems, AI-assisted analytical frameworks, and multimodal bioelectronic interfaces. Among the reviewed platforms, 68.7% were based on electrochemical or electrical sensing, whereas only 9.6% incorporated explicit AI/ML-assisted data analysis, indicating that intelligent analytical functionalities remain relatively limited. AI-assisted platforms have shown promising capabilities for signal discrimination, quantitative analysis, and enhanced analytical performance across diverse neurochemical sensing modalities, but their reported performance remains highly dependent on the sensing architecture, experimental conditions, and level of validation. Rather than providing a conventional technology-centered survey, this review establishes a unified framework for evaluating neurochemical sensing across five dimensions: molecular selectivity, spatiotemporal resolution, operational stability, intelligent data interpretation, and translational readiness. The reviewed evidence indicates a transition from conventional single-modality sensing toward integrated platforms incorporating multimodal detection and intelligent data interpretation, with adaptive and closed-loop interfacing emerging as future directions. By connecting advances in molecular recognition, functional materials, bioelectronics, and AI, this review identifies key design principles, persistent bottlenecks, and realistic priorities for translating next-generation neurochemical sensing platforms into reliable and clinically relevant intelligent interfaces.

title: A homolog of Growth Regulating Factor Targets Protein Synthesis Genes to Regulate Seed Protein Accumulation in Soybean.
authors: Li, Qingyao; Zhang, Xiaomei; Fang, Chao; Zhang, Wei; Liu, Yucheng; Qi, Zhaoming; Peng, Jun; Xu, Jiangyuan; Liu, Min; Wang, Jianhui; Wu, Liang; Yu, Guolong; Xu, Kun; Du, Juan; Miao, Yuchen; Kong, Fanjiang; Chen, Qingshan; Qiu, Lijuan; Feng, Xianzhong; Dong, Zhicheng; Tian, Zhixi; Xiao, Chaowen; Fu, Yong-Fu
abstract: Growth Regulating Factor (GRF) genes encode a family of highly conserved plant transcription factors that control diverse developmental processes. However, no GRF5 orthologs have been directly linked to seed protein accumulation. Here we demonstrate that GmGRF5a, a soybean homolog of GRF5, functions as a key positive regulator of seed protein accumulation. GmGRF5a is preferentially expressed in reproductive tissues, with transcript levels gradually increasing throughout seed development. Overexpression of GmGRF5a driven by its native promoter or the CAB3 promoter increased seed protein content by approximately one percentage point-comparable to the effect of known protein QTLs in soybean-without yield penalty across three independent field seasons, whereas CRISPR/Cas9-generated mutants showed reduced protein and oil contents. Integrative analysis of genome-wide DAP-seq and transcriptome profiling identified hundreds of direct GmGRF5a target genes significantly enriched in pathways related to protein synthesis, ribosomal biogenesis, and energy metabolism. Multiple independent molecular assays, including ChIP-qPCR, EMSA, and dual-luciferase reporter assays, confirmed that GmGRF5a directly activates genes encoding seed storage proteins (e.g., GmCupin1-1) and translational components (e.g., GmRPS4 and GmGOGAT2). Furthermore, natural variation at amino acid position 124 near the WRC DNA-binding domain is associated with seed protein content and exhibits a latitude-dependent distribution pattern consistent with regional breeding priorities. Our findings demonstrate that GmGRF5a coordinates a transcriptional network governing seed protein synthesis and highlight its potential as a promising target for breeding high-protein soybean cultivars without compromising agronomic performance.

title: Protocol for precise large-region haplotype modification for isogenic human iPSC generation using CRISPR-Cas9.
authors: Mishra, Manoj K; Pandey, Rajan; Therani, Bhavika; Geurts, Aron M; Liang, Mingyu; Liu, Yong
abstract: Large genomic region modification, such as precise haplotype reconstitution, remains challenging due to the low efficiency of homology-directed repair (HDR) and difficulties in generating HDR templates. Here, we present a two-stage protocol for genome engineering in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) using CRISPR-Cas9 to generate homozygous, multi-kilobase isogenic haplotypes. We describe steps for in silico experimental design, large haplotype deletion and reconstruction, followed by edited cell line validation. This optimized protocol improves both editing efficiency and screening throughput while reducing turnaround time. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Xue et al.(1).

title: RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction in Therapeutics and Drug Discovery.
authors: Venkat, Karunya Ramaraju; Kanchanapalli, Leelankitha; Varadarajan, Swetha
abstract: RNA-based therapeutics have emerged as a transformative modality in modern medicine, enabling precise modulation of gene expression and offering new treatment strategies for previously intractable diseases. Central to the success and safety of many RNA therapeutics is a detailed understanding of RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs), including both intended target binding and unintended off-target effects. Computational prediction of RRIs plays a critical role in the design, optimization, and validation of therapeutic RNAs such as antisense oligonucleotides, small interfering RNAs, messenger RNAs, and CRISPR-associated RNAs. This chapter examines the role of RRI prediction in therapeutic and drug discovery pipelines, highlighting computational strategies, deep learning models, and validation frameworks. Examples of applications in oncology, infectious diseases, and genetic disorders illustrate how accurate RRI modeling supports efficacy, safety assessment and contribute to evidence generation for therapeutic development. Challenges and future directions for clinically deployable RRI prediction systems are also discussed.

title: Comparative analysis of single and dual sgRNA CRISPR/Cas9 ribonucleoprotein strategies for efficient Park7 gene editing in primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
authors: Suryadevara, Lekhana; Srinivas, Vilasagaram; Barathidasan, Rajamani; Mhaske, Suhas Tukaram; Naik, Ramavat Ravindar; Gupta, Mukesh Kumar; Pramod, Ravindran Kumar
abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurological condition that predominantly affects dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. Mutations or deletions in the Park7 gene may cause a rare autosomal recessive form of early-onset PD. Generating reliable cellular models with specific Park7 disruption is crucial for elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying PD pathogenesis. METHODS AND RESULTS: This study developed a plasmid-free CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing method for targeting the Park7 gene in primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) using single- and dual-sgRNA-mediated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) system. Gene modification through the single sgRNA strategy was confirmed by the detection of indels by T7 endonuclease assay, whereas gene editing by the dual sgRNA strategy was validated through detection of large deletions by junctional PCR and Sanger sequencing. Deep amplicon sequencing showed an overall editing frequency of 50.68% and 24.87% for single-sgRNA and dual-sgRNA editing strategies, respectively. While single-sgRNA editing predominantly generated small insertions and deletions, large deletions constituted the predominant editing outcome in the dual-sgRNA group, accounting for 22.23% of the total reads. Further, Western blot analysis demonstrated a 12.03 +/- 7.6% reduction in PARK7 protein expression following single sgRNA transfection, whereas dual sgRNA transfection showed a significant reduction of 54.89 +/- 9.1% (p < 0.0001). CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates a plasmid-free CRISPR/Cas9 RNP-based approach for targeted Park7 gene editing in primary MEFs. The results underline the importance of considering both the outcomes of genomic editing and the expression of functional protein when evaluating CRISPR/Cas9 approaches. This established approach sets the basis for the development of Park7-edited cellular models to study molecular mechanisms associated with PD and the subsequent development of disease-relevant models.

title: CauYL, encoding a magnesium chelatase H subunit, is required for chlorophyll accumulation and normal leaf coloration in cauliflower.
authors: Huang, Wei; Cui, Jinying; Wen, Zhenghua; Wu, Yuerui; Shan, Xiaozheng; Sun, Deling; Han, Fengqing; Zhang, Xiaoli
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
abstract: Fine mapping and CRISPR/Cas9 validation identified CauYL(BOB03G201420), encoding the H subunit of magnesium chelatase, as the causal gene for the yellow-green leaf phenotype in cauliflower. As the primary photosynthetic pigment in plants, chlorophyll captures light energy to drive photosynthesis and regulate plant growth. In addition, it confers green coloration to plants by absorbing blue and red light wavelengths. Despite the important role of chlorophyll in vegetables, the genetic regulation of chlorophyll accumulation in cauliflower remains largely unknown. In this study, we identified a cauliflower mutant "K-6" from an ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) mutagenized population, that displayed a stable yellow-green phenotype. The mutant showed much lower chlorophyll contents and decreased photosynthetic rate compared with the WT plants. Genetic inheritance analysis revealed that this yellow-green trait was controlled by a recessive gene. The target gene, designated CauYL, was mapped to an approximately 103.07 kb region on chromosome 3, based on BSA-seq and traditional linkage analyses. We identified a candidate gene BOB03G201420 encoding the H subunit of magnesium chelatase. Sequence analysis revealed a non-synonymous single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) within the coding sequence, resulting in an alanine-to-threonine substitution at a highly conserved residue. We employed CRISPR/Cas9 to knockout the CauYL gene in the WT background, and successfully generated CauYL mutants, which showed a yellow-green trait resembling that of the K-6 mutant. Transcriptome analysis showed that differentially expressed genes between K-6 and WT were significantly enriched in photosynthesis, riboflavin metabolism, and related pathways. Collectively, our results demonstrate that the CauYL gene is essential for maintaining the green coloration and photosynthetic competence of cauliflower, providing a valuable genetic target for improving photosynthetic efficiency and leaf color traits in cauliflower breeding.

title: Mdfi overexpression promotes oxidative muscle fiber formation without affecting muscle development in mature skeletal muscles.
authors: Lu, Tingting; Liu, Xulong; Wang, Chao; Huang, Bo; Mo, Ziyuan; Guo, Jiali; Gong, Xuezhu; Zhu, Yifan; Tong, Xiong; Hu, Ching Yuan; Wang, Chong
journal: Cellular and molecular life sciences : CMLS
abstract: Skeletal muscles are composed of multinucleated fibers with distinct metabolic and contractile properties. Skeletal muscles support locomotion and systemic metabolism, and their dysfunction underlies the pathogenesis of muscular dystrophies. The MyoD family inhibitor (Mdfi) has been implicated in muscle biology, yet its function in muscle development and muscle fiber type conversion remains largely unclear. Here, we developed the first tamoxifen (TMX)-inducible, skeletal muscle-specific Mdfi overexpression mouse model using CRISPR/Cas9 and Cre(ERT2) integration, enabling spatiotemporal control of Mdfi activity to mimic therapeutic modulation. This model revealed that Mdfi exerts dual-phase regulatory roles: suppressing early postnatal myogenesis while driving glycolytic-to-oxidative fiber switching in mature muscle. Mechanistically, elevated Mdfi activates the calcium signaling pathway to enhance mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, directly linking its function to improved muscle fatigue resistance. These Mdfi overexpression-induced phenotypic alterations exhibit stable transgenerational inheritance patterns. Our findings establish Mdfi as a key regulator of muscle plasticity and metabolic adaptation, providing a genetically tractable model for investigating muscle development and energy metabolism. Importantly, this study opens new avenues for understanding and potentially modulating fiber-type composition in muscular dystrophies and other disorders involving metabolic insufficiency, offering a conceptual framework for future therapeutic interventions aimed at improving muscle health.

title: Targeted CPSF6 recoding reveals global fitness advantages of SPAD integration targeting and cell type-specific roles for capsid binding in HIV-1 DNA synthesis and nuclear import.
authors: Jang, Sooin; Radhakrishnan, Rajalingam; Greenwood, Juliet; Singh, Parmit K; Bedwell, Gregory J; Robles-Sikisaka, Refugio; Routh, Andrew L; Engelman, Alan N
abstract: As part of the CFIm complex, CPSF6 regulates cellular gene expression via alternative polyadenylation. CPSF6 binds primate lentiviral capsids and has been implicated in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and integration targeting. However, interpretations of the role(s) of CPSF6 during HIV-1 replication are complicated by the transcriptional changes that occur when the protein is depleted from cells. To disentangle the role of CPSF6 in HIV-1 replication from alternative polyadenylation, we selectively recoded its capsid-binding phenylalanine-glycine motif to alanine-alanine in CD4-positive Jurkat T cells, CEM12D7 T cells, and THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells using CRISPR/Cas9-based homology-directed repair. While large variations in single-round HIV-1 infection were observed among isolated T cell clones, en masse comparisons of recoded T cells to cloned control T cells failed to reveal any significant differences in infection levels. Consistent with an overall fitness advantage provided by DNA integration in speckle-associated domains, which was ablated by recoding across cell types, HIV-1 replicated more robustly in control T cell populations. Single-round infection, in addition to spreading replication, was reduced in recoded myeloid/macrophage cells, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription, and more robust blocks to HIV-1 nuclear import. Recoded monocytes/macrophages, however, did not reveal any evidence for enhanced type I interferon production or sensing of HIV-1 nucleic acids. Altogether, we define endogenously recoded cell lines to uncouple capsid binding from CPSF6's role in RNA metabolism, which highlights a global fitness advantage of targeted DNA integration and cell type-specific roles for CPSF6 in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and virus replication proficiency.IMPORTANCEHIV-1 usurps cellular factors to effectively replicate and avoid innate immune sensing. HIV-1 capsid binds CPSF6, but the consequences of this virus-host interaction on HIV-1 biology are necessarily complicated by the cellular role of CPSF6 in pre-RNA processing. By endogenously recoding CPSF6 to selectively disrupt capsid binding while preserving its RNA-processing activity, we demonstrate in two different T cell lines that CPSF6-mediated targeting of HIV-1 DNA integration into nuclear speckle-associated domains correlates with optimal viral replication. Recoded THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells revealed additional single-round and multi-round infection defects, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription and HIV-1 nuclear import. These defects, however, did not correlate with enhanced type I interferon production or detection of HIV-1 nucleic acids by known innate immune sensors. Our work clarifies diverse roles for the capsid-CPSF6 interaction in HIV-1 infection of T lymphocytic versus myeloid cell lines and provides novel cell reagents for future research studies.

title: Natural and engineered bacteriophages against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: current landscape and clinical translation.
authors: Nautiyal, Deeksha; Sahu, Mridul; Jain, Utkarsh
abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.

title: DNA defense systems become a fitness liability during plasmid conjugation.
authors: Martinson, Jonathan N V; Song, Leo C T; Rubin, Benjamin E
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer via conjugative plasmids is a major driver of bacterial evolution. While antibiotic exposure selects for the resistance genes carried by some plasmids, much uncertainty remains about how plasmids persist and spread in microbial communities in the absence of such external selection. Here, we show that conjugative plasmid transfer selectively reduces the fitness of non-permissive recipients through the process of lethal zygosis: a phenomenon in which repeated Type IV Secretion System (T4SS) engagement damages recipients that fail to establish the plasmid. We found that this contact-dependent antagonism effectively clears a niche for plasmid donors by turning recipients' DNA defenses into a liability. Blocking establishment of the plasmid RK2 with CRISPR-Cas or restriction-modification caused strong fitness defects in Escherichia coli recipients by preventing expression of plasmid-encoded exclusion genes and leaving cells exposed to repeated T4SS engagement. We leveraged this insight to resolve an obstacle in bacterial editing by developing transposon vectors that co-deliver exclusion genes, increasing the efficiency of gene editing by orders of magnitude. Our results reveal the role of "coercive assimilation" in horizontal gene transfer, exposing a tradeoff where the advantage of bacterial immunity to foreign DNA is counterbalanced by increased susceptibility to lethal zygosis.

title: Moderate prevalence and evolutionary causes of paralogous compensation in humans.
authors: Shen, Jieyu; Yu, Daqi; Wang, Wenjia; Su, Tianhan; Wang, Dingding; Liang, Junbo; Guo, Yiqiong; Zhao, Shangqi; Ma, Huijing; Wang, Jichang; Wang, Xiaoyue; Zhang, Yong E
abstract: Paralogous compensation drives genetic robustness; however, its in vivo prevalence in humans and the evolutionary forces shaping it remain unresolved. We CRISPR-screened 678 human paralog pairs to identify pairs with negative genetic interactions (nGIs) or compensatory paralogs, and integrated our results with four studies to assemble two complementary resources: the 2168-pair Union and 4859-pair Ito datasets. We extrapolated to the organismal level by classifying paralogs as core (broadly compensating, 99 Union/120 Ito pairs), conditional (111/566) or non-interacting (1958/4173), and testing for enriched compensatory signals in core pairs relative to the latter two groups. Core nGI pairs consistently showed prenatal co-expression, depletion of disease genes and enrichment for upregulation after paralog loss in cancer, though the signals were often moderate. Evolutionary analyses found similar fractions ( approximately 2%) of core compensators among both ancient and young paralogs. Ancient pairs retain overlaps likely under pleiotropic and dosage constraints. Incomplete small-scale duplication mechanisms limit compensation among young pairs, except X-derived retrogenes, which are overrepresented among core nGIs ( approximately 14%). This is consistent with selection to counteract male germline X inactivation and subsequent out-of-testis expansion. Overall, paralogous compensation is moderately prevalent in vivo in humans, shaped by multiple evolutionary forces acting on ancient or young duplicates.

title: CRISPR/Cas genome editing strategies to enhance abiotic stress tolerance in sugar crops.
authors: Liu, Hong-Bo; Kumar, Tanweer; Abu-Ellail, Farrag F B; Lin, Xiu-Qin; Li, Chun-Jia; Xu, Chao-Hua; Arif, Muhammad; Khan, Wajid; Ismail, Muhammad; Zhao, Li-Ping; Sakr, Ebtehag A E; Haq, Nur-Ul; Lu, Xin
abstract: Sugar crops including sugarcane, sugar beets, and sweet sorghum, are fundamental for global sucrose supply and crucial feedstocks for bioethanol production and industrial bioproducts. However, yield and sucrose accumulation are significantly influenced by abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity/alkalinity, heat, chilling/freezing, and heavy metal toxicity. The polygenic complexity of stress tolerance, particularly in sugarcane with its large, polyploid, and haplotype-diverse genome, presents significant challenges for conventional breeding, rendering it slow and imprecise. This review combines advances in genome-editing technologies, including CRISPR/Cas systems (Cas9 and Cas12a), along with transcriptional techniques (CRISPRa/i), base editors, and prime editors. These tools, combined with the progress in reference genomes, haplotype-resolved assemblies, and pangenomes, have facilitated precise gene discovery, genomic selection, and targeted editing. CRISPR-based approaches offer promising avenues for enhancing key stress-responsive pathways governing oxidative homeostasis, membrane integrity, osmotic regulation, hormone signaling, and ion-homeostasis in sugar crops. Prominent candidate targets include transcription factors (TF), signaling components, raffinose biosynthesis genes implicated in freezing tolerance, regulators of salt and alkaline stress, and determinants of heavy metal tolerance and sequestration.
