Translational challenges, such as off-target effects, low transformation efficiencies, and editing multiple homologues or haplotypes, are being addressed such as DNA-free ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, high-throughput screening, haplotype-specific target design, and haplotype-aware guide RNA engineering based on unique genetic variation sites across different gene haplotypes. Collectively, the integration of advanced CRISPR toolkits with enhanced genomic information resources and phenotyping capabilities holds significant potential for accelerating the development of precision-bred, multi-stress-resilient sugar crops that sustain yield, quality, and industrial value under abiotic stress conditions.

title: Recent advances in bacterial detection techniques targeting genetic, protein, and enzymatic biomarkers.
authors: Chen, Hanren; Xiao, Jiayi; Diao, Bihong; Zheng, Shiquan; Shao, Huaze; Liu, Lihong
abstract: Rapid and accurate diagnosis of bacterial infections is essential for effective clinical management, food safety, and environmental monitoring. Traditional culture-based methods are time-consuming and inadequate for addressing urgent challenges such as antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This review categorizes recent bacterial detection strategies into three major biomarker types: genetic, protein, and enzymatic. For each category, we outline the underlying detection mechanisms, evaluate analytical performance, and highlight representative technologies, including polymerase chain reaction (PCR), loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-Cas (CRISPR-Cas) assays, advanced immunoassays, aptamer sensors, and enzyme-based assays. Meanwhile, we provide a detailed description of representative examples for each representative technology. Key metrics such as sensitivity, detection time, portability, and point-of-care (POC) applicability are compared to reveal the strengths and limitations of each approach. Translational progress is discussed with emphasis on commercialized platforms, field-deployable devices, and multimodal workflows. Finally, major technical bottlenecks are identified, and future directions are proposed for developing robust, rapid, and widely accessible bacterial diagnostics.

title: Molecular Technologies for Intracellular mRNA Imaging and Their Recent Biological Applications.
authors: Xia, Ke; Wang, Xiangnan; Wu, Zhenkun; Chu, Xia
abstract: Understanding the spatial and temporal behaviors of individual mRNA molecules is essential for elucidating gene expression regulation and cellular function. Imaging these processes within cells offers unique insights into transcriptional heterogeneity, mRNA transport, translation, and degradation dynamics. In this Review, we summarized the principal molecular technologies for intracellular mRNA imaging and tracking. These approaches are classified based on their compatibility with fixed cells versus live cells. Fixed-cell FISH-based methods provide spatial resolution and multiplex quantification. Live-cell systems, such as RNA stem-loop binding proteins, CRISPR/Cas platforms, fluorogenic RNA aptamers, fluorescent chemical labeling strategies, molecular beacons, and DNA circuits, enable real-time visualization of both endogenous and exogenous mRNA transcripts in live cells. We finally discuss the challenges and potential future directions for intracellular mRNA imaging. We anticipate that this Review will inspire the development of the next generation of mRNA imaging technologies in diverse biological applications.

title: Reshaping the scissors: From directed evolution to AI-driven design for enhanced Cas performance.
authors: Cheng, Xinrui; Ruan, Weimin; Jin, Zheng; Suo, Langda; Ma, Yuehui; Jiang, Lin; Zheng, Wenxin; Li, Ning; Hu, Wenping
abstract: CRISPR/Cas gene editing holds great promise for applications in agricultural breeding and gene therapy; however, native Cas proteins face bottlenecks such as off-target effects, PAM limitations, and delivery challenges. This review explores a three-tiered, progressive, and synergistic analytical framework comprising directed evolution, rational structural design, and integrated protein engineering. Following the logic of "random exploration-precision modification-system integration," it systematically clarifies the principles, advantages, disadvantages, and complementary interactions among these three optimization techniques. By comprehensively mapping the entire technical pathway for Cas protein improvement, this study fills a gap in systematic analysis within the field and provides a theoretical framework for tiered, synergistic modification to support the development of high-performance editors. The paper further analyzes a novel research and development paradigm in which AI and protein language models profoundly empower Cas modification. It summarizes intelligent toolchains such as structure prediction, virtual mutation, and de novo design of artificial Cas proteins, and highlights the unique advantages of AI in overcoming the performance trade-offs inherent in traditional protein engineering. At the same time, it identifies existing challenges, such as data scarcity and insufficient model interpretability, and looks ahead to how multimodal gene-editing large language models and automated closed-loop experimental systems will drive the iterative development of miniaturized, broad-spectrum, and highly precise editing tools, thereby facilitating the clinical and industrial implementation of gene-editing technologies.

title: Structural Empowerment Sensing: Decoding the Structure-Activity Relationship and Detection Application of G‑Quadruplex Aptamer.
authors: Bao, Wenji; Su, Ailing; Ao, Denggerile; Ga, Lu; Yu, Lan; Ai, Jun
abstract: G-Quadruplex (G4) aptamers have emerged as versatile functional nucleic acid architectures for biosensing because of their unique conformational plasticity, programmable topologies, and intrinsic signal-regulation capabilities. Unlike conventional recognition elements that mainly function as passive binding scaffolds, G4 aptamers can actively regulate signal generation and transduction through topology-dependent structural dynamics. Increasing evidence indicates that biosensing performance is closely governed by conformational energetics, folding kinetics, loop organization, ion coordination, and nano-interfacial coupling. This review summarizes recent advances in structure-guided G4 aptamer biosensing from the perspective of "structural empowerment", where conformational architectures directly determine sensing behavior and analytical output. We first discuss the structural fundamentals of G4 aptamers, including topology diversity, thermodynamic stability, folding pathways, and environmental responsiveness, emphasizing their influence on molecular recognition and signal accessibility. We then analyze the mechanistic relationship between G4 conformational transitions and multiple signal transduction modes, including fluorescence, electrochemical, colorimetric, surface-enhanced Raman scattering, photoelectrochemical, and catalytic sensing systems. Particular attention is given to the integration of G4 architectures with CRISPR platforms, nanozymes, DNA amplification circuits, metal-organic frameworks, and nanointerfacial engineering strategies. Importantly, this review establishes a structure-performance framework correlating G4 topological features and kinetic behaviors with analytical outcomes. Current limitations, including structural polymorphism, ionic dependence, reproducibility issues, and limited quantitative predictability, are critically discussed. Finally, future opportunities in adaptive biosensing, intelligent molecular interfaces, and AI-assisted structural design are highlighted. This review establishes a quantitative structure-performance framework by correlating G4 structural descriptors, conformational energetics, kinetic parameters, and analytical outputs, providing a basis for predictive design of G4-based sensing systems.

title: Recent biotechnological advances and technology readiness level of natural products derived from marine fungi.
authors: Chetapalli, Chiranjeevi; Karuppaiah, Nanthini Devi; Garlapati, Deviram; Veeraragavan, Sachithanandam; Sreeharsha, Rachapudi Venkata; Valsalan, Vinithkumar Nambali; Gopal, Dharani; Ramakrishnan, Balaji
abstract: Bioprospecting involves the systematic exploration of natural resources to identify bioactive secondary metabolites with potential for development into commercially valuable products. In this review, more than a hundred bioactive compounds derived from marine fungi were analysed, with emphasis on their chemical diversity, biological activities, commercialisation status, economic relevance, and Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs). The compounds represented diverse metabolite classes, including polyketides, alkaloids, terpenoids, peptides, azaphilones, and other bioactive secondary metabolites with pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, cosmeceutical, industrial, and environmental applications. Among the reviewed compounds, only approximately 10-20 have been marketed, while the majority remain at early stages of development. TRL assessment showed that most marine fungal-derived products are concentrated at TRL 1-3, a smaller number of compounds and bioprocesses have progressed to TRL 4-5, and highly commercialised products reach TRL 9. In India, pharmaceutical applications involving anticancer, antimicrobial, and antiviral compounds were assessed at TRL 3-5, nutraceuticals at TRL 5-7, cosmeceuticals at TRL 6-8, and industrial enzymes at TRL 7-9. The main barriers to commercialisation were low and unstable metabolite yields, structural complexity, regulatory and bioprospecting constraints, inadequate translational investment and industrial infrastructure, and high financial and technical risks during late-stage development. Integrated approaches including strain improvement, fermentation optimization, chemoenzymatic synthesis, OSMAC, in-situ product removal, genome mining, metabolic engineering, Chemi-genomic approaches, and CRISPR/Cas-based pathway engineering offer opportunities to improve production and increase TRLs. Overall, the findings demonstrate a substantial discovery-to-commercialization gap in marine fungal biotechnology. Advancing strain development, scalable bioprocessing, safety and regulatory validation, synthetic biology, industrial partnerships, and translational infrastructure is essential to convert promising low-TRL discoveries into commercially viable products and strengthen the contribution of marine fungi to a sustainable circular bioeconomy.

title: Coxiella burnetii effector CelF reprograms host proteostasis via competitive disruption of the UBQLN1-PSMD4 axis to stabilize autophagic SNARE SNAP29 and modulate lysosomal metabolic maturation.
authors: Zhang, Shan; Jiang, Yufei; Lin, Yinhui; Chen, Xiaoxiao; Zhang, Yuchen; Yu, Yonghui; OuYang, Xuan; Zhou, Dongsheng; Song, Yajun; Jiao, Jun
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) and autophagy-lysosome pathway constitute the core proteolytic metabolic networks that maintain cellular protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and organelle metabolic identity. Intracellular pathogens frequently reprogram host metabolic pathways to establish replicative niches, yet how they manipulate proteostatic metabolism to remodel organelle maturation remains incompletely understood. METHODS: CelF secretion was confirmed by TEM translocation assay. CRISPR-dCas9 was used to generate CelF knockdown and complementation strains, with celF transcription verified by RT-qPCR. Cell infection and SCID mouse models were used to assess intracellular survival, Coxiella-containing vacuole (CCV) maturation, and virulence of Coxiella burnetii. The effect of CelF on late autophagy was examined by dual-fluorescence LC3 and Western blotting. Then, UBQLN1 was identified as a CelF-interacting host protein by co-IP and pull-down, followed by truncation mapping. Finally, co-IP, UBQLN1 knockdown, Western blotting and MST assays were used to analyze the effect of CelF on SNARE assembly, SNAP29 degradation and ubiquitination, and competitive binding of CelF and PSMD4 to UBQLN1. RESULTS: CelF depletion severely impaired the metabolic maturation of CCV, suppressed bacterial proliferation in macrophages, and attenuated virulence in vivo. Mechanistically, CelF acted as a molecular decoy that directly bound the ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain of the proteasomal shuttle factor UBQLN1, competitively displacing the proteasome subunit PSMD4. This competitive interference blocked UBQLN1-mediated proteasomal delivery of SNAP29 without altering its ubiquitination status, thereby enhancing SNAP29 protein stability and promoting assembly of the STX17-SNAP29-VAMP8 fusogenic complex. The augmented SNARE activity drove autophagosome-lysosome fusion, sustained autophagic flux, and facilitated lysosomal metabolic remodeling to support CCV biogenesis. DISCUSSION: Unlike canonical pathogen-encoded UPS modulators that function as E3 ligases or deubiquitinases, CelF operates purely through competitive protein-protein interaction, representing a previously unrecognized paradigm for microbial manipulation of host proteostatic metabolism. Our findings reveal that intracellular pathogens can actively orchestrate organelle metabolic identity by rewiring host proteostasis, and identify the UBQLN1-PSMD4-SNAP29 axis as a novel regulatory checkpoint for SNARE proteostasis and lysosomal metabolic maturation.

title: Direct RNA Targeting by CRISPR/Cas12: Emerging Mechanisms and Diagnostic Applications.
authors: Hall, Tim; Jia, Zhengyang; Cai, Kongzhe; Sang, Rui; Guo, Tianruo; Wang, Yan; Deng, Fei
abstract: RNA detection is essential for molecular diagnostics because it provides dynamic information on gene expression, pathogen activity, and disease progression. Conventional RNA detection methods, particularly reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), remain widely used but require RNA-to-DNA conversion, thermal cycling, and relatively complex workflows, limiting their suitability for rapid and point-of-care testing. In CRISPR diagnostics, Cas13 has traditionally been regarded as the major RNA-targeting system, whereas Cas12 enzymes have been primarily recognized as DNA-targeting nucleases. Recent studies, however, have revealed that several Cas12 variants can directly recognize RNA targets, enabling reverse-transcription-free RNA detection through mechanisms such as RNA-triggered DNase activity. In this review, we summarize the emerging functional diversity of RNA-responsive Cas12 systems, including Cas12a, Cas12a2, Cas12a3, Cas12f, and Cas12g, and discuss their underlying mechanisms for direct RNA sensing. We further highlight strategies for enhancing Cas12-mediated RNA detection, including guide and activator engineering, nanomaterial-assisted readouts, and autocatalytic signal amplification. Finally, we discuss its applications in infectious disease diagnosis, cancer biomarker detection, and environmental monitoring, alongside key challenges and future opportunities for clinical translation and point-of-care testing.

title: AI and the CRISPR Ecosystem: A Mixed Bag.
authors: Barrangou, Rodolphe

title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury.
authors: Zhang, Shimeng; Gong, Xiaoqing; Tian, Songhai; Yang, Yang; Tong, Xinru; Sheng, Kuanwei; Zhang, Yifan; Amatsu, Sho; Zhang, Xi; Yu, Daiyue; Zhao, Hongtao; Ruan, Lin; Sun, Honglu; Wu, Kai; Dong, Min; Xiong, Xiaozhe
abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment(1,2). Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis(3-5), the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

title: An engineered, compact Cas12m variant for multiplexed gene activation in vivo.
authors: Zhang, Hainan; Yang, Lin; Liu, Yuling; Han, Dingyi; Li, Yingnan; Lin, Jiajia; Wang, Bingyan; Hu, Jiaxu; Zhang, Yaru; Zhang, Yi; Li, Jinhui; Wei, Shuping; Liu, Simiao; Li, Tong; Zhong, Na; Zhang, Ganggang; Zhou, Xingtao; Shi, Linyu; Huang, Jinhai; Yang, Hui; Tan, Guohe; Zhou, Yingsi; Li, Guoling
abstract: Achieving coordinated CRISPR-based transactivation (CRISPRa) regulation in vivo remains challenging, as the requisite genetic elements frequently exceed the packaging capacity of AAV vectors. Here we report the identification and engineering of the Cas12m protein family, a naturally nuclease-dead CRISPR system that possesses intrinsic self-processing activity for its precursor crRNA. We develop an optimized variant, denCas12m, and leverage it in the smCRISPRa platform. We show that a single transcriptional unit encoding a multi-gRNA array can be processed into individual functional guides within a target cell, enabling efficient synergistic activation of a single gene through multiple sites or simultaneous activation of distinct endogenous genes from a single all-in-one AAV vector. We demonstrate phenotypic rescue in mouse models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy and Scn1a haploinsufficiency. Furthermore, a single all-in-one AAV vector supports the simultaneous activation of multiple distinct endogenous genes in mice, with a single vector delivering up to eight crRNAs for activation of six different genes, demonstrating the platform's high-order multiplexing.

title: Structural mechanism of programmable gene integration by the R2 retrotransposon coupled with CRISPR-Cas9.
authors: Komatsu, Daisuke; Hiraizumi, Masahiro; Fell, Christopher W; Fujimatsu, Kenta; Nagahata, Naoto; Yamada, Sota; Sapkota, Sworaj; Ramani, Harsh; Arya, Benjamin; Shibata, Mikihiro; Yamashita, Keitaro; Gootenberg, Jonathan S; Abudayyeh, Omar O; Nishimasu, Hiroshi
abstract: R2 retroelements are non-long-terminal-repeat retrotransposons that primarily insert into 28S ribosomal DNA loci across diverse eukaryotes. R2 elements home to their target sites through target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT), in which the R2 protein recognizes and nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription using an R2-encoding RNA as the template. The avian R2 system from Taeniopygia guttata (R2Tg) can insert a payload sequence within an RNA template into 28S ribosomal DNA loci in human cells. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the R2Tg-template RNA-target DNA complex in the TPRT initiation state, both alone and bound to a Cas9-guide RNA complex. These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

title: CRISPR/Cas12a-based simplified lateral flow assay for sensitive detection of OTA and AFB1.
authors: Jiang, Wenjun; Zhu, Yidan; Kang, Jingyi; Zhu, Ziyi; Qian, Kun; Ji, Haiwei; Wang, Qi; Qin, Yuling; Wu, Li
abstract: Mycotoxin contamination in agricultural commodities poses serious health risks, necessitating sensitive and user-friendly detection methods for food safety monitoring. Here, we present a multiplex CRISPR/Cas12a-assisted lateral flow assay (MC-LFA) for the parallel detection of Ochratoxin A (OTA) and Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1). The platform employs a duplex Switch design in which target binding releases an activator sequence (Probe 2), triggering Cas12a trans-cleavage of a half-blocking reporter (HBR). Cleavage generates dsDNA products labeled with Dig/FAM (for OTA) or TAMRA/FAM (for AFB1), which are captured at distinct test lines via specific antibody recognition. An integrated streptavidin (SA) capture line binds intact HBR through biotin-streptavidin interactions, effectively replacing conventional magnetic separation steps. The total assay time is approximately 65 min, including a 45-min target identification and a 15-min Cas12a reaction followed by a 5-min lateral flow readout. This approach achieves visual detection limits of 50 pg/mL for OTA and 250 pg/mL for AFB1. The assay exhibits excellent linear correlation over broad concentration ranges and demonstrates high accuracy in double-blind testing (97.22% for OTA and 94.44% for AFB1). Notably, the platform requires only aptamer replacement for different targets while maintaining the same Cas12a and crRNA sequences, substantially reducing experimental costs. Furthermore, by co-localizing detection probes in a single tube, an "OR" logic gate strategy enables parallel screening for both mycotoxins with a single test line. This cost-effective, sensitive, and operationally simple platform possesses strong potential for on-site food safety monitoring in resource-limited settings.

title: Nanozyme-Driven Next-Generation miRNA Biosensing.
authors: Deshwal, Akanksha; Tripathi, Ravi Mani
journal: Wiley interdisciplinary reviews. Nanomedicine and nanobiotechnology
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small, noncoding RNA molecules nearly 22 nucleotides in length that contribute significantly to regulating gene expression. Their aberrant expression patterns are associated with disease progression, including cardiovascular and neurological disorders and cancer. However, the rapid detection of miRNAs remains challenging due to their low abundance, sequence similarity, and degradation. Conventional methods of detecting miRNAs, such as Northern blotting, microarray analysis, quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR), and next-generation sequencing (NGS), offer significant benefits for miRNA profiling, though they have drawbacks, including limited specificity, complex workflows, relatively high cost, and specialized equipment requirements. Advanced methodologies driven by nanotechnology, especially those that combine clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/Cas approaches, provide revolutionary developments. Nanozymes enhance the stability and biocompatibility of catalytic amplification, while CRISPR technologies enable real-time, multiplex, and ultrasensitive miRNA detection with accurate sequence recognition. The rapidly expanding field encompasses diverse nanozyme architectures, recognition mechanisms, amplification strategies, and signal-transduction platforms, providing a broad basis for critically assessing advances, limitations, and emerging opportunities in nanozyme-enabled miRNA biosensing. Nanozyme-enabled miRNA detection has evolved across diverse sensing platforms, such as colorimetric and optical assays, sophisticated photoelectrochemical (PEC) and electrochemiluminescence (ECL) biosensors, and portable and paper-based diagnostic technologies. The convergence of nanozyme catalysis, CRISPR-based recognition, and advanced sensing strategies holds promise for sensitive, selective, and portable miRNA diagnostics.

title: SCN2B Drives Depression-like Phenotypes in Mice by Suppressing BDNF Signaling via Its Intracellular Domain NICD.
authors: Lu, Min-Nan; Yan, Guo-Ji; Wang, Dan; Huang, Hong-Chen; Zhou, Ying; Li, Shan-Shan; Ye, Chen-Jun; Dong, Xiao-Han; Yang, Chen-Di; Liang, Xi-Wen; Niu, Yong-Min; Hu, Tao; Yang, Xin-Wang; Xiyang, Yan-Bin
abstract: The rising global burden of depression necessitates novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets. Voltage-gated sodium channel beta2-subunit (Navbeta2, coded by SCN2B) has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet its role in depression remains unexplored. Here, we identify SCN2B as a previously unrecognized driver of depression-like pathophysiology. Using SCN2B-overexpressing (SCN2B-OV) mice across different ages (1, 12, and 20 months) and CRISPR- engineered Navbeta2(V173A,V175K) mice with selective reduction of the Navbeta2 intracellular domain (NICD), we combined behavioral phenotyping, electrophysiology, neurotransmitter profiling, and molecular analyses, with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) as an environmental challenge. SCN2B-OV mice exhibited accelerated depression-like phenotypes, including anhedonia (sucrose preference 52.42% reduction, P<0.05), behavioral despair (forced swim test immobility 67.42% increase, P<0.05), and cognitive deficits (Y-maze alternation 50.90% reduction, P<0.05), independent of natural aging. Electrophysiologically, SCN2B overexpression induced a striking prefrontal-hippocampal imbalance: prefrontal cortex (PFC) became hyperexcitable (glutamate release increased by 64.7%; sEPSC amplitude increased 2.05-fold, P<0.05), whereas the hippocampus showed synaptic suppression (GABA release reduced by 32.65%; sIPSC frequency reduced by 66.67%, P<0.05). Mechanistically, SCN2B overexpression suppressed BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/AKT signaling axis (BDNF reduced by 53.17%; p-TrkB reduced by 63.62%, P<0.05), accompanied by decreased synaptic proteins (PSD95 43.45%, synapsin I 40.31%, P<0.05). Remarkably, NICD-reduced Navbeta2(V173A,V175K) mice were fully resistant to CUMS-induced behavioral and neurotransmitter deficits, establishing NICD as a critical mediator of stress vulnerability. Collectively, these findings unravel a causal pathway in which SCN2B overexpression drives NICD-dependent suppression of BDNF signaling, leading to region-specific excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, synaptic disintegration, and depression-like phenotypes. Targeting Navbeta2 proteolysis to block NICD generation may thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.

title: Nucleoredoxin proteins in green lineage: Insights about its roles in biotic and abiotic stress resilience.
authors: Gupta, Arvind; Thakur, Rahul; Yadav, Saurabh
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
abstract: Oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plants are inevitable, and plants employ enzymatic and non-enzymatic system for cell homeostasis. Nucleoredoxins (NRX) are a family of thioredoxin (TRX) superfamily and being nuclear oxidoreductase, NRX are an important class of proteins present in many organisms including plants. Unlike TRXs, plant NRXs are larger proteins comprising of multiple TRX domains and conserved active redox motif 'WCPPC', displayed evolutionary conservation across various plants. NRX maintains oxidative stress tolerance by maintaining the reduced state by thiol-disulphide chemistry via conserved cysteine residues present in active site. Subcellular localization of NRX is mostly cytoplasmic and the putative protein interacting partners predicted their correlation with oxidative stress tolerance. We have also attempted to correlate plant NRXs with the available patent documents and observed that very little information is available. Compared to TRX research that started in 1960s, NRX have been discovered later and their structural complexity, multiple isoforms have led to their functional characterization more challenging. NRXs have roles in abiotic and biotic stresses and emerging roles indicate its role in plant immunity and modulation of plant defense response at molecular level by -OMICS studies. In view of the above, the present review discusses the sequence analysis, structure, and functional genomics associated with NRXs in plants. This is also correlated with the futuristic aspect of NRX roles being delineated in molecular stress response and signaling using CRISPR-Cas genome editing and related techniques.

title: Systems biology and synthetic engineering of probiotic yeasts.
authors: Ali, Saqib; Che Hussian, Che Haznie Ayu; Goh, Hoe-Han
abstract: Yeast probiotics, particularly Saccharomyces boulardii, are used in clinical, nutritional and biotechnological settings, yet their strain-specific mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This review examines how systems biology and multi-omics approaches can improve understanding of probiotic yeast function. We discuss comparative genomics and pangenomics, transcriptomic responses to gastrointestinal stress, cell-surface proteins involved in pathogen interactions, and metabolomic outputs including organic acids and other potential postbiotic metabolites. We then consider genome-scale metabolic models, flux balance analysis, and (13)C metabolic flux analysis as complementary tools for converting omics observations into testable hypotheses about pathway activity and strain-specific metabolic traits. Published comparisons of S. boulardii and S. cerevisiae illustrate this framework. Conserved and strain-specific genomic variation, differential stress responses, acetate production, pathogen binding and host-cell effects can be examined together, while causal links between most variants and probiotic effects remain unresolved. The review also compares the systems-data, metabolic-modeling, and genome-engineering readiness of Kluyveromyces marxianus and Debaryomyces hansenii, two non-conventional yeasts with thermotolerance or halotolerance, but less direct evidence for human probiotic function. Finally, we discuss CRISPR-based engineering, machine learning, data standards, regulatory considerations and future possibilities for strain-specific computational models. Progress will require standardized experimental conditions, well-annotated strain resources, integrated multi-omics datasets, and experimental validation of model predictions.

title: Ultrasound-triggered bio-scaffold integrating engineered stem cells for cartilage regeneration.
authors: Guo, Jiayi; Peng, Yimeng; Xiao, Xiong; Li, Shaobing; Zhu, Junyan; Lin, Juntao; Li, Jian; Wu, Deguang; Yu, Bo; Chen, Yan
abstract: Articular cartilage repair remains a major clinical challenge due to the limited regenerative capacity of the tissue and the poor therapeutic efficacy of current treatments. Although stem cell-based therapies hold promise, their clinical outcomes are often compromised by insufficient chondrogenic differentiation, phenotypic instability, and rapid cell loss in the dynamic joint environment. Herein, we report an ultrasound-responsive, bio-scaffold system (e-BMSCs/Gel) designed to enhance cartilage regeneration through coordinated biochemical and genetic regulation. In this system, bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) are engineered by internalizing nanobubbles (NBs) loaded with TGF-beta3 protein and CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids targeting the YAP (pCas9-YAP), termed T@NBs(pDNA). Additionally, to enhance cell retention and survival, engineered BMSCs (e-BMSCs) are encapsulated within a thermosensitive thiolated-chitosan/hydroxyapatite hydrogel that rapidly forms in situ. Under US stimulation, the synchronized activation of TGF-beta3 release and YAP gene silencing significantly promoted the chondrogenic differentiation of e-BMSCs. Furthermore, in vivo evaluation in a rat articular cartilage defect model demonstrates that US-activated e-BMSCs/Gel effectively promotes hyaline-like cartilage regeneration and improves structural restoration of the defect site. Overall, this work presents a controllable bio-scaffold platform, offering a novel strategy for effective cartilage regeneration.

title: Exonuclease-gated CRISPR/Cas12a biosensing strategy for sensitive detection of lncRNA MIR155HG.
authors: Wang, Qiufeng; Cai, Yongliang; Zhu, Shiyu; Yin, Feifan; Jiang, Yihao; Sun, Heliang; Xiang, Yang; Wang, Zhongyun
journal: Journal of pharmaceutical and biomedical analysis
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been shown to be important regulatory factors in initiation and progression of cancer. However, sensitive detection of lncRNAs remains challenging due to their low abundance, complex structure and susceptibility to nuclease degradation. Among various lncRNAs, MIR155HG has been shown to be involved in the progression of cervical cancer and serve as a potential target for biomarker analysis. Here, we developed an exonuclease-gated CRISPR/Cas12a biosensing platform (E-CRISPR) for the detection of MIR155HG without target pre-amplification. This strategy relies on a bifunctional single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) probe containing both a MIR155HG recognition region and a CRISPR/Cas12a activation region. In the absence of target RNA, exonuclease I (Exo I) degrades the ssDNA probe, thereby reducing background signals. Upon binding to MIR155HG, RNA-DNA hybridization reduces the probe's susceptibility to Exo I digestion and allows the retained probe to activate CRISPR/Cas12a and generate an enhanced fluorescence signal. Under optimized conditions, the E-CRISPR assay achieved a limit of detection of 4.76 pM and a linear range of 4.76 pM to 0.4 nM. The entire assay could be completed within 100 min while maintaining sensitive detection of MIR155HG and showed good sequence specificity and reliable performance in complex biological environment. This exonuclease-regulated CRISPR/Cas12a strategy provides a simple analytical approach for extracellular lncRNA analysis.

title: A sensitive RAA-CRISPR/Cas13a-LFS assay for point-of-care detection of Salmonella.
authors: Xiao, Xiaoliang; Liu, Wenzhe; Lei, Di; Jiang, Chenchen; Li, Tong; Luo, Wenxin; Wang, Xin; Tang, Yi; Fang, Rendong; Wang, Hongzhi
abstract: Salmonella is a major zoonotic pathogen that seriously endangers the poultry industry and threatens public health. Rapid and accurate monitoring is therefore essential for effective prevention and control. In this study, we developed a molecular detection method for Salmonella by integrating recombinase-assisted amplification (RAA) and the CRISPR/Cas13a system. We then adapted this method into a lateral flow strip (LFS) format that allows naked‑eye reading, enabling instrument‑free, rapid on‑site detection. The assay combines the efficient isothermal amplification ability of RAA with the high specificity recognition of CRISPR/Cas13a, targeting the conserved fimY gene of Salmonella. It achieves a detection sensitivity of 10 degrees  copies/muL. When further coupled with LFS for visual detection, the reaction can be finished within 40 min, with a detection limit of 10(2) copies/muL. In clinical sample validation, the method showed 100% agreement with qPCR results and significantly outperformed conventional PCR. This assay provides a sensitive and specific approach for Salmonella detection that is simple to operate and suitable for field deployment, offering a practical tool for rapid Salmonella screening in resource-limited settings.

title: FOSL1-associated condensates modulate superenhancer-mediated selected IL-1 family gene activation in psoriasis.
authors: Qiu, Yueqi; Sun, Ke; Yu, Yaqin; Hou, Huihui; Wu, Ruifang; Lu, Qianjin; Zhao, Ming
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Here we performed multiomics analyses (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA sequencing) on psoriatic lesions, perilesional skin, healthy skin, and M5-stimulated HaCaT cells. Functional validation was performed using CRISPR-mediated superenhancer (SE) editing, epigenetic modulation, circular chromosome conformation capture sequencing, assay for chromatin-bound condensates by exploratory sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. We found widespread activation of enhancers and SEs in lesions, including an interleukin 1 (IL-1)-SE regulating IL1A, IL1B, and IL36G transcription. BET inhibition reduced SE activity, repressed IL-1 cytokines, and relieved psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo. Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) was identified as a key transcription factor enriched in active SEs and associated with condensate formation, contributing to the maintenance of EP300 occupancy and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation deposition. Macrophage-derived IL-1 up-regulated FOSL1 through mitogen-activated protein kinase/ERK signaling, forming a positive feedback loop that amplified inflammation. This study revealed an FOSL1-SE-centered regulatory network driving keratinocyte inflammatory responses, providing previously unknown therapeutic targets for psoriasis.

title: Cbfbeta regulates DNA looping at the Il4-Il13 loci to control their differential expression in Th2 cells.
authors: Wei, Danping; Ge, Guangzhe; Chiang, Chih-Yuan; Cao, Yaqiang; Kline, Zoey J; Jing, Huie; Golec, Dominic; Shibata, Hirofumi; Fang, Difeng; Schwartzberg, Pamela L; Su, Helen C; Zhao, Keji; Cheng, Ken Chih-Chien; Zhu, Jinfang
abstract: Th2 cells play a central role in orchestrating type 2 immune responses by producing type 2 cytokines including IL-4 and IL-13. The master transcription factor GATA3 is essential but not sufficient for type 2 cytokine production. To better define other transcription factors that regulate type 2 cytokine expression, we performed a CRISPR-Cas9 screen after preparing a retroviral library expressing sgRNAs targeting 2,394 mouse transcription factors and cofactors. The screen revealed core-binding factor beta (Cbfbeta) as a specific inducer of IL-13 that simultaneously inhibited IL-4 expression. The effect of Cbfbeta on IL-13 production was confirmed both in vitro and in vivo and was independent of GATA3 induction. Mechanistically, Cbfbeta induced chromatin accessibility at the HS-2 site within the Il13 promoter where the Cbfbeta/Runx complex bound. Hi-TrAC analysis indicated that DNA looping between HS-2 and other enhancers was reduced upon Cbfbeta deletion. Overall, our results indicate that Cbfbeta directly regulates IL-13 expression by binding the Il13 promoter via the Cbfbeta/Runx complex and promoting enhancer-promoter interactions that facilitate Il13 transcription.

title: The Rhizobial Type III Effector NopD Regulates the GmPP2C-ENOD93 Axis to Control Symbiotic Nodulation and Yield in Soybean.
authors: Mi, Liang; Lu, Liying; Sun, Jiake; Li, Yansong; Ma, Chao; Ma, Shengnan; Yang, Mingliang; Hong, Siyan; Wang, Miao; Chen, Lin; Liu, Chunyan; Xin, Dawei; Chen, Qingshan; Wang, Jinhui
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Type III effector proteins (T3Es) are pivotal orchestrators of host-microbe interactions and essential for establishing symbiosis, thereby influencing soybean growth and productivity through modulation of symbiotic nitrogen fixation (SNF). While the central role of the T3E NopD in soybean SNF is recognized, its mechanistic underpinnings have remained elusive. In this study, we determined that GmPP2C, whose expression is regulated by NopD, serves as a regulator of nodulation. Overexpression of GmPP2C suppressed infection-thread formation and markedly reduced nodule number, whereas CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption enhanced infection events and partially rescued nodulation defects of NopD deficiency. Transcriptome profiling and complementation assays indicate GmPP2C inhibits nodulation by repressing ENOD93. Loss of GmPP2C increased per-plant yield without altering plant architecture or seed quality. These findings delineate the NopD-GmPP2C-ENOD93 regulatory module governing soybean nodulation and pinpoint GmPP2C as a compelling target for molecular breeding to enhance nitrogen-fixation efficiency and bolster crop yields.

title: A Chloroplast-Localized SlABCC21 Contributes to Plastid Development and Carotenoid Accumulation during Tomato Fruit Ripening.
authors: Tao, Xuan-Xi; Xiang, Lan-Ting; Zhu, Hong-Liang; Zhu, Ben-Zhong; Qu, Gui-Qin; Luo, Yun-Bo; Zhao, Xiao-Dan; Fu, Da-Qi
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Carotenoids accumulate massively as tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) fruit ripen, a process coupled to the transition of chloroplasts into chromoplasts, yet the membrane transporters that contribute to this plastid remodeling remain poorly understood. Here, we identify SlABCC21, a chloroplast-localized ATP-binding cassette subfamily C transporter that displays a uniquely ripening-associated expression pattern. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of SlABCC21 delayed fruit degreening and produced a mottled red-and-yellow phenotype. Transmission electron microscopy showed that the chloroplast-to-chromoplast transition was delayed in the slabcc21 mutants, with retained thylakoids and fewer plastoglobules. Loss of SlABCC21 redirected carotenoid flux from lycopene and beta-carotene toward xanthophylls and lowered endogenous free abscisic acid (ABA). These findings establish that plant ABCC transporters can act within plastid-associated metabolic networks and identify SlABCC21 as a target for engineering carotenoid composition and nutritional quality in tomato fruit.

title: A targeting delivery platform for the mapping of responses to p53-independent intervention in heterogeneous patient cancer cells.
authors: Qi, Li-Jin; Han, Di; Huang, Qi-Yang; Lei, Jin-Ju; Yang, Chao-Jie; Liao, Xin-Ru; Gao, Qing-Yu; Fu, Fei-Fei; Cheng, Si-Xue
abstract: Developing new cancer therapeutic strategies has become a central focus in precision oncology. However, a major challenge is the lack of robust models to accurately assess target vulnerability in patient-specific heterogeneous cancer cells, which limits the translation of research findings into effective clinical therapies. In this study, we developed an ex vivo blood-based model utilizing a versatile nano-delivery platform to evaluate the responsiveness of MDM2 knockout as a representative therapeutic approach in circulating malignant cells (CMCs) from patients stratified by their p53 status. In our genome editing plasmid delivery system (p@RPA), protamine sulfate was combined with a cell-penetrating peptide to condense the CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid into nano-cores. These nano-cores were then coated with chondroitin sulfate shells functionalized with the AS1411 aptamer, enabling the selective recognition of CD44 and/or nucleolin overexpressing malignant cells. Using the same vector, a molecular beacon delivery system (MBs@RPA) co-loaded with MB(MDM2) for probing MDM2 mRNA, MB(TP53) for probing TP53 mRNA and MB(TP73) for probing TP73 mRNA was constructed for the in situ evaluation of biomarker changes induced by genome editing. p@RPA demonstrates satisfactory efficacy in mediating gene editing for MDM2 knockout in malignant cells. Notably, the knockout of MDM2 induces cell cycle arrest and leads to a marked upregulation of anti-tumor TAp73 irrespective of their p53 status. With efficient gene editing and mRNA probing achieved in patient-derived CMCs, we establish an ex vivo platform capable of in situ therapeutic efficacy assessment at single-cell resolution to explicitly reveal the underlying cellular heterogeneity across individual CMCs.

title: Prediction of therapeutic targets and drug candidates for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by network-based computational framework.
authors: Lu, Jinyuan; Liang, Weishan; Liang, Yixue; Ren, Jiajia; Guo, Chengyang; Li, Xia; Pan, Jianquan; Zhang, Weidong; Tian, Saisai
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies, with limited therapeutic options and an urgent need for novel treatment strategies. This study presented a network-based computational framework for in silico genome-wide therapeutic target identification and drug discovery. METHODS: A network-based computational framework was developed that integrates transcriptomic data from multiple independent PDAC cohorts to construct gene co-expression networks. Prognostic gene signatures were incorporated to identify feature modules via hypergeometric enrichment analysis. Key regulatory genes within these modules were prioritized using multi-metric centrality analysis. Functional relevance of candidate targets was assessed using single-cell ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing, genome-wide clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) dependency datasets, and clinical survival analyses. To enable therapeutic translation, this study implemented a transcriptome-guided drug discovery strategy to systematically match pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)-specific gene expression signatures with compound-induced transcriptional profiles from the Library of Integrated Network-based Cellular Signatures (LINCS) database. Candidate compounds were ranked using a cross-cohort consensus scoring approach and subsequently evaluated in vitro using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), Western blotting, and cell viability assays. RESULTS: Comprehensive analysis of multi-cohort PDAC transcriptomic data identified 14 key genes with high network centrality, including three potential oncogenic drivers: Cytoskeleton associated protein 2 like (CKAP2L), kinesin family member 18A (KIF18A), and minichromosome maintenance 10 replication initiation factor (MCM10), which exhibited tumor-specific overexpression and poor prognostic associations. Single-cell RNA sequencing (ScRNA-seq) revealed their predominant expression in epithelial tumor cells, while CRISPR screening confirmed functional essentiality. The transcriptome-guided drug discovery approach matched these targets with LINCS perturbation profiles, identifying mitoxantrone/OTSSP167 (CKAP2L inhibitors), PF-3758309 (KIF18A inhibitors), and vorinostat (MCM10 inhibitors) as candidate therapeutics. Experimental validation using qRT-PCR, Western blotting, and cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assays collectively demonstrated the dose-dependent therapeutic effects of these compounds, showing significant mRNA suppression, corresponding decreases in protein levels, and potent anti-proliferative activity in PDAC cells. CONCLUSION: This study establishes a robust, network-based framework for therapeutic target discovery and transcriptome-driven drug prediction in PDAC. It identifies three novel, functionally essential oncogenic drivers and proposes clinically actionable compounds, offering a scalable approach for addressing undruggable targets in cancer therapy.

title: GESV: a bioinformatic pipeline for genome editing sequence variants analysis.
authors: Hu, Peiyao; Liu, Hao; Ye, Shangqi; Ma, Weihua; Zhang, Jianwei; Xie, Kabin
journal: Molecular breeding : new strategies in plant improvement
abstract: Rapid and accurate identification of sequence modifications is essential in genome editing, yet user-friendly bioinformatic tools for processing amplicon data remain limited. Inspired by amplicon-data processing strategies in microbiomics, we developed GESV (Genome-Edited Sequence Variants), a simple and flexible pipeline for the direct extraction of sequence variants from amplicon data of genome-edited organisms. Unlike conventional methods that adopt traditional single-nucleotide variant calling pipelines to analyze editing outcomes of genome-edited organisms, the GESV workflow directly extract sequence variants through the following core steps: merging paired-end reads, removing low-quality and short reads, dereplicating sequences to generate unique sequences with abundance, filtering out potential PCR/sequencing errors, and finally calling sequence modifications to profile edited sequence variants (ESVs). We demonstrate that this pipeline simplifies amplicon-based genotyping while maintaining high accuracy and flexibility. Both online and standalone versions of the GESV tool are available at http://crispr.hzau.edu.cn/gesv. Together, this study presents a novel and flexible data analysis pipeline for amplicon-based genotyping of gene-edited organisms, which will facilitate the application of gene editing in crop breeding. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-026-01736-8.

title: Engineering next-generation CAR-NK cells for hematological malignancies: genome editing, synthetic biology, and precision immunotherapy.
authors: Bahr, Ahmed Reda; Basem, Youssef; Alhejely, Amani; Alaa, Abdel Rahman; Abozeid, Saifallah Mabrouk; Basem, Amira; Khormi, Mohsen A; Abo-Zaid, Mabrouk A
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment by enabling engineered immune cells to selectively recognize and eliminate malignant targets, with CAR-T cells establishing the first major clinical success in this field. However, severe associated toxicities, logistical complexities of autologous manufacturing, and high rates of antigen-loss relapse have accelerated the development of alternative effector platforms such as CAR-NK cells. CAR-NK cells combine antigen-directed cytotoxicity with the innate antitumor functions of natural killer cells, offering a potentially safer and more readily available off-the-shelf therapeutic strategy. Nevertheless, the clinical efficacy of CAR-NK therapy is constrained by key biological and translational hurdles: brief in vivo persistence, inadequate trafficking and solid tumor infiltration, severe susceptibility to tumor microenvironment-mediated immunosuppression, and antigen escape driven by tumor heterogeneity. These biological constraints are compounded by technical bottlenecks, including cell source variability, limited large-scale expansion capacity, ex vivo functional exhaustion, and an absence of standardized manufacturing protocols. To address these multi-faceted barriers, recent advances in genome engineering, systems biology, and computational modeling provide promising routes forward. Given that prolonged exposure to immunosuppressive niches induces functional impairment, genome-editing strategies targeting inhibitory checkpoints and persistence programs are crucial; however, enhancing persistence requires stringent safeguards to mitigate toxicity risks from constitutive signaling or genomic instability. Thus, engineering next-generation CAR-NK cells necessitates balancing extended longevity, potent cytotoxicity, and safety. Multiomics approaches facilitate deeper characterization of CAR-NK functional states and tumor-immune interactions, whereas artificial intelligence-guided engineering integrates high-dimensional biological and manufacturing data to optimize receptor design, predict therapeutic performance, and accelerate translational workflows. Collectively, these innovations support a paradigm shift toward programmable CAR-NK cells that can dynamically sense, adapt, and respond to tumor evolution, driving the transition toward autonomous, highly scalable, and precisely controllable cellular immunotherapies in precision oncology.

title: Antiangiogenic Drug Testing Using Proangiogenic and Hypoxia Zebrafish Model.
authors: Vinoth, S; Santhakumar, Kirankumar
abstract: Zebrafish is an excellent in vivo model for high-throughput antiangiogenic drug testing, commonly known as the zebrafish angiogenesis assay. Conventional zebrafish angiogenesis assays are performed in wild-type zebrafish to evaluate the vascular changes in intersegmental and subintestinal vessel regions of the zebrafish larvae at 2 and 3 dpf stages, respectively. However, wild-type zebrafish larvae do not adequately mimic the hypoxia microenvironment and ectopic vessel branching characteristics of cancer. To overcome this limitation, we developed a genetically engineered zebrafish model with constitutive activation of the hypoxia signaling pathway by targeting the vhl, a tumor suppressor, by negative regulation of the hypoxia pathway, using CRISPR mutagenesis. This model exhibits robust ectopic blood vessel branching throughout the larval body, thereby recapitulating pathological angiogenesis. The utility of this zebrafish model system for drug screening was validated with the sorafenib treatment, a known antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Overall, this proangiogenic hypoxia zebrafish model provides a physiologically relevant platform for testing antiangiogenic drugs. Key features * Generate a vhl mutant zebrafish line with constitutive activation of the hypoxia signaling pathway using CRISPR-CAS9 mutagenesis. * The generated model exhibits extensive ectopic neovascular branching and abnormal vascular growth resembling pathological angiogenesis observed in solid tumors. * Mimics the chronic hypoxic microenvironment commonly associated with cancer progression and angiogenesis. * Provides an economical alternative to mammalian tumor models for early-stage antiangiogenic drug testing.

title: Knockout and re-expression system for mutant analysis in primary mouse T cells.
authors: Morfos, Vasileios; Frie, Meredith C; Peschkov, Daniel; Wagner, Juliana; Lillemeier, Bjorn F; Brzostek, Joanna
abstract: We describe here an efficient method for gene editing in mouse T cells, based on well-established, high-efficiency retroviral transduction protocols. Our platform allows analysis of mutant phenotypes in primary murine T cells in vitro and in vivo. This approach uses a single retroviral vector to simultaneously knockout an endogenous gene and ectopically express its mutant version. This knockout/re-expression vector can be used as the only plasmid to transduce Cas9-expressing T cells, or used together with a Cas9 retroviral vector to transduce T cells from any mouse strain. We validated the system for analysis of murine T cells by targeting key molecules in proximal T cell signaling, i.e. CD3gamma and Zap70. We obtain high knockout and re-expression efficiencies in both Cas9-expressing and non-Cas9 T cells. Knockout efficiencies can be further improved by gRNA multiplexing. Endogenous proteins compete with their ectopically expressed mutants or tagged versions for cellular location, protein interactions and cellular functions. Here, we quantified the incorporation of CD3gamma-GFP into surface T cell receptor (TCR) complexes. Our data shows that the knockout and re-expression platform improves integration of CD3gamma-GFP into the TCR. Therefore, eliminating competition between endogenous and ectopic proteins benefits analyses of protein assemblies and signaling pathways in primary T cells. Furthermore, we validated advantages of our system for mutant analysis using wild-type and mutant Zap70s. Zap70 mutants deficient in TCR binding or kinase activity show their phenotypes only in the absence of endogenous protein, further validating our knockout/re-expression approach. Most importantly, this system can be used to generate gene-edited primary T cells for in vivo studies, such as the quantification of anti-tumor responses. Our knockout and re-expression platform provides a useful gene editing tool for primary T cells in fundamental research and immunotherapy development.

title: Type IV-Dominated Plasmid-Encoded CRISPR-Cas Systems Are Enriched in Multireplicon and Multi-Stressor Resistance Plasmids Across the Global Plasmidome.
authors: de Souza, Hannay Crystynah Almeida; Dos Santos, Anamaria Mota Pereira; Almeida, Arlen Carvalho de Oliveira; Conte Junior, Carlos Adam; Panzenhagen, Pedro
abstract: Plasmids are central vectors of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). However, the features that distinguish the most epidemiologically successful resistance plasmids remain incompletely understood. CRISPR-Cas systems are classically regarded as barriers to horizontal gene transfer, which makes their occurrence within resistance plasmids yet unexplored at large scale. Here we analyzed 72,555 curated plasmid sequences from the Plasmid database (PLSDB) to test whether plasmid-encoded CRISPR-Cas systems are non-randomly associated with plasmid architecture and multi-stressor resistance across a large scale plasmidome. Using a three-tier classification of CRISPR-Cas system integrity based on array quality and Cas gene presence, we found that intact systems, defined by the co-occurrence of a high-confidence array and cas genes within the same replicon, were rare (1.03%) but strongly and specifically enriched in multireplicon plasmids (OR = 12.36) and in plasmids resistant to multiple stressor classes (MSR; OR = 6.25). These associations were robust to clonal redundancy: after dereplicating near-identical sequences over 100 iterations, both remained significant in every iteration, whereas the association with antimicrobial multidrug resistance (MDR) collapsed, identifying it as an artifact of clonal expansion. Intact systems were concentrated in high-risk IncF and IncH backbones and were more prevalent in plasmids from environmental sources than in those from clinical sources. Type IV-A was the predominant subtype (38.8% of intact systems), consistent with its near-exclusive association with mobile genetic elements and its proposed role in inter-plasmid competition rather than host defense. Together, these findings suggest that plasmid-encoded CRISPR-Cas systems, whether retaining defense-associated functions or acting as intra-MGE competition elements, are non-randomly retained in structurally complex, multi-stressor plasmid backbones that are particularly effective at accumulating and disseminating antimicrobial resistance.

title: "Illuminating" the silkworm chassis: Synthetic biology-driven evolution of genetic-based sexing circuits.
authors: Li, Chenyang; Cao, Mingjie; Li, Bing
abstract: The silkworm (Bombyx mori), a classical lepidopteran model, is evolving into a highly tractable synthetic biology chassis. In modern sericulture, genetic sexing circuits provide a rational design framework for efficient all-male rearing, effectively overcoming the gene dosage disruptions and fitness costs associated with traditional radiation-induced chromosomal translocations. This review systematically summarizes the construction strategies and industrial applications of these circuits. We outline the optimization of sex determination elements and highlight the advantages of far-red optical markers in penetrating host physical barriers and reducing cytotoxicity. Furthermore, we trace the evolution of genomic manipulation tools from random transposon insertions to targeted CRISPR/Cas9 integration into genomic safe harbors (GSHs). To address circuit instability during multigenerational rearing, protective molecular strategies-including boundary insulators, conditional expression, and automatic excision networks-are evaluated. We also explore the industrial interface that integrates standardized biological optical reporters with artificial intelligence and high-throughput optoelectronic sorting hardware. Ultimately, engineering principles derived from the silkworm chassis can provide a molecular framework for the sterile insect technique in global pest management, with future directions pointing toward footprint-free genome editing and dynamic conditional regulation.

title: Rapid resolution of a complex locus via CRISPR-mediated chromosome-walking knockout.
authors: Jin, Minghui; Shan, Yinxue; Peng, Yan; Zhang, Junzheng; Xiao, Yutao

title: Phenotype rescue through the restoration of full-length dystrophin using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing in Duchenne muscular dystrophy patient-derived iPSCs carrying the deletion of two exons.
authors: Rovina, Davide; Milasi, Sofia; Di Giuseppe, Giusy; Pioner, Jose Manuel; Langione, Marianna; Giammarino, Lucrezia; Ferrantini, Cecilia; Chiesa, Mattia; Canonico, Francesco; D'Amario, Domenico; Mercuri, Eugenio Maria; Pompilio, Giulio; Sommariva, Elena; Gowran, Aoife; Maione, Angela Serena
abstract: BACKGROUND: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a X-linked disease affecting skeletal and cardiac muscle and is caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene (DMD). Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) serve as reliable in vitro disease models. Their genetic correction by CRISPR/Cas9 allows the generation of isogenic controls and holds promises for gene therapy. However, restoring full-length dystrophin, especially when deletions involve multiple exons, constitutes a technological challenge. This study aimed to fully repair the dystrophin gene from a DMD iPSC line carrying the deletion of exons 49-50 and to characterize the rescue of the cardiac phenotype. METHODS: We developed an innovative CRISPR/Cas9-based approach involving the insertion of coding sequences of the deleted region, at the 3' of exon 48, thereby generating a single continuous coding sequence encompassing exons 48-49-50. Subsequently, iPSCs were differentiated into cardiomyocytes and cardiac fibroblasts. Cardiac phenotypes were analysed by western blot, immunofluorescence, ELISA, FACS, Ionoptix, 3D engineered heart tissue (EHT) and single-nuclei RNA-seq. RESULTS: The correction of a two-exons DMD gene deletion in Duchenne iPSCs, using CRISPR/Cas9, enabled the re-expression of a stable and functional full-length dystrophin in cardiomyocytes resulting in the rescue of cardiac pathological phenotypes. Edited cardiomyocytes showed improved morphology, reduced release of the cardiomyocytes damage marker troponin I, and decreased ROS production. Moreover, dystrophin restoration enhanced contractility and ameliorated the Ca(2+) kinetics. Notably, edited iPSC derived fibroblasts showed reduced pro-fibrotic stimuli response. In parallel, we also observed enhanced functioning of a 3D engineered heart tissue and profound change in the transcriptomic profile in both cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts after the re-expression of full-length dystrophin. CONCLUSIONS: We developed an innovative approach that enabled the re-expression of full-length dystrophin in a DMD iPSC line with consequent complete rescue of in vitro DMD cardiac phenotypes. On the long term, these results could lay a foundation for future applications of cell therapy or in vivo CRISPR/Cas9-based intervention to treat DMD.

title: A CRISPR-based 'dam-break drainage' sensing architecture for rapid, affordable and ultrasensitive pathogen detection.
authors: Liu, Kai; Li, Xiang; Zhao, Meng; Yang, Zhuo; Wen, Jingshuai; Liu, Jinpeng; Zhang, Haoli; Zhao, Yuecan; Sun, Yang; Li, Zhengping
abstract: Nucleic acid testing is important for infectious-disease diagnosis, but combining high sensitivity with accessible testing remains challenging. Here we show a chip-based visual detection strategy for one or two viral RNA targets that involves only sample loading, without further instrumentation or manual actuation. Target-activated CRISPR-Cas13a alters the wettability of a molecular barrier, causing liquid to cross a preset threshold and generate a dam-break drainage signal. The chip detects a single target at 10 aM within 2 min and two targets at 100 aM within 5 min, with costs of $0.20 and $0.30 per test, respectively. We further establish a practical clinical-sample workflow combining room-temperature lysis with RNase inhibition and validate the platform across 40 nasal-swab samples tested for SARS-CoV-2, influenza A virus and influenza B virus, with results concordant with RT-PCR. This threshold-based fluidic strategy provides a route towards rapid, low-cost and instrument-free molecular testing outside centralized laboratories.

title: Non-canonical function of SCIMP restricts JAK1 activity to counteract immune evasion in bladder cancer.
authors: You, Yongqiang; Zhang, Hui; Sun, Jiayin; Shuai, Yujun; Shi, Xin; Yuan, Ye; Hong, Sijia; Wang, Ning; Wang, Miao; Wang, Liang; Huang, Chao; Jiang, Guosong
abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite the fact that immunotherapy is reshaping the therapeutic landscape of bladder cancer, immune evasion remains a major obstacle to durable clinical benefit. Therefore, elucidating the mechanisms underlying immune resistance is essential for developing novel therapeutic strategies. METHODS: In this study, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in bladder cancer cells co-cultured with CD8(+) T cells and identified the SLP adaptor and CSK-interacting membrane protein (SCIMP) as a key gene that enhances CD8(+) T cell antitumor immunity. RESULTS: SCIMP serves as a favorable prognostic biomarker in patients with bladder cancer treated with immunotherapy. Mechanistically, SCIMP restricts JAK1 phosphorylation in an adaptor-independent manner, suppressing the IFN-gamma/JAK1/STAT5A/PD-L1 signaling axis. Meanwhile, YTHDF2 destabilizes the m6A-tagged SCIMP transcripts to reduce their expression. Remarkably, SCIMP synergizes with PD-1 blockade in suppressing tumor growth. CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unexplored non-canonical role of SCIMP in preventing immune evasion and provide a potential therapeutic target for bladder cancer.

title: Enhanced Plasmin Generation Due to PAI-1 Deficiency Impairs Regulated Vascular Endothelial Cell Motility.
authors: Sano, Hideto; Ito, Masahiko; Suzuki, Tetsuro; Urano, Tetsumei; Suzuki, Yuko
journal: Journal of thrombosis and haemostasis : JTH
abstract: BACKGROUND: Plasminogen activator (PA) inhibitor (PAI)-1 plays crucial roles in the plasminogen activation system and fibrinolysis. Congenital PAI-1 deficiency in humans is characterized by severe bleeding and delayed wound healing, indicating dysregulated plasmin activity. However, how PAI-1 controls pericellular plasmin generation and endothelial cell (EC) behavior remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To elucidate the specific effects of enhanced plasmin generation caused by PAI-1 deficiency on human ECs. METHODS: PAI-1-deficient human ECs (PAIKO-ECs) were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 and compared with wild-type ECs. The effects of enhanced pericellular plasmin generation caused by PAI-1 deficiency on endothelial cell migration and angiogenic tube formation were evaluated, and transcriptome analyses were performed to investigate the molecular mechanism. RESULTS: PAIKO-ECs showed markedly increased plasmin generation compared to wild type ECs. They exhibited increased overall uncoordinated motility with multidirectional migration trajectories and impaired directional wound closure, while cell proliferation remained unaffected. This aberrant migratory phenotype was reversed by aprotinin, recombinant PAI-1, or the lysine analog epsilon-aminocaproic acid (EACA). EACA notably reduced plasminogen accumulation on the cell surface while preserving fluid-phase plasmin generation, suggesting enhanced EC motility is driven by pericellular rather than fluid-phase plasmin activity. In tube formation assays, PAIKO-ECs displayed increased extremities and branches, which was normalized by EACA or aprotinin. Transcriptome analyses revealed differential gene expression related to fibrinolysis, angiogenesis, and endothelial-mesenchymal transition. CONCLUSIONS: Pericellular plasmin activity is essential for EC motility and angiogenic behavior under PAI-1-deficient conditions, highlighting the importance of spatially regulated plasmin activity in vascular remodeling.

title: Functional double-emulsion droplets enable multiplexed CRISPR quantification of cancer-related miRNAs.
authors: Zhang, Yang; Deng, Fei; Sang, Rui; Liu, Ling; Barber, Tracie J; Goldys, Ewa M; Li, Ming
abstract: Accurate, multiplexed microRNA detection is critical for early cancer diagnosis. We present a droplet-based digital CRISPR/Cas13a platform for simultaneous, amplification-free detection of multiple miRNAs. By integrating double emulsion (DE) microfluidics with programmable crRNAs, the system achieves orthogonal, interference-free readouts, enabling precise absolute quantification in complex biological samples. The assay demonstrates high sequence specificity, robust orthogonality, and consistent performance across target combinations and matrices. Fluorescence-positive droplet counts correlate linearly with input concentrations, allowing quantification of miRNA-21, miRNA-29a, and miRNA-92a with 10 copies/muL representing the lowest concentration experimentally evaluated in this study. The applicability of the platform is further evaluated in a small proof-of-concept cohort of plasma samples from healthy controls and colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. This platform provides an amplification-free approach for multiplexed miRNA quantification and supports further development for clinical biomarker analysis.

title: Two paralogous seed protein trait-associated genes influence light and phytohormone signaling, maturity, and seed storage in soybean.
authors: Quach, Truyen; Nguyen, Hanh; Meyer, Olivia; Sato, Shirley; Yang, Weilong; Kumar, Vikranth; McDaniel, Lauren; Hancock, C Nathan; Parrott, Wayne; Stacey, Minviluz Bing; Hudson, Matthew E; Diers, Brian W; Butler, Nathaniel M; Cahoon, Edgar B; Clemente, Tom Elmo; Zhang, Chi; Guo, Ming
abstract: The soybean gene Glyma.20G085100 (Gm20P), contributing to the cqSeed protein-003 QTL, and its paralog Glyma.10G134400 (Gm10P), were edited using the CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing reagents. Two mutants, a gm20p single mutant and a gm10p gm20p double mutant devoid of editing reagents, were identified. Additional gm10p and gm20p single mutants were isolated from F2 population of the cross between the gm10p gm20p double mutant and the wild-type Thorne. The above mutants were characterized in different growing conditions. Seed protein content of the gm10p single and the gm10p gm20p double mutant were significantly reduced relative to the gm20p single mutant and Thorne, with a concomitant increase in oil and starch content. A delayed maturity phenotype was observed in the gm20p single, the gm10p single, and gm10p gm20p double mutants under field conditions across multiple environments. Under controlled conditions in a growth chamber, prominent delayed maturity was only observed under short-day conditions, while long-day conditions induced phenotypic changes in growth in the gm10p gm20p double mutant, but slight delay in maturity. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the gm10p gm20p double mutant exhibited repression of genes involved in light signaling, enhanced expression of JAZs in JA signaling, suppression of ABA-responsive and senescence-related genes, and elevation of genes that inhibit IAA signaling. Furthermore, the gm10p gm20p double mutant displayed higher sensitivity to salt and ABA during germination. Collectively, these results suggest that both Gm10P and Gm20P modulate light signaling and impact soybean development, maturity and seed reserve content.

title: CDH1 loss remodels gene expression and lineage identity in human mammary epithelial cells.
authors: Musick, Maggie; Ufondu, Chinasa A; Rowland, Carmen E; Brown, Micaela E; Sottnik, Joseph L; Shackleford, Madeleine T; Nesiba, Camryn S; Danis, Etienne P; Goodspeed, Andrew E; Zera, Richard; Johnson, Arthur T; Schwertfeger, Kathryn L; Nelson, Andrew C; Ostrander, Julie H; Sikora, Matthew J
abstract: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) is a common subtype of breast cancer, molecularly defined by genetic loss of CDH1, and subsequent loss of cell adhesion protein E-cadherin, in ~95% of ILC. Though CDH1 loss occurs early in ILC oncogenesis, it is unclear how this facilitates transformation. We modeled early CDH1 loss using "normal" human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC), i.e., finite lifespan cells reflecting early hyperplasia, and targeted E-cadherin signaling using antibodies versus causing genetic CDH1 loss using siRNA or CRISPR/Cas9-knockout. Transcriptome analysis across four HMEC models showed that the mode of E-cadherin targeting is critical for the subsequent phenotype. Antibody-mediated inhibition of cell-cell contacts induced gene signatures of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), consistent with the role of E-cadherin suppression during the EMT process. Conversely, genetic CDH1 loss - as in ILC oncogenesis - repressed EMT signatures, and instead remodeled gene expression toward a luminal epithelial phenotype. RNA-seq, single cell transcriptomics, flow cytometry, microscopy, and ATAC-seq analyses support that CDH1 loss induces lineage remodeling to a luminal state, which is mirrored in transcriptomic analysis of clinical ILC precursor lesions. By isolating luminal versus basal cells prior to CDH1 knockout, we found that CDH1 loss led to remodeling of lineage identity in both populations, converging on a new lineage homeostasis with a luminal progenitor-like phenotype. Consistent with the shift to a luminal progenitor phenotype, CDH1 loss enhanced proliferative capacity over the finite lifespan of the HMECs, highlighting a feature of early CDH1 loss that may contribute to clonal advantage during tumor initiation. Moreover, CDH1 loss enhanced anoikis resistance, a defining feature of ILC cells. Our findings support that genetic loss of CDH1 in mammary epithelial cells induces transcriptional and phenotypic changes consistent with lineage identity remodeling toward a luminal progenitor-like state, which may underpin the mechanism by which early CDH1 loss mediates ILC oncogenesis.

title: Heterogeneous contributions of APOBEC3 deaminases to substitution and indel mutagenesis in lung adenocarcinoma.
authors: Striepen, Josefine; Culibrk, Luka; Dananberg, Alexandra; Rozowsky, Jacob S; Petljak, Mia; Maciejowski, John
abstract: APOBEC3 cytosine deaminases are major sources of cancer mutations. In lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), APOBEC3 activity drives tumor evolution and therapy resistance, nominating these enzymes as therapeutic targets. Although APOBEC3A drives most APOBEC3-associated mutational signature burden across cancers, the relative contributions of individual paralogs in LUAD remain unclear. Here, we define the roles of endogenously misregulated APOBEC3 deaminases using CRISPR-Cas9 knockouts and whole-genome sequencing of 197 long-term propagated single-cell clones. APOBEC3 mutagenesis falls into three patterns, driven predominantly by APOBEC3A, by both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B, or minimal despite detectable enzyme expression. Commonly used surrogate measures, including mRNA and protein levels and in vitro deaminase activity, do not predict these contributions. We also provide the first causal evidence that endogenous APOBEC3A generates the indel signature InD9a, linking it to uracil excision following cytosine deamination. These heterogeneous contributions highlight the need for biomarkers that resolve individual APOBEC3 activities to guide therapeutic targeting.

title: Advances in Diagnostic Technologies of Major Avian Respiratory Viruses: A Review.
authors: Hu, Zhiqiang; Hailai, Ase; He, Huiling; Yang, Chaoyun; Chen, Yiqun; Huang, Zengwen; Li, Xinhong; Xu, Shangen; Guan, Ran
abstract: Avian respiratory diseases, particularly those induced by the avian influenza virus (AIV), Newcastle disease virus (NDV), infectious bronchitis virus (IBV), and infectious laryngotracheitis virus (ILTV), represent a substantial economic threat to the global poultry industry. Several of these viruses can also transmit across species, posing risks to public health security. Given the challenges posed by similar clinical symptoms from different pathogens, the prevalence of co-infections, and rapid viral mutations, rapid, precise, and highly sensitive diagnostic techniques are imperative for effective disease prevention and control, epidemic surveillance, and epidemiological research. This review provides an overview of molecular and immunological diagnostic techniques for major avian respiratory viruses. All covered technologies are evaluated and compared across key performance metrics: target type, analytical sensitivity, multiplex capacity, turnaround time, point-of-care diagnostic techniques (POCT) suitability and application scenarios. Specifically, the review details real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) and its multiplex formats, isothermal amplification methods including loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), recombinase-aided amplification (RAA) and recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA), and innovative CRISPR-Cas-based nucleic acid detection systems. It also examines high-throughput sequencing, microarray technologies, and advanced immunological assays enhanced by nanomaterials, recombinant proteins, and single-domain antibodies. The review further discusses integrated, automated, and portable diagnostic platforms, including microfluidics, and smartphone-assisted systems. Finally, the review outlines future trends in avian diagnostic technologies, providing a practical reference for building more efficient and accessible avian disease surveillance and early warning systems.

title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Genome-Wide CRISPR-Cas Screens to Identify Host Factors Involved in HIV-1 Infection.
authors: Zhu, Min; Sun, Zhou; Xu, Ke; Ye, Ling
abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) replication depends on a complex interplay between viral proteins and host cellular factors, which represent promising therapeutic targets. However, systematic integration of results from genome-wide CRISPR screens for HIV host factors remains limited. Here, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens to identify host dependency, restriction, and latency-promoting factors in HIV-1 infection. Following PRISMA guidelines, we identified 11 eligible studies from which we extracted 26 gene lists. These were classified into three phenotypic categories, including dependency (5 lists), restriction (10 lists), and latency-promoting (7 lists), and integrated using meta-analysis by information content (MAIC). GO over-representation analysis and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis were performed on MAIC-ranked gene lists to characterize pathway architectures. MAIC successfully recovered well-established host factors, including the entry receptors CD4, CCR5, and CXCR4; the integration cofactor PSIP1 (LEDGF/p75); and the restriction factors TRIM5, TRIM22, PML, G3BP1, and EIF2AK2. RNF114 emerged as the top-ranked restriction factor, supported by four independent publication-level categories. Additional high-confidence hits included TRIM56, BIRC3, DTX3L, and components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system across the dependency and latency datasets, further supporting the robustness of the MAIC framework. Beyond these canonical factors, we identified multiple undercharacterized genes and pathways, including coagulation and IL-17 signaling in dependency factors, SUMOylation and DNA damage response in restriction factors, and the Integrator complex and proteasome-granule co-enrichment in latency-promoting factors. Leading-edge analysis confirmed that most of these non-canonical enrichments are driven by coherent gene modules rather than a small set of pleiotropic hubs.
