These findings reveal distinct pathway architectures across the three infection states and highlight previously unrecognized host processes that may serve as targets for antiviral therapy. Our analysis provides a comprehensive resource for guiding future mechanistic studies of host-HIV interactions and developing strategies to enhance immunity, block viral replication, and reverse latency.

title: Assessment of TLR3-TRIF-NF-kappaB Innate Immune Signaling Pathway Induced by Newcastle Disease Virus and Construction of TLR3-Deficient BHK-21 Cells.
authors: Dong, Bingmei; Cai, Jing; Zhao, Haiqi; Gao, Pengyan; Xu, Qingqing; Meng, Weiqin; Tang, Na
abstract: The innate immune system plays a significant role in inhibiting viral infection and proliferation. To explore the signaling pathway of the innate immune response induced by Newcastle disease virus (NDV) in BHK-21 cells, the mRNA expression levels of pattern recognition receptors such as TLR3, TLR7, TLR8, and NOD2, as well as those of cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-1beta, IL-10, IL-17, TRIF, TRAF3, and NF-kappaB were determined by transcriptome sequencing, qRT-PCR, and ELISA. All these results indicated that the NDV LaSota strain primarily induces the TLR3-TRIF-NF-kappaB signaling pathway in BHK-21 cells. Subsequently, an NF-kappaB inhibitor, a TLR3 inhibitor, and a TRAF3 inhibitor were separately used, and the viral titer was measured during the NDV LaSota strain infection of BHK-21 cells. The results displayed that the inhibition of TLR3 or NF-kappaB effectively increased the viral titer of NDV. Hence, the CRISPR/Cas9 system was used to create a BHK-TLR3(-) cell clone in which TLR3 was knocked out, and the cells were assessed for morphology, cell density, cell viability, and genetic stability. Finally, the cells were infected with the NDV LaSota strain. The results showed that the BHK-TLR3(-) cell line is a stable cell line with markedly enhanced NDV LaSota strain production. Furthermore, the knockout of the TLR3 gene significantly inhibited the expression of IFN-alpha, IFN-beta, IL-1beta, and TNF-alpha, especially that of IL-1beta and TNF-alpha. In summary, the present research revealed the main signaling pathway of the innate immune response induced by the NDV LaSota strain and provides a promising basis for NDV production.

title: CRISPR/Cas12a-Based Aptasensor for Cas9 Protein Detection in Spiked Food Matrices.
authors: Wang, Zizhao; Wang, Jing; Li, Ling; Chen, Guofeng; Wen, Hongtao; Liu, Baohai; Dong, Yiyang
abstract: Residual gene editors are a concern associated with the widespread application of CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Here, we developed a CRISPR/Cas12a-based fluorescent aptasensor for the qualitative and quantitative detection of Cas9 protein. Secondary structure prediction and molecular docking were combined to identify potential binding sites of the Cas9-specific aptamer. A fluorescence aptasensor was constructed based on competitive binding: in the presence of Cas9, the aptamer binds to the target and releases complementary DNA (cDNA), which activates the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a. Cas12a subsequently cleaves a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) reporter labeled with a fluorophore and a quencher, generating a fluorescence signal, expressed in relative fluorescence units (RFU), that increases with Cas9 concentration. The optimized conditions comprised a trans-cleavage reaction time of 20 min, a Cas12a:CRISPR RNA (crRNA) molar ratio of 1:1, a final aptamer concentration of 180 nM, and a combination of low- and high-salt buffers to balance molecular recognition and protein stability. The proposed assay enabled Cas9 protein detection in buffer and Cas9-spiked soybean milk and cereal matrices. These results represent a proof-of-concept evaluation in complex food matrices rather than validation of authentic residual Cas9 detection. Further studies using unspiked gene-edited samples with independently verified Cas9 residues and an orthogonal reference method are required.

title: A Review of Recombinase-Aided Amplification (RAA) in Veterinary Medicine.
authors: Li, Shaomei; Gao, Jieqi; Miao, Yongqiang; Chen, Qianlin; Mu, Hao; Zheng, Hua; Zhang, Yifan; Zhou, Jie; Huang, Chunhua; Li, Mingwen; Yu, Yuandi; Yang, Liu
abstract: Rapid and accurate pathogen detection is crucial to mitigating the significant economic impacts of infectious animal diseases. Recombinase-aided amplification (RAA) has emerged as a highly promising isothermal diagnostic tool, characterized by its rapid turnaround time, robust amplification efficiency, and single-copy analytical sensitivity. In veterinary diagnostics, RAA has evolved from single-pathogen proof-of-concept assays to become a promising technology for point-of-care scenarios. This review critically evaluates the integration of RAA with real-time fluorescence, CRISPR-Cas systems, lateral flow dipsticks (LFDs), and suspension microarray technologies, highlighting their impact on assay sensitivity and point-of-care (POC) applicability. Despite recent advancements, including encouraging progress in multiplexing and expanded applications in companion animal medicine, inherent challenges such as matrix effects in crude clinical samples, aerosol contamination risks, and commercialization barriers remain. By benchmarking RAA against traditional molecular methods and structurally similar technologies like recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA), this review outlines future trajectories for optimizing RAA platforms, aiming to maximize their utility in routine veterinary surveillance and epidemiological control.

title: Enhanced Scytonemin Biosynthesis in Engineered Nostoc flagelliforme with ScyR Overexpression and Cultivation Optimization.
authors: Xie, Hao; Zhang, Yue; Yuan, Xiaolong; Xia, Wanxia; Gao, Xiang
abstract: Scytonemin, a lipid-soluble indole-alkaloid pigment unique to cyanobacteria, is a bioactive small molecule with UV-shielding, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory activities. Nostoc flagelliforme represents a promising strain for scytonemin biosynthesis, yet engineering to boost its yield remains challenging. Two genes encoding a histidine kinase (COO91_00772) and a response regulator (COO91_00771, ScyR) putatively constitute a two-component regulatory system governing the UV-induced biosynthesis of scytonemin. Here, we employed CRISPR/Cpf1 technology to achieve the insertion of an additional ScyR expression cassette into the N. flagelliforme genome and evaluated its effect on scytonemin yield. The engineered strain was designated Nf-psbA-ScyR, in which the ScyR gene was expressed under the PpsbA promoter. This strain exhibited a markedly enhanced accumulation of scytonemin, reaching 4.6 mg g(-1) dry weight under UV-B radiation after 15-day cultivation with exogenous tryptophan supplementation, representing a 1.9-fold increase compared with the MAAs-deficient (Nf-MAAs-D) strain. Upon transition from indoor UV-B exposure to outdoor solar radiation, scytonemin production further increased to 5.4 mg g(-1) dry weight. These findings indicate that the ScyR regulator can highly promote scytonemin biosynthesis under UV induction, providing an engineering strategy for the exploitation of N. flagelliforme.

title: Surveillance, Detection and Therapeutic Innovation in Antimicrobial Resistance in the Age of Polycrisis: From Genomic and Digital Innovation to One Health Integration.
authors: Branda, Francesco; Maria, Francesco De; Alexiev, Ivailo; Demir, Ayse Banu; Limon, Onder; Ceccarelli, Giancarlo; Scarpa, Fabio; Russo, Alessandro; Spoto, Silvia; Ciccozzi, Massimo
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance is increasingly strained by interconnected global crises, i.e., pandemics, climate change, armed conflicts, population mobility, and health inequalities, that disrupt healthcare delivery, diagnostic capacity, and laboratory infrastructure. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, whole-genome sequencing, metagenomics, and digital surveillance offer the potential to shift from reactive reporting to predictive intelligence that anticipates resistance threats, although current implementations remain sector-specific, retrospective, and project-funded. Environmental surveillance, particularly wastewater monitoring coupled with genomic epidemiology, provides early warnings at population and ecosystem levels. The future integration of AI across human, animal, and environmental sectors could enable unified One Health intelligence; no such integrated platform is currently operational. This review focuses primarily on bacterial AMR. It examines how global drivers strain surveillance, how genomic, metagenomic, digital, and AI-enabled technologies reshape AMR detection and prediction, and the emerging non-antibiotic therapeutic landscape, including bacteriophage therapy, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-based antimicrobials, antimicrobial peptides, microbiota-directed interventions, nanomedicine, host-directed therapies, photodynamic therapy, and vaccines. It then explores how these innovations can be integrated within a One Health framework to support coordinated global preparedness. Addressing the AMR crisis will require not only technological innovation but also equitable implementation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and resilient systems.

title: Genomic Characterization of the Probiotic Limosilactobacillus mucosae CRL2069 Isolated from Feedlot Cattle Feces.
authors: Aristimuno Ficoseco, Cecilia M; Carrasco, Natalia; Montemurro, Marco; Chieffi, Daniele; Fadda, Silvina G; Nader-Macias, Maria E F; Fusco, Vincenzina; Vignolo, Graciela M; Fanelli, Francesca
abstract: Limosilactobacillus mucosae (L.) CRL2069, isolated from feedlot cattle feces, has previously exhibited high performance when used as a probiotic in animals. To investigate the genetic bases underlying its probiotic potential, complete genome sequencing and comparative analyses were performed. The CRL2069 genome showed a total length of 1.93 Mb, with an average GC content of 46.76%. No evidence of plasmid sequences was detected, while CRISPR-Cas elements, as well as twelve genomic islands, were identified in the genome. Pan-genomic and clustering analysis among L. mucosae strains showed a lack of partitioning according to their isolation origin, revealing a niche specialization. CRL2069 genes related to stress and those conferring probiotic character were identified. In addition, the absence of acquired antimicrobial resistance genes and virulence determinants evidenced the safety of this strain. Genomic determinants conferring the ability to metabolize a diverse array of carbohydrates, particularly those present in cattle feed, were annotated. Phenotypic analysis supported the genomic prediction and demonstrated the capacity of CRL2069 to metabolize 39 out of 95 carbon sources tested and to produce folate. Based on the results obtained, L. mucosae CRL2069 evaluated in this study is confirmed to be a promising candidate for use as a probiotic in cattle.

title: H3 Subtype Avian Influenza Virus: Ecology, Cross-Species Evolution, and Public Health Threats.
authors: Cheng, Kaihui; Yu, Zhijun
abstract: H3 subtype avian influenza virus (AIV) is one of the most widely distributed and frequently detected low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (LPAIVs) in wild birds and poultry worldwide. Wild waterfowl are the natural reservoir of this virus. In recent years, driven by frequent genetic reassortment and continuous evolution, H3 subtype AIV has expanded its host range to include various mammalian species-dogs, cats, horses, seals, pigs (experimental infection), and humans. Among these, the H3N8 subtype shows the broadest cross-species transmissibility, having established sustained transmission lineages in horses and dogs, while also causing sporadic infections in seals and humans. Avian-origin H3N2 canine influenza virus has circulated stably in dog populations across Asia and North America for nearly two decades. Between 2022 and 2023, China reported three human cases of H3N8 subtype AIV infection, one of which was fatal (Guangdong, March 2023), indicating that this virus poses a potential zoonotic transmission risk. Novel triple-reassortant strains, including genotype G25 of H3N8 and H3N3, first detected in chicken flocks in late 2022, have continued to emerge. Their HA genes originate from H3 subtype viruses of wild bird or chicken origin, whereas their internal gene segments are predominantly acquired from H9N2 subtype AIV, resulting in enhanced mammalian adaptability. This review summarizes the global epidemiology of H3 subtype AIV (covering wild birds, poultry, and live poultry markets), its genetic evolution and reassortment patterns, and the molecular mechanisms underlying cross-species transmission. This review particularly highlights the regulatory roles of key amino acid mutations-such as PB2-D701N, M1-M192V, and HA-Q226L/G228S-in receptor binding preference, polymerase activity, and pathogenicity. This review also summarizes recent advances in detection techniques (multiplex RT-PCR, quantum dot-based immunochromatographic strips, RT-RAA, and CRISPR-Cas13a) and vaccine development (inactivated, adenovirus-vectored, and mRNA vaccines). Key prevention and control challenges-including covert circulation, surveillance gaps, and limited subtyping diagnostic capacity at primary laboratories-are also discussed. This review proposes that H3 subtype AIV should be recognized as a potential zoonotic threat warranting continued surveillance, although no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission has been documented to date. Better understanding of cross-species mechanisms, stronger surveillance and early warning, and evidence-based control strategies are needed to inform future risk assessment.

title: Probiotic Characteristics and Whole-Genome Profiling of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum V2 Isolated from Tibetan Plateau Traditional Yogurt.
authors: Zhang, Lanxin; Chen, Man; Wen, Zhaohai; Li, Junmei; Chen, Binghao; Ju, Xianghong; Ma, Yi; Yong, Yanhong; Ma, Xinbin; Yan, Shuping; Li, Youquan
abstract: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum V2 is a probiotic strain isolated from yogurt by Tibetan Plateau herdsmen in China. In this study, we systematically evaluated the probiotic potential and genome-wide features of L. plantarum V2. The cell-free supernatants (CFSs) of strain V2 exhibited broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against at least 13 species of pathogenic bacteria. Moreover, L. plantarum V2 showed excellent gastrointestinal tract adaptability: it maintained a survival rate of 83.02 +/- 1.64% at pH 3.0 an retained a survival rate of 20.34 +/- 0.48% after 24 h exposure to 0.3% bile salts. Strain V2 adhered to Caco-2 cells with an efficiency of 1.83 +/- 0.54%. It displayed non-hemolytic activity, was susceptible to clinically relevant broad-spectrum antibiotics, and harbored no transferable antimicrobial resistance genes. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) analysis revealed that strain V2 possesses one circular chromosome and one linear plasmid, which collectively encode 3,041 coding sequences (CDSs), 16 rRNA genes, 71 tRNA genes, 12 CRISPR arrays, and a complete prophage region. Key functional genetic elements of strain V2 include five gene clusters encoding broad-spectrum antimicrobial peptides, six regions associated with environmental adaptability, 129 carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) genes, and one specialized metabolic cluster. Functional annotation further highlighted enriched pathways involved in transcriptional regulation, as well as the transport and metabolism of carbohydrates and amino acids. Collectively, our in vitro data demonstrate that L. plantarum V2 exhibits favorable acid and bile tolerance, potent bacteriostatic activity, and genomic safety, making it a promising candidate for applications in the livestock breeding and feed industries.

title: SaCas9-Mediated CrtYB Disruption Coupled with Heterologous alpha-Bisabolol Production in Rhodotorula mucilaginosa JY1105.
authors: Sun, Wenyi; Liu, Haoyang; Dong, Yaqi; Li, Haoyu; Wang, Yanan; Cai, Qian
abstract: Rhodotorula mucilaginosa is a promising host for terpene biosynthesis, but its rational engineering remains constrained by limited genome-editing tools. Here, we developed a Staphylococcus aureus Cas9 (SaCas9) workflow in R. mucilaginosa JY1105 for CrtYB disruption and demonstrated heterologous alpha-bisabolol production. Five sgRNAs targeted CrtYB, encoding bifunctional phytoene synthase/lycopene cyclase; its disruption provided visible depigmentation for preliminary screening. Among 25 sequenced transformants per guide, CrtYB3 and CrtYB5 yielded 10 (40%) and 4 (16%) white colonies, respectively; each white colony carried an on-target deletion of 11-26 bp, whereas all red colonies retained the wild-type target sequence. No white colonies or target-site deletions were detected for CrtYB1, CrtYB2, or CrtYB4. A codon-optimized chamomile TPS1 cassette encoding alpha-bisabolol synthase was integrated by random integration into wild-type JY1105 and the edited R1-DeltaCrtYB derivative. The selected highest producers produced 37.52 +/- 3.09 and 41.45 +/- 2.08 mg L(-1) alpha-bisabolol, respectively. To our knowledge, this is the first report of heterologous alpha-bisabolol production in R. mucilaginosa. This study demonstrates the potential of R. mucilaginosa as an editable chassis for heterologous sesquiterpene biosynthesis and provides a foundation for further development of SaCas9-assisted metabolic engineering in this non-conventional yeast.

title: Integrated Multi-Omics Analyses Identify Core Determinants Governing Newcastle Disease Virus Oncolytic Therapy Efficacy Under Tumor Heterogeneity.
authors: Feng, Shufeng; Zhu, Yongxin; Cui, Lu; Yang, Hongchun; Duan, Huimin; Li, Xuefeng; Li, Hai; Ou, Changbo
abstract: Newcastle disease virus (NDV) is a promising oncolytic virus, but tumor heterogeneity constrains its clinical translation. The key determinants driving variable NDV oncolytic potency amid tumor heterogeneity remain incompletely elucidated. The main scope of this study included analyzing 22 human cancer cell lines representing 11 tumor types and identifying five gene co-expression modules associated with NDV susceptibility through weighted gene co-expression network analysis. Integrative multi-omics analyses of NDV-infected HCT116 cells, the least-susceptible cell line in our panel, predicted metabolic processes, innate immune defenses, and multiple forms of cell death as candidate pathways modulating NDV oncolytic efficacy. These key bioinformatic findings were further validated by genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening, which uncovered POLR2G and SREBF1 as central components of the pro-oncolytic network and TNFRSF1A, TNFAIP3, and CASP9 as core mediators of the anti-oncolytic network. Their functional roles were further verified via genetic manipulation and pharmacological perturbation of JAK-STAT, TLR4, and apoptotic signaling. In conclusion, our findings support a bidirectional model wherein host metabolic programs promote NDV replication and oncolysis, whereas antiviral-innate immune signaling restricts them, providing candidate targets for host-directed combination therapy amid tumor heterogeneity.

title: Regulatory Pathways of Endophytic Fungi in Promoting Flavonoid Biosynthesis in Medicinal Plants.
authors: Gao, Yuan; Dong, Haonan; Fang, Zesen; Liu, Silin; Xu, Yan; Guo, Yuyang; Yang, Yang; Luo, Jianghan; Yan, Lijun
abstract: Endophytic fungi form complex symbiotic associations with medicinal plants via long-term coevolution. Such cross-kingdom interactions substantially modulate flavonoid biosynthesis in host plants. This review dissects the mechanisms through which endophytic fungi elevate flavonoid accumulation in medicinal plants. We first summarize symbiotic and growth-promoting relationships between endophytic fungi and medicinal plants, outlining four core synergistic functions: nutrient supply, phytohormone homeostasis, stress resistance enhancement, and secondary metabolism activation. We then elaborate on three primary regulatory patterns underlying endophyte-modulated flavonoid biosynthesis, including direct activation of plant flavonoid biosynthetic pathways, indirect regulation via stress mitigation and host metabolic reprogramming, and autonomous flavonoid production by endophytic fungi. Notably, most current evidence for autonomous flavonoid biosynthesis by endophytic fungi is derived from axenic cultures, whereas its occurrence and quantitative contribution within colonized plant tissues remain to be established. We further discuss state-of-the-art technologies for untangling plant-fungus symbiotic interactions, including multi-omics integration, spatial metabolomics, single-cell sequencing, synthetic microbial consortia, and CRISPR-Cas genome editing. Lastly, we propose future research perspectives covering green cultivation of medicinal plants, targeted improvement of medicinal quality, and efficient microbial biosynthesis of flavonoids.

title: Pathophysiology and Comprehensive Pharmacological Management of ATTR Cardiac Amyloidosis: Knowledge Gaps, Ongoing Clinical Trials, and Future Research Directions.
authors: Bains, Sareen; Atwal, Harry; Sidhu, Ashbir; Singh, Harpreet; Sodhi, Gurpreet
abstract: The purpose of this review article is to discuss the current treatment modalities and ongoing clinical trials regarding cardiac amyloidosis (CA), specifically transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA). Amyloidosis refers to the extracellular deposition of insoluble amyloid fibrillar proteins. When these proteins are deposited in the heart's myocardium, it is referred to as cardiac amyloidosis. CA can be divided into two main groups: light chain cardiac amyloidosis (AL-CA) and transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA), which can be further subdivided into wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRwt) and hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv). ATTR-CA is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure in the setting of progressive restrictive cardiomyopathy, particularly among older adults, males, and individuals of African descent, with remarkable advances in the therapeutic landscape. TTR stabilizers, including Tafamidis (approved in 2019) and Acoramidis (approved in 2024), have demonstrated significant reductions in mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations. Gene silencing therapies, including Vutrisiran (approved in 2025), represent a new drug group that targets TTR production at the RNA level. Meanwhile, CRISPR-based gene editing with nexiguran ziclumeran (nex-z or NTLA-2001) and amyloid-depleting monoclonal antibodies offer the prospect of one-time curative treatments and active fibril clearance, respectively. However, despite these advances, substantial knowledge gaps persist: no head-to-head trials have compared stabilizers to silencers, optimal combination therapy regimens remain undefined, and the role of conventional guideline-directed medical therapy in ATTR-CA has only been supported by observational data.

title: Integrated Molecular and Physiological Mechanisms Underlying Rice Adaptation to Heat, Salinity, and Drought Stress.
authors: Khan, Atika; Mas-Ud, Md Atik; Ahmad, Shahab; Ullah, Shafi; Matin, Mohammad Nurul
abstract: Rice faces increasing threats from climate change, driven by heat, salinity, and drought stresses. Although researchers have extensively studied individual stresses, growing evidence indicates that combined stresses elicit unique physiological, biochemical, and molecular responses that single-stress studies cannot predict. This review comprehensively synthesizes current knowledge of the integrated signaling networks and adaptive mechanisms underlying rice responses to heat, salinity, and drought stress, with particular emphasis on stress crosstalk and multi-stress responses. We examine the roles of mechanosensitive ion channels, calcium signaling, salt overly sensitive (SOS) pathway, heat shock response regulators, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades, and ABA-dependent and -independent signaling networks in stress tolerance systems. Furthermore, we discuss major adaptive responses involving reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis, osmoprotectant accumulation, antioxidant defense systems, and phytohormone crosstalk involving abscisic acid, auxin, salicylic acid, cytokinin, brassinosteroids, ethylene, and gibberellins. Particular attention is given to the detrimental effects of combined stresses on growth, development, and yield. In addition, recent advances in enhancing stress tolerance through CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing, marker-assisted breeding, and molecular marker technologies are also highlighted. Despite significant progress, critical knowledge gaps remain regarding primary stress-sensing mechanisms, epigenetic stress memory, organelle-specific signaling, and the translation of laboratory findings to field conditions. By integrating current knowledge across molecular, physiological, and breeding perspectives, we provide a comprehensive integrated signaling network model and crosstalk among signaling pathways for understanding rice adaptation to combined stresses and highlight potential strategies for enhancing crop resilience and global food security.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 Editing of Grapevine Clade V-Related MLO Genes: Grapevine Powdery Mildew Resistance (Erysiphe necator) and Plant Development Effects.
authors: Gouthu, Satyanarayana; Deluc, Laurent G
abstract: Clade V-MLOs are associated with powdery mildew susceptibility in several plants. In grapevine, four MLO genes (MLO3, MLO4, MLO13, and MLO17) belong to clade V and have been studied to determine their contribution to susceptibility to Erysiphe necator (Grape Powdery Mildew-GPM). Using somatic embryogenesis to generate knockout mutants in grapevine, we performed a series of multiplex gene-editing-mediated transformations to determine each clade V-related MLO's contribution to GPM resistance. We characterized a hierarchy of contributions from the four MLOs to GPM, with MLO17 playing the largest role, followed by MLO3 and MLO13. In addition, MLO4 was a less essential modifier of GPM resistance: its loss-of-function, in combination with other MLOs, conferred a modest but consistent improvement in GPM resistance, and mlo mutants with a fraction of WT MLO4 allele chimerism lacked the mlo-associated developmental pleiotropic effects. Defects in flower development in most mlo4 mutant lines suggest a role for this gene in reproductive tissues. Our data also indicated functional redundancy within the clade V-MLOs, particularly between MLO13 and MLO17. Ultimately, our results show that a certain degree of chimerism (wild-type background in the mutants) is necessary to achieve resistance to GPM without major growth defects or yield penalties. Ultimately, this approach offers a viable strategy for breeding powdery mildew-resistant grapevines while maintaining agronomic fitness.

title: Type III Effectors of Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000: Molecular Mechanisms, Host Manipulation Networks, and Implications for Plant Disease Resistance.
authors: Zhong, Xiaoju; Huang, Jianzhong
abstract: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 (Pst DC3000) is a reference system for dissecting how type III-secreted effectors (T3Es) suppress plant immunity and reconfigure host physiology. Here, we reassess the DC3000 effector repertoire through an evidence-graded framework that links experimentally resolved effector-target mechanisms to repertoire-level genetic interactions and, ultimately, to disease-resistance strategies. We distinguish findings demonstrated with Pst DC3000 from mechanistic examples derived from other P. syringae pathovars and from computationally generated hypotheses. At the molecular level, validated DC3000 effectors perturb pattern-recognition receptor signaling, protein turnover, vesicle trafficking, plasmodesmatal communication, organelle function, and hormone-associated processes. At the repertoire level, deletion and reconstruction studies reveal functional redundancy, specialization, conditional suppression, and context-dependent interactions; importantly, convergence on a common host phenotype is not treated as evidence of direct physical cooperation between effectors. We further evaluate how effectoromics, multi-omics, single-cell and spatial approaches, structure prediction, and machine-learning tools can prioritize new hypotheses while emphasizing their need for genetic, biochemical, and infection-based validation. Finally, we consider how conserved effector targets, susceptibility factors, NLR engineering, and CRISPR-based editing may translate mechanistic knowledge into more durable bacterial-disease resistance. This synthesis positions the DC3000 system as a bridge between mechanistic effector biology, quantitative effector-network analysis, and experimentally testable strategies for crop protection.

title: Beyond Homologous Recombination: Functional Modules of Olaparib Resistance Revealed by CRISPR Screens.
authors: Dildabayeva, Dana; Samarkhanova, Diana; Lezina, Larissa
abstract: Clinical use of PARP inhibitors (PARPi), including olaparib, has improved outcomes for patients with BRCA1/2-mutant and homologous recombination (HR)-deficient tumors. However, acquired resistance remains a major limitation to their efficacy. CRISPR-Cas9 screening approaches have been developed to identify genetic drivers of PARPi resistance. However, differences in experimental conditions, library coverage, and selection design complicate comparisons across studies. In this review, we present a harmonized reanalysis of CRISPR knockout olaparib resistance screens to identify recurrent resistance-associated genes and pathways. Datasets with raw data were collected from the BioGRID ORCS database. Resistance hits identified in at least two screens were subjected to Reactome pathway-enrichment analysis and organized into functional modules. Using this approach, we identified eight modules: DNA-damage repair and replication stress; cell-cycle regulation; chromatin remodeling and histone modification; post-translational regulation; mitochondrial function; TGF-beta and mTOR signaling; RNA processing and nucleocytoplasmic transport; and emerging adaptive mechanisms. Importantly, mitochondrial function genes were observed as recurrent hits, but their relation to olaparib resistance is underinvestigated. Our integrative analysis suggests that PARPi resistance is a complex, adaptive phenotype shaped by recurrent but context-dependent vulnerabilities across multiple cellular programs. This framework prioritizes candidate resistance drivers for validation and highlights directions for the design of combination therapies aimed at overcoming PARPi resistance.

title: Neurobiological Pathways Underlying Opioid Addiction and Overdose: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Targets, and Insights from Zebrafish Model.
authors: Duric, Jovana; Williams, Frederick E; Schiefer, Isaac T
abstract: The worldwide opioid epidemic continues to claim thousands of lives each year and remains one of the most urgent global public health challenges, driven by the high abuse potential and overdose risk of potent, fully synthetic mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists such as fentanyl. While fentanyl is highly effective in pain management, it also carries severe risks including respiratory depression, addiction, and fatal overdose. Understanding the neurobiological pathways underlying these risks is essential for developing safer analgesics and effective interventions. The MOR, a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that modulates neuronal excitability and synaptic transmission in important brain circuits like the ventral tegmental area (VTA), nucleus accumbens (NAc), and prefrontal cortex (PFC), is the primary receptor through which opioids exert their therapeutic effects. Dopaminergic dysregulation, transcriptional remodeling, and altered synaptic plasticity are neuroadaptations brought on by long-term opioid exposure that contribute to dependence and relapse. Life-threatening opioid toxicity is primarily driven by MOR-mediated suppression of respiratory networks, with risk shaped by dose, pharmacokinetics, receptor efficacy, and circuit sensitivity. Zebrafish (Danio rerio) provide a powerful complementary system for dissecting opioid-related neurocircuitry and screening for potential therapeutics. Zebrafish share conserved opioid-signaling components with mammals, and larval transparency facilitates in vivo imaging of neuronal activity at cellular resolution. Behavioral paradigms capture reward-related and drug-seeking phenotypes, while CRISPR-based approaches offer a means to investigate receptor-specific functions in validated models. In addition, zebrafish larvae provide an efficient platform for high-throughput screening of compounds that modulate opioid signaling and respiratory-related phenotypes. Together, insights from human, rodent, and zebrafish studies provide a more integrated understanding of opioid overdose and addiction neurobiology. This review incorporates current knowledge on the molecular and circuit-level mechanisms driving these processes and discusses how zebrafish models accelerate the discovery of safer analgesics and novel treatments for opioid use disorder and overdose.

title: Terpenoids: A Comprehensive Review on Biosynthesis, Applications and Enhancement Strategies for Translational Research.
authors: Irum; Tripathi, Gyanendra; Ahmad, Suhail; Fatima, Nida; Puri, Paridhi; Ahmad, Naved; Dissanayake, Kasun Kumara; Ahmad, Khurshid; Ahmad, Saheem; Farooqui, Alvina
abstract: There is growing interest in natural bioactive compounds as potentially safer and more sustainable sources of therapeutic agents. Terpenoids, one of the most structurally diverse and biologically active classes of natural products, are derived from repeating isoprene units and possess a broad range of pharmacological and industrial applications. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in terpenoid biosynthesis, structural classification, and therapeutic applications. It also discusses emerging approaches for enhancing large-scale production, improving functional efficacy, and overcoming pharmacokinetic limitations. Attention is given to terpenoids currently undergoing clinical evaluation, along with their progress toward commercial development. Despite substantial preclinical evidence supporting their therapeutic potential, the clinical translation of many terpenoids remains limited. Key challenges include poor aqueous solubility, low permeability, slow dissolution, and high lipophilicity, which can collectively restrict systemic bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, only a relatively small proportion of biologically active terpenoids have progressed to advanced stages of clinical development, highlighting a considerable gap between experimental findings and clinical application. This review integrates current knowledge of terpenoid biosynthesis, biological activities, production strategies, and translational development while highlighting sustainable and scientifically driven approaches that may facilitate their future therapeutic and commercial utilization.

title: CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL Signaling Drives TGF-beta2-Mediated Immune Evasion and Pancreatic Cancer Progression.
authors: Zhang, Biyu; Li, Yaxin; Fan, Simiao; Zhang, Jiamei; Zhang, Yu; Wang, Wen; Luo, Liang; Xiao, Wanying; Xie, Xinlei; Jian, Xiaoxiao; Han, Qiuying; Huang, Shaoyi; Wu, Min; Song, Zengqing; Wen, Yuqi; Tu, Haiqing; Li, Sen; Hu, Huaibin
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by extensive neural remodeling and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, both of which contribute to disease progression and therapeutic resistance. However, whether nociceptor-derived signals directly reprogram PDAC cells to promote immune evasion remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized tumor-intrinsic neuroimmune mechanism driven by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) signaling through the receptor complex RAMP1/CALCRL on PDAC cells. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of Ramp1 or Calcrl did not alter PDAC cell proliferation in vitro but markedly suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in immunocompetent mice. These antitumor effects were lost in immunodeficient hosts, indicating that the pro-tumorigenic function of CGRP signaling depends on an intact host immune system. Consistently, tumor cell-specific loss of Ramp1 or Calcrl remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment, enhancing CD4(+) and CD8(+) T-cell effector activity. Mechanistically, CGRP stimulation promoted TGF-beta2 expression and secretion by PDAC cells in a RAMP1-dependent manner. Tumor-derived TGF-beta2 subsequently acted in a paracrine fashion to suppress CD8(+) T-cell activation and cytotoxic function, whereas genetic disruption of RAMP1 or pharmacological inhibition of TGF-beta signaling relieved this immunosuppression. Together, these findings define a CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL-TGF-beta2 signaling axis through which nociceptive input is converted into tumor-driven adaptive immune evasion in PDAC. This pathway reveals a previously underappreciated mechanism linking neural signaling to PDAC progression and identifies CGRP receptor signaling as a potential therapeutic vulnerability for restoring antitumor immunity and improving the responsiveness of PDAC to immunotherapy.

title: HDAC Inhibitors Potentiate Doxorubicin Cytotoxicity in HepG2 Cells and Alter DNA-Repair- and p53-Associated Transcriptional Programs.
authors: Guo, Kaidi; van Herwijnen, Marcel; Caiment, Florian; van den Beucken, Twan
abstract: Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACis) can enhance responses to DNA-damaging chemotherapy, but how they alter doxorubicin (DOX)-induced transcriptional programs remains incompletely understood. We investigated the effects of valproic acid (VPA) and vorinostat (SAHA) on DOX cytotoxicity and associated molecular responses in HepG2 cells. HDAC inhibition, cell viability, apoptosis, and DOX IC(50) values were assessed using histone H3 acetylation, cell counting, Alamar Blue assays, and cleaved caspase-3 immunofluorescence. Transcriptomic responses were analyzed by RNA sequencing, differential expression analysis, and Hallmark gene set enrichment analysis, with selected findings evaluated by RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and comparison with published CRISPR/Cas9 DOX-response data. Both HDAC inhibitors increased histone H3 acetylation and enhanced DOX cytotoxicity, markedly reducing DOX IC(50) values. VPA co-treatment also increased DOX-induced cleaved caspase-3 signaling. RNA-seq showed broad transcriptional remodeling, including depletion of the DNA-repair gene set following VPA treatment and attenuation of canonical p53-responsive genes during HDACi-DOX co-treatment. Several HDACi-repressed DNA-repair genes overlapped with genes whose loss sensitized cells to DOX in a published CRISPR screen. HDAC inhibition therefore enhances DOX cytotoxicity and is accompanied by alterations in DNA-repair-associated and p53-responsive transcriptional programs.

title: The Role of SOD1 and Oxidative Stress in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: An Overview.
authors: Gomez-Perez, Carlos Alberto; Ramirez-Garcia, Miguel Angel; Yescas-Gomez, Petra
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. The median survival time after diagnosis is 2 to 5 years. Oxidative stress (OS), driven mainly by reactive oxygen species (ROS), plays a central role in motor neuron (MN) degeneration. In this narrative review, we analyse the pathogenic role of SOD1 variants and their contribution to OS in ALS. SOD1 mutations alter the Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase enzyme, thereby promoting oxidative damage and triggering neuroinflammatory cascades via the MAPK, NF-kappaB and Nrf2/ARE signalling pathways. We also discuss emerging proteomic and machine-learning biomarkers, as well as the current therapeutic landscape. Riluzole and edaravone are approved treatments, while AMX0035 was approved in 2022 but withdrawn in 2024. Masitinib and EPI-589 remain investigational. In the realm of genetic therapies, the antisense oligonucleotide tofersen received accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for SOD1-ALS, primarily due to its ability to reduce plasma neurofilament light chain levels. However, the clinical benefit remains modest. RNA interference has reached human trials, while CRISPR/Cas9 remains in the preclinical stage. Both approaches have shown promising results in experimental models. Further research into ALS pathogenesis is needed to develop treatments that integrate antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and gene-editing strategies.

title: IndelQuant: A Workflow for Cost-Efficient Amplicon Sequencing Analysis of Genome-Edited Chickens.
authors: Duan, Yujuan; Xu, Ke; Zhou, Hao; He, Chuan; Ding, Jinmei; Qin, Chao; Zhang, Yan; Han, Chengxiao; Meng, He
abstract: Accurate quantification of Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9-induced insertions and deletions (indels) is essential in chicken genome-editing studies, where low editing efficiencies and mosaicism can complicate the assessment of target-site modifications. Existing assays often involve a trade-off between affordability and the sensitivity orsequence information needed for detailed analysis. Here, we introduce IndelQuant, a cost-efficient workflow integrating sample-specific barcode PCR, pooled amplicon library construction, AdapterRemoval3-based read processing, and CRISPResso2-based indel quantification. The workflow provides graphical and tabularsummaries of editing efficiency, indel positions, indel-size distributions, and sample-level mutation profiles. We evaluated the workflow in TYR-edited DF-1 cells and genome-edited chickens. In edited chickens, IndelQuant detected tissue-specific indel signals, most below 5%, while negative controls showed background frequencies from 0 to 0.03%. These findings indicate that IndelQuant retains the sequence-level information provided by amplicon sequencing while simplifying sample processing and analysis, offering a practical approach to routine screening for low-frequency and mosaic indels in poultry genome-editing studies.

title: Genome-Wide Identification and Characterization of the Rboh Gene Family in Populus trichocarpa Reveals PtrRbohB Positively Regulates Adventitious Root Development.
authors: Shi, Run; Ding, Yanping; Guo, Peng; Shang, Fude; Cao, Shenquan
abstract: Adventitious roots (ARs) are essential for clonal vegetative propagation of woody tree species. Extensive studies have focused on phytohormone and transcription factor regulatory networks during AR development in poplar, yet the regulatory roles of reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling during AR development remain poorly understood. In this study, we performed a genome-wide identification and systematic characterization of the Respiratory Burst Oxidase Homolog (Rboh) gene family in Populus trichocarpa. A total of 10 PtrRbohs were identified and phylogenetically classified into five subfamilies. Expression profiling revealed distinct tissue-specific and stress-responsive expression patterns among PtrRbohs. Functional validation via CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout showed that disruption of PtrRbohB significantly reduced AR length, diameter, and lateral root density in poplar. Heterologous overexpression of PtrRbohB in Arabidopsis thaliana enhanced ROS accumulation, confirming its conserved function in ROS generation. Furthermore, knockout of PtrRohB down-regulated the expression of several AR-positive regulators and up-regulated that of AR-negative regulators in poplar. Collectively, this study provides the direct genetic evidence that Rboh regulates AR formation in poplar, and identifies PtrRbohB as a key positive regulator of AR development. These findings enrich our understanding of woody plant AR formation and provide candidate genes for molecular breeding of poplar rooting traits.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-Mediated Knockout of the Chorion Gene s36 Impairs Ovarian Development and Abolishes Egg Hatching in the Melon Fly Zeugodacus cucurbitae.
authors: Sun, Lina; Fan, Xinlin; Chen, Ting; Shi, Qingxing; Qi, Guojun; Tang, Bin; Chen, Jie
abstract: The melon fly, Zeugodacus cucurbitae (Coquillett), is a globally invasive pest of cucurbit crops whose concealed larval feeding limits chemical control and has driven interest in reproduction-based management. The chorion gene s36 encodes an eggshell protein conserved among dipterans. However, whether s36 is required for female reproduction in Z. cucurbitae remains unknown. We generated a homozygous s36 mutant line by CRISPR/Cas9 and characterized its reproductive phenotype. Disruption of s36 strongly reduced transcript abundance and truncated the predicted protein. Mutant females showed elevated mortality after sexual maturation, fecundity was approximately halved, and none of the eggs laid hatched. Ovaries were markedly reduced in size and were scored as abnormal in every mutant female examined, and eggs were smaller, dull and shriveled rapidly in air, indicating compromised chorion integrity. Both vitellogenin genes were down-regulated in the ovary. Whole-body transcriptomics identified 179 differentially expressed genes enriched in lipid and hormone-related metabolism. Tissue-resolved RT-qPCR showed vitellogenin and yellow-g2 transcripts elevated in the fat body yet depleted in the ovary; whether this pattern reflects impaired delivery of yolk precursors to the oocyte or the secondary loss of the follicular tissue in which these genes are normally expressed remains to be determined. These findings identify s36 as required for normal ovarian maturation and egg viability in Z. cucurbitae, and as a candidate target for genetic control of this pest.

title: Inherited Anemia: A Contemporary Clinical and Lab Review.
authors: Qadah, Talal
abstract: Inherited anemias represent a diverse group of genetic disorders characterized by impaired red blood cell production, increased destruction, or abnormal hemoglobin synthesis. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the contemporary clinical landscape, diagnostic workflows, and therapeutic advancements for both major and rare inherited anemias. Major hemoglobinopathies, including thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD), continue to impose a significant global health burden, while rare conditions such as hereditary hemolytic anemias (HHAs), congenital dyserythropoietic anemias (CDAs), and Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) present unique diagnostic challenges. Recent years have seen a paradigm shift in laboratory investigations, primarily driven by the integration of next-generation sequencing (NGS) and third-generation sequencing (TGS) into clinical practice. These technologies have revolutionized the identification of causative variants, particularly in complex or multiallelic cases that elude traditional biochemical assays. Furthermore, specialized flow cytometry, such as eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding, remains critical for the diagnosis of red cell membrane defects. Therapeutic management is also undergoing a transformation. Beyond traditional supportive care and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), groundbreaking gene-editing therapies, most notably CRISPR/Cas9-mediated BCL11A enhancer editing, offer the potential for curative outcomes in beta-hemoglobinopathies. Novel pharmacological agents, such as luspatercept for thalassemia and mitapivat for pyruvate kinase deficiency, are providing targeted options to improve erythropoiesis and reduce transfusion burden. Despite these advances, challenges remain in ensuring equitable access to these high-cost interventions and addressing the diagnostic gaps in resource-limited settings.

title: Advancing the Translational Pipeline: From In Vivo and In Vitro 2D Models to Next-Generation Cell Culture Models for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Modelling and Drug Discovery.
authors: Carata, Elisabetta; Mariano, Stefania; Tenuzzo, Bernardetta Anna; Panzarini, Elisa
abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is still a global health challenge, as there is no effective treatment due to the inadequacy of conventional experimental platforms for comprehending pathogenic mechanisms and developing therapy. Objectives: This review details the recent progress and clinical utility of next-generation iPSC-derived 3D in vitro systems integrated with microfluidics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, multi-omics readouts, and AI-based machine learning, which are emerging as transformative platforms for recapitulating key ALS pathological hallmarks. Methods: A literature search was performed using PubMed and Web of Science, including only English-language publications. All the published papers collected covered the period from January 2015 to June 2026. Results: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cerebral organoids, assembloids, and organ-on-a-chip technologies are revolutionizing research into ALS by providing a way to model the complex spatial organization, cellular heterogeneity, and neural network dynamics of the human brain. Moreover, recent bioengineering advancements enable the inclusion of functional neurovascular units, the integration of resident immune cells (microglia), and the use of 3D bioprinting to accelerate the functional maturation of age-related phenotypes. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, OMICS, and machine learning improve tools for studying ALS and identifying therapeutic targets. Conclusions: Novel cell culture models may bridge the gap between preclinical animal models and human clinical trials and reduce the duration and costs of translation. Future work is likely to integrate bioprinting with organ-on-chip microfluidics, CRISPR-based genetic editing, and multi-omics readouts to build increasingly faithful, patient-specific ALS models for both basic research and precision therapeutics.

title: Gene-Editing in Respiratory Disease: From Pre-Clinical Human Models to Future Therapeutics.
authors: Duffy, Amy; Schweikert, Anja; Tan, Sze Ying; Murphy, Cormac; Dowling, Catriona M; Hurley, Killian; Ozaki, Mari
abstract: Chronic lung diseases arise from complex interactions between environmental exposures and host genetic factors. However, these interactions are not fully understood, and despite decades of study, effective curative therapies remain unavailable for many patients. Recent breakthroughs in therapeutic gene-editing have become a reality for some inherited blood diseases and are a promising approach for monogenic lung diseases. Early-phase clinical studies are now ongoing for AATD, primarily through liver-directed editing of hepatocytes to restore circulating functional AAT and for COVID-19 using gene-edited immune cell approaches. However, direct in vivo gene-editing of pulmonary epithelial cells remains largely at the preclinical stage. Expanding this therapeutic pipeline requires overcoming the unique biological barriers of the lung and developing human-specific models that faithfully recapitulate human disease mechanisms. Advances in gene-editing technologies, including CRISPR-Cas9 systems, base and prime editors, and emerging compact nucleases, have increased the feasibility of precise genomic correction. However, safe and efficient delivery directly to the lung remains a major unmet challenge due to mucus, surfactant, epithelial tight junctions, and innate immune surveillance. Delivery systems such as engineered AAVs, lentiviral vectors, selective organ targeting lipid nanoparticles and aerosolizable formulations like nebulised or dry powder nanoparticles are beginning to address these obstacles. In parallel, human preclinical models have evolved from traditional cell lines to more sophisticated platforms such as iPSC-derived airway and alveolar cells, organoids, precision-cut lung slices, air-liquid interface cultures, organ-on-a-chip devices, and patient-derived primary cells. These models enable mechanistic interrogation, variant-specific functional assessment, and preclinical evaluation of gene-editing strategies with increased physiological relevance. In this review, we detail current and emerging gene-editing tools, delivery strategies, and human-relevant disease models. We highlight key translational barriers and discuss how advanced human models combined with improved delivery technologies can accelerate the development of safe and effective gene-editing therapeutics for chronic respiratory disease.

title: Current Evidence on Gene-Based and Epigenetic Therapeutic, Diagnostic, and Prognostic Strategies in Epithelial-Derived Carcinomas: A Scoping Review.
authors: Thomas, Joshua George; Ayyub, Mohammed; Annamma, Lovely M; Prasad, Prathibha; Azim, Sabrin Ali; Varma, Sudhir; George, Biji Thomas; Khair, Al Moutassem Billah
abstract: Background: Epithelial-derived carcinomas exhibit genomic instability due to genetic mutation and epigenetic dysregulation. Mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, and noncoding RNA regulation may lead to tumor progression, immune evasion, and treatment resistance. Presently, gene-based and epigenetic therapies, including CRISPR systems, RNA interference, and chromatin-modifying agents, are reported to be effective in targeted cancer treatment. Objectives: This scoping review aims to map the evidence on gene-based technologies in epithelial-derived carcinomas, including therapeutic, diagnostic, prognostic, screening, and disease-modeling applications, and to identify molecular targets, translational outcomes, and gaps in the current evidence base. The review will characterize the molecular targets, gene-based approaches, cancer types, translational applications, and reported outcomes to identify evidence gaps, translational challenges, and priorities for future research. Methods: The scoping review was conducted as per PRISMA-ScR by conducting a literature search in databases such as PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar, covering studies published between 2016 and 2026. In the inclusion criteria, all studies and reviews related to investigating gene-based, RNA-mediated, and epigenetic therapies in epithelial cancers were included. Thirty-six studies met the eligibility criteria. Results: Amongst the studies reviewed, the most common epithelial cancers reported were hepatocellular carcinoma, ovarian carcinoma, lung carcinoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Among the epithelial-derived carcinomas identified in this review, HCC was the most frequently represented cancer; epigenetic alterations and therapies used were RNA-based therapies, CRISPR diagnostics, and epigenetic drugs. Ovarian and breast cancers targeting BRCA pathways and chromatin remodeling produced clinical translation outcomes. Lung and colorectal cancers showed moderate epigenetic involvement, often managed through combined therapeutic strategies. Pancreatic cancer therapies were limited by challenges in drug delivery despite identifiable molecular targets. Gene therapies such as CRISPR-based gene editing, RNAi/siRNA therapies, miRNA/lncRNA targeting, and HDAC inhibition were commonly reported. Conclusions: The present study indicates that the majority of epithelial-derived carcinomas can benefit from gene-based and epigenetic therapies. Though the majority of carcinomas, such as hepatocellular, have good clinical outcomes, pancreatic cancer has limited clinical translation.

title: Epigenetic Memory in Human Diseases: Acquired Chromatin States as Targetable Drivers of Disease Evolution.
authors: Khan, Shahper Nazeer; Danishuddin; Isah, Salamatu Tijjani; Siddiqui, Mohammed Haris; Ahmad, Aamir; Kim, Jong-Joo
abstract: Clinical heterogeneity remains a major challenge across human diseases, where patients with similar genetic backgrounds frequently exhibit striking differences in disease progression, therapeutic response and clinical outcome. Increasing evidence indicates that these differences cannot be explained by genetic variation alone, positioning epigenetic memory as a critical non-genetic determinant of disease behavior. Epigenetic memory refers to the stable yet reversible propagation of transcriptional states through mechanisms including DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, enhancer dynamics and higher-order chromatin organization. In this review, we synthesize emerging mechanistic and translational evidence demonstrating how epigenetic memory integrates environmental, metabolic, inflammatory, infectious and therapeutic cues into persistent cellular programs that drive inter-patient, intra-tumoral and temporal heterogeneity. We discuss its disease-specific manifestations across cancer, immunological, neurological, and metabolic disorders, with particular emphasis on cellular plasticity, stemness, immune evasion, drug-tolerant persister states and relapse. Furthermore, we highlight recent advances in single-cell and spatial epigenomics, liquid-biopsy-based epigenetic biomarkers, CRISPR-mediated epigenome editing and targeted chromatin therapies that collectively establish epigenetic memory as both a measurable biomarker and a therapeutically actionable vulnerability. By framing epigenetic memory as a dynamic interface between genome and environment, this review provides a unified conceptual framework for understanding disease evolution and advancing precision epigenetic medicine.

title: Transthyretin Amyloidosis: From Mechanisms to Treatment.
authors: Triposkiadis, Filippos; Xanthopoulos, Andrew; Georghiou, Georghios P; Stephanou, Anastasis; Patrikios, Ioannis
abstract: Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) is a progressive systemic disorder driven by the misfolding of transthyretin (TTR) proteins and their deposition as amyloid fibrils. It manifests as hereditary ATTR (ATTRv), caused by pathogenic variants, and wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt), linked primarily to aging. These deposits preferentially affect the myocardium and peripheral nerves, producing severe cardiomyopathy and polyneuropathy. The amyloidogenic cascade is initiated by the dissociation of TTR tetramers into misfolded monomers that aggregate into insoluble fibrils. Historically, treatment was limited to supportive care or organ transplantation; however, it has been transformed by TTR stabilizers, RNA interference (RNAi) agents, and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). More recently, CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has emerged as a potential single-dose strategy for durable TTR suppression. In parallel, anti-fibril therapies, including amyloid-depleting monoclonal antibodies designed to clear existing tissue deposits, are being developed as a complementary disease-modifying strategy. This review delineates the molecular mechanisms of amyloidogenesis and evaluates current clinical management strategies. Recent advances in noninvasive diagnostics and targeted molecular therapies, enabled by precision medicine, have markedly improved disease management and clinical outcomes.

title: In Vitro Chromosome Translocations: Modeling Critical Drivers of Human Neoplasms.
authors: Tynyshtykbayeva, Nuray; Varga, Kamilla; Lukacsi, Szilvia; Fabian, Zsolt
abstract: Chromosomal abnormalities are among the most common molecular characteristics of human cancer cells and are believed to play an essential role in the genesis of tumor driver molecules. Chromosome translocations are one of the first recognized tumor-related chromatin alterations; many of them are so typical to certain neoplasms that they are used as diagnostic biomarkers in contemporary clinical histopathology. Understanding their molecular roles in carcinogenesis is essential to the development of novel targeted therapeutics but this has been hindered by the difficulties in establishing appropriate in vitro models. Here, we review the recent advances of the field covering its historical background, medical relevance and most recent technological breakthroughs in chromosomal translocation modeling that may facilitate the innovations of related tumor-agnostic therapeutic modalities.

title: SUGP1 Deficiency Leads to Splicing Dysregulation and Reduced piRNA Abundance in Insects.
authors: Liu, Dan; Guo, Yongkang; Wang, Liting; Shen, Mengting; Lv, Jing; Wei, Peng; Ma, Sanyuan; Jia, Ling
abstract: SUGP1 (SURP and G-patch domain containing 1) participates in splice-site recognition through its interaction with SF3B1, and loss of this factor leads to aberrant splicing. While its role in pre-mRNA splicing is well-documented, its impact on small RNA pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we used CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SUGP1 editing in Bombyx mori BmE cell populations and RNAi to systemically knock down SUGP1 in Drosophila melanogaster. SUGP1 loss caused widespread splicing abnormalities in both species and reduced transposon-derived piRNA abundance as shown by small RNA-seq. Notably, the expression and splicing patterns of known piRNA pathway genes remained largely unchanged. Integrating silkworm transcriptomic data with the Flag-SUGP1 Co-IP/MS interactome revealed no direct association with the components of the piRNA biogenesis pathway, but identified a physical interaction with the Y-box protein (YBX), suggesting a potential link connecting splicing surveillance to RNA metabolism and proteostasis. Collectively, these correlative findings suggest that SUGP1 depletion perturbs global RNA processing, and piRNA reduction may represent a secondary outcome associated with cellular stress or dysregulated RNA metabolism within these two tested insect systems. These results suggest a potential indirect link between SUGP1-dependent splicing regulation and piRNA abundance in the tested insect models.

title: Targeting Peripheral T-Cell Lymphomas with Chimeric Antigen Receptor Therapy: Mechanistic Challenges, Clinical Landscape and Future Engineering Perspectives.
authors: Irimia, Ruxandra; Piccaluga, Pier Paolo
abstract: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL) comprise a biologically diverse and clinically aggressive family of mature T/NK-cell neoplasms, for which outcomes remain poor in the majority of patients treated with conventional anthracycline-based frontline regimens. Contemporary classifications (WHO-HAEM5 and ICC) increasingly incorporate immunophenotypic and molecular information, underscoring that "PTCL-NOS" is not a single disease but rather a diagnostic umbrella that includes biologically distinct entities and molecular subgroups. Among these are the TBX21- and GATA3-driven PTCL-NOS subsets, the latter associated with inferior survival and a distinctive cytokine/microenvironmental program. These advances, many of which were shaped by long-standing contributions from the Bologna group, support a rational shift from empiric chemotherapy toward mechanism-based and immune-based interventions. CAR-engineered cellular therapies have revolutionized the care of B-cell malignancies, yet translation to PTCL has been delayed by lineage-specific barriers: (i) fratricide during manufacturing when targeting shared T-cell antigens (e.g., CD5, CD7), (ii) the risk of profound and prolonged T-cell aplasia (a markedly less "replaceable" toxicity than B-cell aplasia), and (iii) product contamination by malignant T-cells in autologous platforms. Recent progress in genome editing (CRISPR/Cas9 and base editing), intracellular antigen "blocking" strategies, and alternative effectors (allogeneic "universal" CAR-T, CAR-NK, and iPSC-derived platforms) has begun to address these obstacles at the manufacturing level, while their downstream clinical consequences (e.g., prolonged cytopenias, infectious risk and delayed immune reconstitution) remain incompletely resolved. Early-phase clinical trials now demonstrate clinically meaningful responses for select targets, particularly CD7, CD5, TRBC1 and CD30, for the pan-T targets. However, the strongest efficacy data remain largely derived from T-cell lymphoblastic malignancies (T-ALL/T-LBL), whereas evidence in mature PTCL remains limited and at an earlier stage, with target-specific differences in safety, immune reconstitution and relapse patterns. This review synthesizes the biological rationale for antigen selection in PTCL, the emerging clinical evidence for leading CAR targets, and the engineering strategies most likely to improve the therapeutic index. It also proposes an integrated hematology perspective on how CAR-based therapies might be positioned relative to transplant and evolving targeted agents in relapsed/refractory PTCL.

title: Engineering of the High-Precision Cas12m Dual Base Editor-Loaded Virus-like Particles for A-to-G and C-to-T Conversions.
authors: Aliev, Timur; Imatdinov, Almaz; Prudnikova, Elena; Imatdinov, Ilnaz
abstract: Background/Objectives: CRISPR/Cas-dependent base editing enables the precise correction of genomic sequences by direct modification of DNA bases without creating potentially mutagenic DNA double-strand breaks. Base editing is considered a therapeutic approach for rare monogenic disorders or viral infections. However, many variants of base editors suffer from limited specificity because they induce bystander edits within a broad editing window. However, nucleotide substitution is sufficient to correct a mutation or to achieve a therapeutic effect. Methods: PCR, cloning by restriction digest, and ligation were used to create genetic constructs. The editing efficiency was evaluated using NGS. Virus-like particles were produced in HEK293T cells using transient expression. VLPs were visualized by electron microscopy. Results: Using dual base editors that induce C-to-T and A-to-G substitutions, we show that high editing precision can be achieved by engineering the linker between the MmCas12m domain and the deaminase domain of the editor. By testing different linker sequences, we have created high-precision dual base editors with narrowed editing windows that can edit a single nucleotide at a target position with high accuracy. Conclusions: We found that shortening the linker to an acceptable length provides a single-nucleotide substitution in vitro with minimal bystander activity (less than 0.8%), while the high-precision MmCas12m dual base editor retains up to 90% of the editing efficiency of the original base editor. These high-precision base editors will be useful in cases where high precision is required, and editing of adjacent nucleotides is undesirable.

title: Long Non-Coding RNA LINC01614 Promotes Aggressive Phenotypes and Ferroptosis Resistance in Papillary Thyroid Cancer Through a Putative miR-4521/IGF2/PI3K-AKT Signaling Axis.
authors: Quaranto, Danielle; DeSouza, Nicole R; Carnazza, Michelle; Dadafarin, Sina; Moscatello, Augustine; Iacob, Codrin; Islam, Humayun K; Li, Xiu-Min; Tiwari, Raj K; Geliebter, Jan
abstract: Background/Objectives: Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) is the most common endocrine malignancy and is generally associated with favorable clinical outcomes. However, a subset of tumors develops aggressive phenotypes characterized by increased proliferation, migration, therapeutic resistance, and disease progression. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as important regulators of tumor biology, yet the role of Long Intergenic Non-Protein Coding RNA 1614 (LINC01614) in PTC remains poorly understood. This study investigated the functional role of LINC01614 in PTC and its potential involvement in ferroptosis-associated molecular pathways. Methods: RNA sequencing data from a repository of 44 paired PTC and adjacent normal thyroid tissue samples were analyzed to identify differentially expressed lncRNAs. LINC01614 expression was evaluated in thyroid cell lines, and CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) was used to generate stable LINC01614 knockdown K1 cell lines. Cellular proliferation, migration, clonogenicity, intracellular iron accumulation, lipid peroxidation, cytokine secretion, and ferroptosis-associated gene expression were assessed using qRT-PCR, RNA sequencing, Western blotting, cytokine array analysis, iron quantification assays, and BODIPY C11 lipid peroxidation imaging. Results: LINC01614 was significantly overexpressed in PTC tissues and thyroid cancer cell lines. CRISPRi-mediated repression of LINC01614 reduced cellular proliferation, migration, and clonogenic capacity. Mechanistically, LINC01614 knockdown resulted in an 8.8-fold increase in miR-4521 expression and a 23-fold decrease in IGF2 expression, supporting a potential competing endogenous RNA mechanism. Reduced LINC01614 expression was associated with decreased AKT, GPX4, SLC7A11, and SLC3A2 expression, increased IL-6 secretion, a 3.4-fold increase in intracellular ferrous iron accumulation, and a marked increase in lipid peroxidation following erastin treatment, indicating enhanced sensitivity to ferroptosis. Conclusions: These findings identify LINC01614 as a novel regulator of aggressive PTC phenotypes and ferroptosis resistance. The data support a model in which LINC01614 contributes to thyroid cancer progression through modulation of a miR-4521/IGF2/PI3K/AKT signaling axis and downstream anti-ferroptotic pathways. LINC01614 may represent a promising biomarker and potential therapeutic target in papillary thyroid cancer.

title: CRISPR/Cas-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Intestinal Parasites: From Proof-of-Concept to Point-of-Care Testing.
authors: Alsaady, Isra M
abstract: Intestinal parasitic infections remain a significant global public health concern, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where timely and accurate diagnosis is essential for effective disease management and control. Although conventional diagnostic methods, including microscopy, antigen detection, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), are widely used, each possesses inherent limitations related to sensitivity, turnaround time, laboratory infrastructure, or point-of-care applicability. Recent advances in clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas) systems have led to the development of highly sensitive and rapid molecular diagnostic platforms suitable for decentralized testing. This review summarizes current applications of CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostics for intestinal and foodborne parasitic infections, with particular emphasis on assays developed for Giardia duodenalis, Cryptosporidium parvum, Clonorchis sinensis, Fasciola hepatica, and Schistosoma spp. Published studies have predominantly employed Cas12a, with additional applications of Cas12b and Cas13a and, more recently, a type I-A Cascade-Cas3 system, generally coupled with isothermal amplification methods such as recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) or recombinase-aided amplification (RAA), enabling highly sensitive detection within 60-90 min using fluorescence or lateral-flow strip readouts. The available evidence indicates high analytical sensitivity and specificity, with several assays demonstrating substantial agreement with conventional molecular methods and potential for point-of-care development. However, current CRISPR-based assays remain limited by dependence on nucleic acid extraction, relatively small clinical validation cohorts, lack of standardized protocols, and the persistence of false-negative results associated with low parasite burdens and pre-analytical variables. Emerging strategies, including simplified or extraction-free sample preparation, one-pot sample-to-answer platforms, and detection of parasite-derived cell-free DNA, may further enhance the clinical utility of CRISPR diagnostics. Overall, CRISPR/Cas-based technologies represent a promising next-generation approach for intestinal parasite diagnosis, although large-scale clinical validation and workflow optimization are still required before widespread implementation in routine clinical and field settings.

title: Fluorescence Encoding-Enabled Multiplexed Droplet Digital Recombinase Polymerase Amplification-CRISPR/Cas12a Assay for Rapid Screening of Lower Respiratory Tract Infection-Associated Bacterial Pathogens.
authors: Wang, Yifan; Huang, Enqi; Zhang, Ziyi; Zhu, Xicong; Zhang, Ting; Yang, Na; Chen, Zhenhua; Cai, Dongyang; Liu, Dayu
abstract: Digital RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a assays enable accurate nucleic acid quantification; however, their multiplexing capacity is inherently limited by signal confounding arising from the promiscuous trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a effectors. To overcome this limitation, we developed a fluorescence encoding-enabled multiplexed droplet digital RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a (FLEMD-CRISPR) assay that integrates combinatorial fluorescence encoding, deterministic droplet pairing within a calabash-shaped microwell array, and a machine learning-assisted decoding pipeline. In FLEMD-CRISPR, small-volume fluorescence-encoded CRISPR/Cas12a droplets, each assigned a unique spectral signature corresponding to a specific crRNA, are one-to-one paired with large-volume RPA droplets. Following RPA amplification and droplet merging, Cas12a-mediated reporter cleavage occurs only in droplets containing target amplicons. The decoding pipeline then localizes droplets, classifies their colors to assign crRNA identities, and finally detects positive signals, enabling high-throughput, hands-off analysis of the entire droplet array. FLEMD-CRISPR enabled simultaneous quantification of nucleic acid targets from eight major lower respiratory tract infection-associated bacterial pathogens, showing strong linear correlation (R2 = 0.9987-0.9998) and consistent detection efficiency (slopes = 0.9849-1.0198) relative to single-plex digital PCR. The complete workflow, from sample preparation to final readout, can be completed within 2 h. Clinical validation using 30 bronchoalveolar lavage fluid samples showed that the bacterial detection outcomes of FLEMD-CRISPR were highly concordant with standard-of-care culture, achieving 100% (20/20) positive percent agreement and 99.1% (218/220) negative percent agreement. By enabling panel reconfiguration through simple modifications of the droplet encoding library, FLEMD-CRISPR provides a flexible platform for the development of highly multiplexed digital CRISPR assays.

title: Microbial approaches to cadmium stress in the soil-plant interface: current understanding and biotechnological solutions for sustainable remediation.
authors: Yousef, Asma E; Khare, Tushar; Manikandan, Soumya Koippully; Elnaggar, Attiat; Badar, Zarreen; Hamdy, Rania; Zhou, Yaoyu; El-Keblawy, Ali; Mosa, Kareem A
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) contamination poses a critical threat to agriculture, food security, and human health due to its high solubility, toxicity, and bioavailability. Conventional remediation methods are often expensive, inefficient, and environmentally damaging, highlighting the urgent need for sustainable, biotechnology-based alternatives. This review explores microbial remediation as a promising strategy for Cd detoxification, focusing on the mechanisms that confer microbial Cd tolerance, including cell wall modification, biofilm formation, efflux systems, intracellular chelation, and genetic adaptation. Special emphasis is placed on plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) and endophytes, which mitigate Cd stress in plants by enhancing nutrient uptake, producing phytohormones, modulating antioxidant activity, and regulating metal transporter gene expression. The co-application of PGPR with soil amendments such as biochar and nanoparticles is shown to further improve Cd immobilization, plant resilience, and crop yield. Advancements in omics technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) offer deeper insights into microbial Cd resistance pathways, enabling the development of tailored bioinoculants and genetically engineered strains through tools like CRISPR. By integrating traditional microbiology with modern innovations, this review outlines next-generation solutions for effective Cd remediation, positioning Cd-tolerant microbes as key tools for sustainable agriculture and environmental protection.

title: A one-step LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12a platform targeting lytA and cpsA for rapid parallel identification and virulence stratification of Streptococcus pneumoniae.
authors: Luo, Wanying; Fan, Linping; Wei, Dandan; Xiang, Chunxiang; Xu, Hengyi; Liu, Yang; Zhang, Wei
abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae (S. pneumoniae, SPN) is the primary pathogen causing community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), purulent meningitis, sepsis, and acute otitis media. Accurate species identification and rapid differentiation of invasive strains are critical for clinical management and infection control. Based on loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and CRISPR/Cas12a technologies, this study established a parallel dual-target detection platform targeting the S. pneumoniae-specific lytA gene and the capsular polysaccharide synthesis regulatory gene cpsA. A dual-readout mode combining fluorescence detection (FD) and lateral flow test strip (LFTS) was adopted to meet diverse laboratory testing requirements. For each target-specific reaction, LAMP amplification and CRISPR/Cas12a cleavage were sequentially performed in a single closed tube using paraffin-oil stratification to suppress solvent evaporation, effectively preventing aerosol contamination. Range-finding serial-dilution assays revealed that the lowest gDNA concentrations producing positive signals in all three technical replicates reached 1 fg muL(-1) (FD) and 10 fg muL(-1) (LFTS). This assay specifically distinguished S. pneumoniae from other common clinical pathogens and preliminarily identified encapsulated invasive strains, with 100% sensitivity and specificity consistent with conventional PCR. This LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12a platform, with its closed-tube design, avoids contamination, while FD and LFTS dual readouts cater to diverse testing needs. Featuring high sensitivity, excellent specificity, simplicity, and speed, it provides an innovative and practical solution for the rapid diagnosis of S. pneumoniae and holds great clinical potential.

title: Aquaporin-4 Orchestrates Muscle Cell Differentiation and Satellite Cell Preservation: A Novel Target in Age-Related Muscle Decline.
authors: Giron, Maria D; Manzano, Manuel; Pereira, Suzette L; Reinoso, Antonio; Burgio, Chiara; Montero-Martin, Nora; Jimenez-Jimenez, Guillermo; Argiles, Josep M; Rueda, Ricardo; Lopez-Pedrosa, Jose M; Salto, Rafael
journal: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle
abstract: BACKGROUND: Impaired muscle regeneration is a key contributor to age-related muscle decline, yet the molecular mechanisms linking muscle water homeostasis to regenerative failure remain incompletely understood. Aquaporin-4 (AQP4), a major skeletal muscle water channel, may have functions beyond water transport that are relevant to muscle maintenance and repair. We investigated whether altered AQP4 expression contributes to age-related defects in skeletal muscle regeneration and whether AQP4 may represent a targetable pathway for muscle dysfunction associated with ageing. METHODS: Skeletal muscle from young adult (25-week; n = 9) and aged (85-week; n = 8) rats was analysed for extracellular and intracellular water content by bioimpedance. AQP4, AQP1 and myogenic markers were measured by Western blot. Satellite cells isolated from skeletal muscle were assessed for proliferation, differentiation and expression of differentiation markers. To define the mechanistic role of AQP4 in myogenesis, CRISPR-generated AQP4-silenced L6 rat myoblasts were evaluated for proliferation, differentiation, senescence and Akt/PKB signalling.
