Rescue experiments were performed by restoring AQP4 expression in silenced cells. Data are reported as mean +/- SEM. RESULTS: Compared with young rats, aged rats showed an altered intracellular water-to-lean mass ratio (0.94 vs. 0.62, p < 0.05), a 33% reduction in AQP4 expression (p < 0.05) and reduced muscle strength (3.1 vs. 2.6, p < 0.05), with AQP4 levels correlating with muscle performance. Satellite cells from aged muscle exhibited 29% lower AQP4 expression and 39% lower Pax7 expression (both p < 0.05), together with reduced myogenic differentiation (30% decrease, p < 0.05). In L6 myoblasts, AQP4 silencing reduced proliferation (20% decrease, p < 0.05), impaired myotube differentiation (50% decrease, p < 0.05), increased senescence (30% increase, p < 0.05) and decreased Akt/PKB signalling by 42% (p < 0.05). AQP4 silencing was also associated with decreased dystrophin localization at the plasma membrane (50%, p < 0.05). Re-expression of AQP4 reversed these abnormalities and restored the phenotype toward wild-type levels (all p < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Reduced AQP4 expression is associated with impaired muscle regeneration and functional decline in aged skeletal muscle. Experimental AQP4 loss disrupts myogenic signalling, membrane organization and increases progression to senescence, whereas AQP4 restoration rescues these defects. These findings identify AQP4 as a biologically plausible therapeutic target for strategies aimed at preserving or restoring muscle health and regenerative capacity in ageing-associated muscle dysfunction.

title: Protocol for non-viral HDR-based CRISPR/Cas9 platform for small custom editing in primary T cells.
authors: Mamia, Katariina; Matheson Sollano, Anniken Solveig; Lundberg, Vanja; Vakkilainen, Svetlana; Kekalainen, Eliisa; Schalin-Jantti, Camilla; Leinonen, Eira; Fevang, Borre; Gronholm, Juha; Martelius, Timi; Dahal-Koirala, Shiva; Haapaniemi, Emma Maria
abstract: CRISPR/Cas9 enables precision gene editing via homology-directed repair (HDR) for mutation correction and disease modelling. Here we present a customizable T cell single nucleotide variant (SNV) correction platform based on non-viral HDR, previously described in Mamia et al. Precision T Cell Correction Platform for Inborn Errors of Immunity. Molecular Therapy, 2025. To enable reproducible application, we provide a comprehensive, step-by-step 8-day HDR workflow for editing primary T cells, covering CRISPR/Cas9 reagent design, custom genomic editing from start to finish, optimization and validation strategies, on-target detection, and flow cytometric assessment of T cell phenotype and exhaustion. The platform separates locus-specific reagent optimization from a fixed cellular workflow, enabling implementation of new genomic targets without modifying the downstream T cell editing pipeline. Using this workflow, we have achieved up to 80% editing efficiency across multiple loci and donors. We have further optimized the T cell culture platform for PBMC stimulation to promote CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cell activation and proliferation. We validated this culture platform in 33 patients with Inborn Errors of Immunity using flow cytometry and observed that the defined culture conditions maintain low T cell exhaustion and support persistence of memory T cell populations. The protocol was developed under research-grade conditions but supports scalability and transition to preclinical and clinical GMP workflows. Overall, this adaptable platform is a broadly applicable framework for precision T cell engineering across diverse genomic targets offering opportunities for both in vitro disease modeling and therapeutic genome correction.

title: xNNPCD identifies regulators of programmed cell death by integrating perturbation transcriptomes with cancer dependency profiles.
authors: Yin, Qingyang; Chen, Liang
abstract: Programmed cell death (PCD) encompasses regulated processes whose dysregulation shapes cancer fitness, yet computational studies use known PCD genes for prognosis rather than discovering regulators. We developed xNNPCD, an interpretable neural-network framework that links CRISPR-Cas9 perturbation signatures from CMap to gene dependency profiles from DepMap. The model constrains hidden neurons to five PCD pathways and iteratively refines a prior gene-PCD pathway mask matrix derived from GO, KEGG, and Reactome using pathway-neuron ablation. This converts binary gene-pathway relationships into continuous-valued associations and improves dependency prediction over random forests, fully connected multi-layer perceptrons, and its own non-iterative variant. The learned mask matrix recovers annotated death regulators and nominates candidate regulators, including RPL23A, HSPA5, SNRPA1, SLC6A2, and ASAH1; combined with dependency scores, it separates pathway coupling from regulatory direction. Transferring the refined mask matrix and learned weights to compound-induced perturbation data enables in silico drug screening, identifying BRD-K19103580 and decitabine as therapeutic agents for apoptosis and ferroptosis, respectively. The pathway-resolved drug profiles can facilitate the design of combination therapies targeting complementary PCD pathways to overcome single-pathway resistance. Overall, xNNPCD offers a pan-cancer, interpretable approach that generalizes across perturbation modalities for mapping the regulatory landscape and elucidating the molecular processes of PCD in cancer.

title: Advanced soilless cultivation of medicinal plants: integrating dynamic LED lighting, elicitation, and smart technologies for sustainable biomass and phytochemical production.
authors: Kumar, Amit; Kanika; Rani, Shashi; Warghat, Ashish Rambhau
abstract: Countries with limited water and land resources confront a significant problem due to the growing demand for medicinal plants. These plants are used worldwide to extract and isolate therapeutically important bioactive molecules, known as secondary metabolites. Many medicinal plant species are currently facing significant conservation challenges due to excessive, unregulated harvesting, driven by rapidly growing demand for plant-derived therapies. Soilless farming techniques like hydroponics, aeroponics, and vertical farming offer a sustainable alternative for generating high-quality planting material on a large scale in a considerably shorter period and with less space. Soilless farming revolutionises agriculture and food production, making it particularly well-suited for urban agriculture by reducing maintenance requirements and maximizing crop yields. Soilless farming of numerous medicinal herbs, fruit crops, and vegetables has become increasingly popular in recent years, particularly for its ability to produce large amounts of biomass, high yields, and a wide range of pharmacologically active metabolites. These high-tech systems have significant promise for increased crop yields, cleaner produce, season-independent cultivation, and reduced environmental impact, particularly in water use and disease, compared to traditional soil-based systems. This review article rigorously evaluates recent advancements in soilless agriculture, including LED spectral regulation, nano-elicitation, microbial biostimulants and precursor-feeding strategies, reusable substrates, computational technologies, and CRISPR/Cas-based editing, with respect to their efficacy in generating high-quality plant biomass, improving automation, and optimizing shoot architecture. Implementing soilless farming to produce and synthesize bioactive molecules is expected to be crucial in enhancing sustainability and human well-being.

title: Immortalisation of human airway epithelial cells for genome editing applications.
authors: van Grinsven, Emma J; Ithakisiou, Georgia N; Cleijpool, Pim; Bosch, Bram M; Tziouvelis, Marinos; Amatngalim, Gimano D; van Beuningen, Sam F B; Nijenhuis, Wilco; Yetkin-Arik, Bahar; Kapitein, Lukas C; Beekman, Jeffrey M; Akhmanova, Anna
abstract: AIM: In vitro air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures of human airway epithelial cells are widely used to study respiratory biology and disease, as they recapitulate key features of the pseudostratified airway epithelium and reduce reliance on animal models and repeated patient biopsies. However, the limited proliferative capacity of primary airway basal cells restricts long-term studies and genome editing. This study aimed to generate stable, immortalised human airway basal cell lines that retain differentiation capacity and support genetic manipulation. METHODS: Human airway epithelial basal cells from bronchial and nasal origin were immortalised by lentiviral expression of human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) followed by polyclonal expansion. A panel of cell lines derived from three independent nasal donors was established. Differentiation capacity was assessed in ALI cultures and compared with primary airway epithelial cells. Suitability for genetic manipulation was evaluated using lentiviral overexpression and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene knockout and knock-in strategies. RESULTS: All immortalised cell lines displayed sustained proliferative capacity and efficiently differentiated into major airway epithelial cell types, including multiciliated and secretory cells. Differentiation patterns and functional characteristics closely resembled those of primary airway epithelial cultures. The cell lines supported efficient lentiviral transduction and CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, enabling stable gene overexpression, targeted gene disruption, and precise genomic modification. CONCLUSIONS: hTERT-immortalised human airway basal cell lines preserve key features of primary airway epithelium while enabling long-term culture and versatile genome editing. This resource provides a robust platform for airway biology research, disease modelling, and therapeutic development.

title: Deletion of a rheumatoid arthritis risk enhancer in mouse disrupts Bim expression and immune homeostasis.
authors: Rossi, Stefano; Hayes, Kelly S; Butler, Jake; Ding, James; Richards, Ellie L; Frantzeskos, Antonios; Howell, Gareth J; Grencis, Richard K; Adamson, Antony D; Eyre, Stephen; Orozco, Gisela
abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to characterise the in vivo function of a murine regulatory region syntenic to the human rheumatoid arthritis (RA)-associated enhancer at the ACOXL locus and its role in immunity. METHODS: Using CRISPR-Cas9, we generated the Bim-eDelta mouse model by excising a 15 kb genomic region syntenic to the human RA-associated locus tagged by rs13401811 from C57BL/6J zygotes. Bim expression was assessed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Thymocytes and splenocytes were profiled by flow cytometry, and whole-spleen RNA-seq was used to define transcriptional changes. Immune responses were tested using a Trichuris muris infection model and an antigen-induced arthritis (AIA) protocol. RESULTS: Bim-eDelta mice show reduced Bim expression vs wild-type counterparts. This indicates that Bim is a transcriptional target of this region. Enhancer loss was correlated with differences in T cell proportions across age- and sex-stratified cohorts consistent with altered thymic selection. Splenic T and B cells were altered, and the transcriptome skewed toward inflammation. Bim-eDelta and wild-type mice mounted comparable responses to T. muris, whereas Bim-eDelta mice developed a severe adverse response during the sensitisation phase of the AIA protocol. CONCLUSIONS: A murine noncoding regulatory region modulates Bim expression and immunity in vivo. Enhancer deletion altered the splenic transcriptional profile and lymphocyte composition while revealing a context-dependent phenotype upon inflammatory in vivo challenge. These findings support a role for RA-associated regulatory architecture in shaping immunity and point to BIM regulation as a potential therapeutic lever for restoring immune balance.

title: Development of a multiplex detection system for toxic Amanita species based on isothermal recombinase polymerase amplification and CRISPR/Cas12b technology.
authors: Li, Hao; Ying, Xinyu; Luo, Zhidan; Lu, Chen; Zhang, Ping
abstract: BACKGROUND: Toxic Amanita species are a major cause of fatal mushroom poisoning worldwide. Their morphological similarities to the edible species of mushrooms increase the risk of accidental ingestion, highlighting the need for rapid and accurate identification. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to develop a multiplex detection system using isothermal recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) and CRISPR/Cas12b technology for rapid and specific detection of multiple toxic Amanita species. METHODS: Species-specific RPA primers and single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) were designed and optimized for six toxic Amanita species (A. exitialis, A. pallidorosea, A. subjunquillea, A. rimosa, A. molliuscula, and A. fuligineoides). The detection system combined RPA with Cas12b-mediated fluorescence readout to evaluate the specificity and sensitivity, and the results were visualized using lateral flow strips and a microfluidic disc chip for parallel detection. RESULTS: The selected primer-sgRNA combinations showed high specificity values without cross-reactivity and a low detection limit of 10 pg of genomic DNA per reaction. The lateral flow strips enabled intuitive and reliable detection. Furthermore, the microfluidic disc chip enabled multiplex detection for both single-species and four-species mixed samples. CONCLUSION: We successfully established a rapid, sensitive, and specific multiplex detection system for toxic Amanita species using purified genomic DNA from authenticated specimens, providing a proof-of-concept analytical strategy for informing future development of instrument-light species identification tools in mushroom poisoning cases. We also summarize the evaluations required for further optimization of the current design prior to practical application.

title: Gene therapy as an upcoming technique in the treatment of cancer: A cellular solution to a cellular problem.
authors: Bedada, Abdisa Tufa; Genet, Solomon
abstract: Cancer remains a formidable global health challenge, representing the second leading cause of mortality worldwide. In 2023, there were approximately 18.5 million new cancer cases and over 10 million deaths globally, with projections estimating 30.5 million new cases and 18.6 million deaths annually by 2050. In the US, an estimated 2,114,850 new cases and 626,140 deaths are projected for 2026. Cancer arises from accumulated genetic and epigenetic alterations that progressively transform normal cells into malignant counterparts, with mutations in proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and DNA repair machinery as fundamental drivers of carcinogenesis. Gene therapy has emerged as a therapeutic modality that addresses cancer at its genetic core. This review examines the genetic basis of cancer pathogenesis and analyzes contemporary gene delivery platforms viral vectors, bacterial vectors (bactofection), physical methods (microinjection, electroporation, hydroporation, and gene gun), and chemical approaches (lipofection, polymer based systems, and nanoparticles)alongside their advantages, limitations, and clinical applications. Particular emphasis is placed on suicide gene therapy and immunomodulatory approaches, with focused examination of chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy as the most clinically advanced gene therapy strategy to date. Recent advances, including expanded regulatory designations for CAR-T therapies targeting solid tumors and next-generation vector platforms, underscore the field's rapid evolution. Despite persistent challenges safety concerns, high costs, and limited efficacy in solid tumors, gene therapy represents a transformative approach that may ultimately achieve durable remissions. We conclude by discussing future directions, including next-generation delivery systems, genome editing technologies such as CRISPR-Cas9 base and prime editing, and strategies to improve accessibility and affordability.

title: Comparative Analysis of Poly(Ethylene Glycol) (PEG) and Poly(2-Ethyl-2-Oxazoline) (PEtOx) for Organic Solvent-Free Lipid Nanoparticle Formulations.
authors: Streiber, Michael; Holick, Caroline T; Gath, Lucas; Tsarenko, Ekaterina; Bachmann, Vivien; Litsiou, Stavroula; Harder, Lukas; Rosenberger, Laura J; Rusevski, Aleksandar; Kimmig, Julian; Culemann, Stephan; Franke, Christian; Waskow, Claudia; Hoeppener, Stephanie; Schubert, Stephanie; Bros, Matthias; Werz, Oliver; Nischang, Ivo; Bauer, Michael; Press, Adrian T; Schubert, Ulrich S; Traeger, Anja
abstract: Efficient, biocompatible, and flexible application of CRISPR-Cas9 remains a major challenge in gene therapy. This study addresses a novel formulation method, focusing on organic solvent-free lipid nanoparticles for the efficient delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 components. Therefore, novel stealth lipids comprising the lipid anchor cholesterol hemisuccinate conjugated to poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx) were synthesized and evaluated as a promising in vitro alternative to commercially available poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based lipids. Our study identified PEtOx-lipids as markedly more biocompatible compared to PEG-based analogues (12-fold reduction in cytotoxicity; 99% reduced hemolytic effect) with high efficiency for mRNA gene delivery. We demonstrate successful CRISPR-Cas9 activity ex vivo and efficient uptake of PEtOx nanoparticles by macrophages in vivo (66.5% pos. F4/80(+) macrophages). Our data demonstrate that PEtOx-based stealth lipids are a promising alternative to PEG. The resulting LNPs, optimized for fully aqueous manufacturing, address key limitations of current LNP systems, including immunogenicity and the reliance on ethanol-based production processes.

title: OSCAR: an omics atlas of paired single-cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq for decoding cell-specific gene regulation.
authors: Song, Chao; Zhou, Yao; Feng, Chenchen; Dai, Xintong; Xiao, Jiaxin; Fan, Xuan; Wang, Kewei; Xiao, Pengxiang; Zheng, Yixin; Luo, Wenxi; Li, Chunquan; Wang, Qiuyu
abstract: Paired single-cell chromatin accessibility and transcriptome profiles provide a powerful framework for dissecting cell-specific regulatory programs underlying diverse biological processes and human diseases. The rapid accumulation of paired single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (scATAC-seq) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data has led to an urgent need to comprehensively integrate these data to illustrate the regulatory landscape at single-cell resolution. To address this need, we developed OSCAR (an Omics atlas of paired Single-Cell ATAC and RNA-seq, https://bio.liclab.net/OSCAR/) to curate large-scale paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data and to provide comprehensive regulatory annotations and analyses. The current version of OSCAR catalogs 7749 898 human cells from 1136 samples across 30 tissue types. Importantly, OSCAR integrates paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq profiles for joint cell clustering and peak-to-gene linkage identification, and provides detailed (epi)genetic annotations for marker peaks and regulatory elements of marker genes, including super-enhancers, enhancers, enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), common and risk single nucleotide polymorphisms, expression quantitative trait loci, transcription factor binding sites, transcription factor/transcription co-factor binding peaks, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 target sites, DNase I hypersensitivity sites, chromatin accessibility regions, DNA methylation sites, chromatin interaction regions, and topologically associating domains. Furthermore, OSCAR provides three online analysis tools, including cell type enrichment analysis, sequence-based peak regulatory analysis, and peak-to-gene linkage analysis. Hence, OSCAR is a useful platform to query, browse, analyze, and visualize cell-specific regulatory programs across diverse human tissues and diseases.

title: Genetic architecture of low-temperature germinability in rice revealed by integrated maps of SNPs and structural variation.
authors: Shi, Youshuai; Xu, Kai; Lv, Yamei; He, Xiaoyu; Yu, Tingting; Wu, Fengcai; Liang, Lunping; Feng, Ting; Zhang, Liang; Liu, Erbao; Li, Zhikang; Wang, Wensheng; Li, Min; Zhang, Chaopu
journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology
abstract: Low-temperature germinability (LTG) limits rice direct seeding, yet its genetic architecture and regulatory roles of structural variations (SVs) remain largely unclear. We evaluated LTG in 403 rice accessions at four temperatures (13 degrees C, 15 degrees C, 18 degrees C, 21 degrees C). Integrating SNP/SV-GWAS, RNA-seq, gene editing, population genetics, and machine learning, we dissected the genetic basis of LTG and built a genomic selection (GS) prediction model. The panel showed extensive LTG variation, which was negatively correlated with origin latitude. SV- and SNP-based GWAS for LTG detected 119 and 127 QTLs, respectively, with 25 loci overlapping between the two datasets. Combining GWAS and RNA-seq, we screened 30 candidate genes and 48 favorable haplotypes, with high-LTG favorable alleles enriched in low-latitude Xian (Indica) accessions. We identified a deletion in the qLTG3-1 coding region that negatively regulated LTG, and gene editing (CRISPR/Cas9) confirmed qLT11d is a key gene for LTG. Population genetic analysis identified 29 inter-subspecies (Xian-Geng) and 37 intra-Xian divergent regions for LTG, implying shared selected regions across and within subspecies under low temperature. Using SNP and SV data, we built corresponding genomic selection (GS) models with the machine learning-based MFGP method, achieving high prediction accuracy across all temperatures. All cross-temperature prediction correlations exceeded 0.55, with optimal performance at 18 degrees C. Our results clarify rice LTG genetic architecture and suggest potential regulatory roles for SVs that merit further investigation, providing candidate genes, favorable haplotypes, and a GS model for LTG genetic improvement in direct seeding rice.

title: An Integrated Framework Coupling Hierarchical Hyperspectral i-trait Screening, Gene Identification, and Functional Validation for Genetic Dissection of Salt Tolerance in Cotton.
authors: Xu, Bowei; Liu, Le; Yu, Mengli; Guo, Yuling; Ye, Junli; Zhang, Jun; Zhao, Rumeng; Yang, Jiajie; Yang, Wanneng; Xu, Yameng; Fan, Liqiang; Yang, Zuoren
abstract: Cotton is an economically pivotal fiber crop worldwide, but its growth and yield are critically limited by soil salinity. Salt tolerance is a complex quantitative trait, and conventional destructive phenotyping methods have long hindered the efficiency and accuracy of gene discovery and genetic dissection. To overcome this phenotyping bottleneck and establish a streamlined workflow from phenotype to gene, we developed an integrated framework coupling dynamic hyperspectral phenomics, hierarchical trait selection, genome-wide association study (GWAS), and functional validation, and applied it to dissect the genetic basis of salt tolerance using a natural population of 419 upland cotton accessions. We first confirmed abundant salt tolerance phenotypic diversity in the population via four core physiological traits and their phenotypic plasticity indices. Using time-series hyperspectral imaging (HSI), we extracted large-scale image-derived traits (i-traits) capturing dynamic physiological responses to salt stress. A three-tiered screening strategy integrating t-test, broad-sense heritability (H(2)) estimation, and multi-algorithm machine learning consensus was applied to identify core salt-responsive i-traits with biological relevance, genetic stability, and low redundancy. Using these core i-traits as phenotypic inputs for GWAS, we successfully mapped GhST7 as a key candidate gene. Functional validation via CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout and haplotype-specific overexpression demonstrated that GhST7 acts as a key regulator of cotton salt stress responses, and natural variation in its promoter region confers differential salt tolerance by modulating gene expression levels. Collectively, this study not only identifies a functionally verified salt tolerance gene with breeding application value, but also establishes a coherent phenomics-genomics-functional validation framework, providing an efficient paradigm for high-precision genetic dissection of complex stress-tolerance traits in crops.

title: Identification of STYXL1 as novel susceptibility gene for anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity in breast cancer patients.
authors: Velasco-Ruiz, Alejandro; Nunez-Torres, Rocio; Pita, Guillermo; Torres-Ruiz, Raul; Diaz-Talavera, Alberto; Tejera-Perez, Hugo; Wildiers, Hans; Lambrechts, Diether; Hatse, Sigrid; Delombaerde, Danielle; Van Brussel, Thomas; Alonso, M Rosario; Alvarez, Nuria; Herraez, Belen; Alonso-Gordoa, Teresa; Talavera-Calle, Pedro; Serrano-Antolin, Jose Maria; Campos-Olivas, Ramon; Robledo, Mercedes; Vulsteke, Christof; Rodriguez-Perales, Sandra; Zamora, Pilar; Lopez-Fernandez, Teresa; Gonzalez-Neira, Anna

title: Microfluidic platforms for CAR-T cell engineering: a multidisciplinary review on potential next generation intracellular delivery method.
authors: Aparecida de Araujo Andreotti, Isabela; Griep, Gabriel; Patino Narino, Edgar Andres; Ribeiro Batista-Silva, Leonardo; Gongora-Rubio, Mario Ricardo; Bonamino, Martin Hernan; Balbino, Tiago Albertini
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapies have transformed the treatment landscape for hematological malignancies, yet their large-scale manufacturing still faces significant technical, economic, and regulatory constraints. Microfluidic-mediated mechanical poration (MMP) has emerged as a promising non-viral strategy for intracellular delivery in cell engineering, offering high-throughput operation, reduced reagent consumption, and the possibility of preserving cell viability compared with conventional physical delivery methods. MAIN BODY: This review provides a structured assessment of the main MMP modalities, including constriction-based squeezing, volume exchange convective transfection (VECT), vortex shedding, spiral/viscoelastic hydroporation, and droplet mechanoporation, highlighting how device geometry, flow regime, and deformation mechanism influence delivery efficiency and cell integrity. Across the studies analyzed, reported delivery efficiencies frequently range from 60% to >95%, with cell viabilities commonly above 80-90% and processing capacities reaching from approximately 1 x 10(6) to 2.5 x 10(8) cells/min, depending on the device design, cargo, cell type, and operating conditions. Compared with viral vectors, MMP avoids complex vector production and may reduce biosafety and manufacturing burdens, while compared with electroporation, it may offer advantages in continuous-flow processing, cytotoxicity reduction, and cell recovery. CONCLUSIONS: Microfluidic-mediated mechanical poration shows strong potential as a next-generation intracellular delivery strategy for CAR-T cell manufacturing, combining efficiency, scalability, and reduced cytotoxicity. However, the current evidence remains uneven: many studies still rely on model cell lines or surrogate cargos, and direct validation in primary human T cells using CAR-encoding mRNA, DNA, or CRISPR-Cas9 components remains limited. Further optimization, regulatory alignment, and GMP-compatible integration are required to translate MMP from high-performing laboratory prototypes into reliable components of next-generation CAR-T cell manufacturing workflows.

title: Expansion of the Asgard archaeal virome and defensome provides insights into virus-host interactions.
authors: Gu, Chengxiang; Zhang, Rui; Rao, Yang-Zhi; Zhang, Xinxu; Zhou, Zhichao; Liu, Yang; Dong, Xiyang; Wang, Long; Wang, Yinzhao; Hua, Zheng-Shuang; Krupovic, Mart; Li, Meng
abstract: BACKGROUND: Asgard archaea, broadly considered as a group of archaea that exhibit the closest evolutionary relationship with eukaryotes, encode diverse defense systems and are infected by distinct viruses. However, the diversity of Asgard archaeal viruses and their interactions with the hosts remain poorly explored. RESULTS: Here, using CRISPR spacer-protospacer matching, we predict 23 viruses associated with Asgard archaea from various habitats. Apart from clusters with known viruses, we report three previously undescribed groups of Asgard viruses with predicted head-tailed virions of the realm Duplodnaviria and filamentous virions characteristic of the archaea-specific realm Adnaviria. Mapping of metagenomic reads to viral and host genomes suggested that most Asgard viruses display relatively low virus-to-host ratios, typically below 10. In addition, we considerably expanded the known defensome of Asgard archaea, among others, detecting putative PARIS and Prometheus defense systems. Finally, the diversity of anti-defense proteins and putative archaeal type IV pilins encoded by some Asgard viruses provide additional insights into the interactions between Asgard archaea and their viruses. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, this work sheds new light on the Asgard archaeal virome and defensome, and virus-host interactions. Video Abstract.

title: Multifaceted role of genetic and epigenetic architecture of glucose homeostasis and diabetes.
authors: Khokhar, Manoj
abstract: Glucose homeostasis depends on coordinated genetic and epigenetic regulation of pancreatic beta-cells, insulin-sensitive tissues, and neuroendocrine circuits. This review synthesises evidence from over 600 GWAS loci and the primary literature published between 2008 and 2026, and emerging single-cell functional genomics, CRISPR-based perturbation screens, deep-learning variant-effect predictors (DeepSEA, Enformer, AlphaGenome), and polygenic risk frameworks to explain insulin secretion, insulin signalling, and diabetes susceptibility, converting GWAS associations into mechanistic insight and genotype-guided precision therapies.

title: The 9-1-1 complex protects ssDNA gaps in BRCA2-deficient cancer.
authors: Grimsley, Helen E; Courtemanche, Katherine; Cox, Shane; Calder, Anthony; McDermott, Niamh; Pei, Xin; Sharma, Aman; Bright, Jackson; Riaz, Nadeem; Setton, Jeremy; Orman, Mehmet; Powell, Simon N
abstract: Single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps are a hallmark of BRCA-deficient cells, yet the mechanisms that safeguard these lesions remain unclear. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen in isogenic BRCA2-proficient and -deficient cancer cells, we identified the RAD9A-HUS1-RAD1 (9-1-1) complex as essential for BRCA2-deficient cell survival through an ATR-independent mechanism. In this context, loss of 9-1-1 leads to accumulation of PRIMPOL-dependent gaps that fail to undergo post-replicative repair, resulting in pathological expansion and increased DNA damage. Excessive EXO1-mediated degradation drives this genomic instability, as EXO1 depletion rescues the phenotype. We further demonstrate that the 9-1-1 complex contributes to POLzeta-dependent gap filling. We propose a model in which ssDNA gaps, when extended beyond a critical length, become inaccessible to translesion synthesis (TLS)-mediated repair and rely entirely on homologous recombination. These findings establish the 9-1-1 complex as a key regulator of ssDNA gap stability and as a promising therapeutic target in BRCA2-deficient cancers.

title: In vivo genome-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Preclinical studies and first-in-human trial.
authors: Li, Guoling; Han, Feng; Wang, Cuijin; Jin, Ming; Lin, Jiajia; Zhang, Hainan; Yan, Xiudong; Wang, Xing; Sun, Xinyan; Yuan, Yiqun; Zhang, Siyuan; Zhang, Shuaishuai; Zhu, Jingyan; Xu, Yichao; Wang, Yingyan; Deng, Yujiao; Li, Fangxin; Shi, Linyu; Luk, Alvin; Wang, Ning; Yang, Hui; Wang, Jiwen
abstract: We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector. In humanized DMD mice, systemic administration achieved targeted genome editing, partial dystrophin restoration, and improved muscle function. In non-human primates, efficient on-target editing was achieved with no dose-limiting toxicity identified under the conditions tested. In an open-label, dose-escalation, first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06594094), post-treatment muscle biopsies provided early molecular evidence of hfCas12Max-mediated genome editing and detectable dystrophin expression in participants with DMD. However, at the higher dose level (1.0 x 10(14) vg/kg), one participant experienced a treatment-related fatal serious adverse event, characterized by marked complement activation and systemic cytokine response shortly after dosing. This work provides initial human proof-of-concept for muscle genome editing while crucially highlighting the critical role of immunologic risks and the narrow therapeutic window of systemic adeno-associated virus (AAV)-CRISPR therapies, underscoring the need to develop safer dosing and immunomodulation strategies.

title: CRISPR-based functional screening of noncoding regulatory elements.
authors: Roh, Heejin; Liau, Brian B
abstract: The vast majority of trait-associated genetic variants reside in noncoding cis-regulatory elements (CREs), yet most regulatory sequences remain functionally uncharacterized. CRISPR-based screens enable direct perturbation of CREs in their native genomic context and have expanded into a diverse toolkit, including CRISPRi/CRISPRa, nuclease-mediated editing, base editing, prime editing, and continuous mutagenesis. Moreover, these approaches can be paired with phenotypic, transcriptomic, or chromatin readouts at single-cell resolution. However, a limitation of conventional pooled CRISPR screens is that cells are assigned by sgRNA identity rather than by the genotype installed. New genotype-resolved approaches address this gap by directly reading the edited endogenous sequence. Because sequence variants in CREs are associated with human disease, continued development of CRISPR-based technologies may help advance new therapies. In this review, we discuss diverse CRISPR-based modalities and their limitations, emerging genotype-resolved techniques, their applications in gene therapy, and computational approaches for predicting the function of regulatory sequences.

title: Cascade DNA walker-driven photo-controlled CRISPR/Cas12a nanorobot enabling ultrasensitive one-pot detection of dual miRNAs in triple-negative breast cancer.
authors: Yu, Luhu; Li, Xiaoyu; Huang, Leming
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are critical biomarkers for the early diagnosis of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), but sensitive simultaneous detection of multiple miRNAs remains a clinical challenge. Herein, we report an innovative biosensing method based on a cascade DNA walker-driven photo-controlled CRISPR/Cas12a nanorobot for one-pot, rapid, and ultrasensitive dual miRNA detection. Target miRNAs trigger the cascade DNA walker, which integrates catalytic hairpin assembly and enzyme-mediated strand displacement, to generate abundant single-stranded DNA (ssDNA). These ssDNA then activate the photo-controlled CRISPR/Cas12a nanorobot under light illumination, enabling amplified fluorescence signaling for dual-target quantification. The assay exhibits a linear range of 100 aM to 1 pM with a limit of detection of 48.7 aM. Serum recovery experiments and cell line tests confirm its reliability in complex matrices. Clinical validation using 30 plasma samples (15 TNBC patients, 15 healthy controls) demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy (area under the curve, AUC = 0.964). This method features simple operation and strong clinical translational potential, offering a reliable tool for the early diagnosis of TNBC.

title: Genomic resequencing of low nicotine tobacco germplasm identifies novel allelic variations contributing to reduced alkaloid accumulation in tobacco.
authors: Yuan, Cheng; Tong, Zhijun; Chen, Xuejun; Zhang, Yihan; Di, Yingtong; Wang, Yuehu; Wang, Ruixue; Sui, Xueyi
abstract: In response to proposed regulations on non-addictive nicotine levels in tobacco products, researchers are screening tobacco germplasm for natural alleles associated with reduced alkaloid accumulation. Here, we re-evaluated total alkaloid contents in 15 low-nicotine accessions and identified associated allelic variations through whole-genome resequencing. Two novel nic1 alleles, nic1-5 and nic1-6, were identified and associated with suppressed nicotine biosynthetic gene expression and reduced alkaloid accumulation. Furthermore, we also identified a single-nucleotide deletion in NtMYC2a and a C-to-A substitution in NtNUP2, both causing frameshifts and resulting in premature termination codons. The NtMYC2a mutant was associated with dramatically reduced alkaloid levels in low-nicotine accessions, whereas CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of NtNUP2 did not significantly reduce nicotine content in the edited lines. These findings expand our known nic1 allelic diversity and facilitate allele pyramiding as a strategy for breeding ultra-low-nicotine tobacco cultivars.

title: T7 Ribonucleic Acid Polymerase-Triggered CRISPR/Cas13a and Branched HCR Cascade Amplification with Machine Learning for SERS Detection of Cardiac Troponin I.
authors: Zhou, Na; Ma, Yueyue; Wang, Yunxia; Zhai, Fuheng; Li, Yuanyuan; Luo, Xiaojun; Shao, Bing
abstract: Cardiac troponin I (cTnI) serves as a critical biomarker of acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Its serum level is extremely sparse, and the clinical cut-off value reaches merely 0.2 ng mL-1. This poses a significant challenge, requiring highly sensitive analytical techniques for reliable quantification. This study proposes a powerful surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) sensing strategy integrating multistage signal amplification and machine learning to enhance detection performance. By combining T7 RNA polymerase, CRISPR/Cas13a, branched hybridization chain reaction (bHCR), and Fe3O4@COF@Ag magnetic substrate, the strategy constructs an efficient "recognition-amplification-signal output" closed loop for cTnI detection. Experimental results demonstrate that the platform has a linear calibration range of 0.1-104 pg/mL for cTnI, with an estimated limit of detection (LOD) of 0.1 pg/mL, holding promise for future AMI-related biomarker analysis. It also shows excellent selectivity against common serum interferents, good reproducibility (intra-batch RSD = 2.87%, inter-batch RSD = 7.96%), and reliable recovery (100.1%-110%) in human serum samples. Based on Raman signals, the k-nearest neighbor (kNN) classifier demonstrated high accuracy in classifying cTnI concentration levels, while the artificial neural network (ANN) model exhibited strong quantitative predictive performance with an R2 of 0.9997. This platform overcomes the limitations of conventional cTnI assays in terms of sensitivity and signal amplification efficiency, providing a promising analytical platform for future AMI-related biomarker studies.

title: scDRP: disentangled representation learning for predicting single-cell responses to perturbations and estimating individual treatment effects.
authors: Sun, Jianle; Stojanov, Petar; Zhang, Kun
abstract: Dissecting cell-state-specific changes in gene regulation induced by perturbations is crucial for understanding biological mechanisms. However, single-cell sequencing provides only unmatched snapshots of cells under different conditions. This destructive measurement process hinders the estimation of individualized treatment effects (ITEs), which are essential for pinpointing these heterogeneous mechanistic responses. We develop scDRP, a generative framework that leverages disentangled representation learning with asymptotic correctness guarantees to separate perturbation-induced and perturbation-invariant latent variables via a sparsity regularized $\beta $-variational autoencoder. Assuming quantile-preserving effects of perturbations conditional on confounders, scDRP performs conditional optimal transport in the disentangled latent space to infer counterfactual states and estimate ITEs. Applied to simulated and real single-cell perturbation data, scDRP accurately estimates treatment effects and individual counterfactual responses, with subsequent biclustering analysis further elucidating cell-type-specific functional gene module dynamics. Specifically, it captures distinct cellular patterns under rhinovirus and cigarette-smoke extract exposures, reveals heterogeneous responses to interferon stimulation across diverse immune cell types, and identifies distinct functional module activation in chronic myeloid leukemia cells following CRISPR activation targeting different genes. scDRP also generalizes to unseen perturbation doses and combinations. Our framework provides a principled computational approach to extracting heterogeneous causal relationships from single-cell perturbation data, enabling a deeper understanding of cellular and molecular mechanisms.

title: CRISPR/Cas13a-Regulated SERS Biosensor Based on Plasmonic-Enhanced Magnetic Rods with Intensified Electromagnetic Field Generation for Breast Cancer Associated miRNA Detection.
authors: Sim, Sang Baek; Haizan, Izzati; Ahn, Ha Rim; Choi, Jin-Ha
abstract: Early and sensitive detection of breast cancer biomarkers is essential for improving patient prognosis, yet rapid and amplification-free analysis of low-abundance circulating miRNAs remains challenging. Herein, we report a CRISPR/Cas13a-regulated surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) biosensor, termed the CaRER sensor, for on-site detection of miRNA-511-5p, a clinically relevant breast cancer-associated biomarker. To enhance plasmonic activity and SERS performance, Ag, known for its strong SERS amplification capability, was incorporated into Au-Ni-Au magnetic rods to construct plasmonic-enhanced magnetic rods (PEMRs), which generated markedly stronger Raman signals than conventional Au-Ni-Au rods. Integration of PEMRs with the CRISPR/Cas13a system enabled amplification-free and highly sensitive detection through target-triggered trans-cleavage-induced modulation of the SERS signal after sequence-specific recognition of miRNA-511-5p. The CaRER sensor achieved femtomolar-level detection with high selectivity and reproducibility, and reliably distinguished clinical plasma samples from breast cancer patients and healthy controls. In addition, the magnetic properties of PEMRs enabled efficient separation and robust signal readout, improving assay practicality and operational reliability. The incorporation of Au also enhanced antioxidative stability relative to Ag-dominant plasmonic structures, supporting long-term chemical stability and sensing reliability. Owing to the programmability of crRNA, this platform can be readily adapted to diverse nucleic acid biomarkers through simple sequence redesign, highlighting its potential as a versatile point-of-care testing (POCT) tool for cancer diagnostics and liquid biopsy applications.

title: Functional impact of PCSK9 variants on LDL uptake in a knockout hepatic model.
authors: Li, Hongmei; Liu, Huili; Xu, Wenxin; Zeng, Yuanjun; Huang, Pengfei; Guo, Jiawang; Cai, Binxiang; Chen, Yajing; Lin, Yanyan; Zhang, Chunbin
abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a central regulator of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol metabolism, yet the functional consequences of many clinically observed PCSK9 variants remain unknown. To establish a rigorous system for quantitative variant assessment, we generated a PCSK9 knockout (KO) HepG2 cell line through CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of exons 2-8, effectively removing both the prodomain and catalytic regions required for PCSK9 function. This null background enabled systematic functional mapping of wild-type (WT) PCSK9 and multiple clinically relevant variants representing well-characterized, recurrent, and previously understudied alleles. Functional assays revealed pronounced heterogeneity among variant activities. The classical gain-of-function (GOF) variants D374Y and R496W exhibited robust suppression of LDL uptake, whereas A443T-an infrequently reported and previously uncharacterized variant-demonstrated a loss-of-function (LOF)-like phenotype with significantly enhanced LDL uptake. Additional poorly characterized variants, including V4I, R104C/V114A, and R496W/N425S, displayed varied functional profiles, providing novel mechanistic insights. Surface LDL receptor (LDLR) levels generally correlated with LDL uptake but revealed unique patterns for specific variants. This KO-based rescue system provides a high-resolution framework for mechanistic classification of both established and poorly characterized PCSK9 variants, bridging the gap between genetic discovery and functional interpretation while supporting precision lipid-lowering strategies.

title: Promoter editing of OsGTL1 improves instantaneous water use efficiency via targeted stomatal reduction in rice.
authors: Fajariani, Widya; Hungsaprug, Kansinee; Chaidee, Anchalee; Lynagh, Peter G; Purnama, Putut R; Comai, Luca; Chadchawan, Supachitra
abstract: OsGTL1 promoter modification decreases stomatal density (SD) and is inherited as a recessive trait compared to the wild type. Lower SD increases water use efficiency but lowers yield components. GT2-LIKE1 (GTL1) is a predicted drought-responsive gene in rice involved in stomatal development, yet its regulatory relationship with putative targets like Stomatal Density and Distribution 1 remains complex. Here, we employed CRISPR/Cas-based editing to alter GTL1 expression by designing a tRNA-based CRISPR to mutagenize its promoter, targeting ~ 1,500 bp 5' of the transcription start site with 7 gRNAs. Two promoter-edited lines with decreased stomatal density were selected and tested for inheritance by crossing with wild type and demonstrated to be recessive alleles, which regulated the lower expression of OsGTL1 in the developing leaves, leading to a tendency of OsSDD1 higher expression. Lower OsGTL1 expression did not significantly affect meristemoid formation, but it prevented some guard mother cells from completing symmetrical division to form mature guard cells. Lower stomatal density did not decrease the photosynthesis rate, but increased water use efficiency in the tillering stage under normal conditions and in the reproductive stage under drought stress. However, yield components in the edited lines were lower than in WT under normal conditions, but drought stress at the reproductive stage reduced yield components in the edited lines less than in WT. These findings indicate that altered OsGTL1 expression can affect stomatal development and water-use efficiency, while also revealing a trade-off between water conservation and yield components under different water regimes.

title: Construction of Recombinant PRV Expressing PRRSV Antigens and Evaluation of Their Protective Efficacy in Pigs Against Homologous Challenge.
authors: Wang, Shanghui; Liu, Yunfei; Han, Longfei; Gao, Liguo; Ye, Guangqiang; Zhao, Xiang; Liu, Yi; Liu, Hongyang; Zhang, Zhaoxia; Weng, Changjiang
abstract: Background/Objectives: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) remains a major threat to the global swine industry, while the emergence of variant pseudorabies virus (PRV) strains has further complicated disease control in China. This study aimed to develop a PRV-based viral vector platform for PRRSV antigen delivery and evaluate its safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy. Methods: A five-gene-deleted variant PRV strain, PRV-JM-DF, was used as the vector backbone. Candidate genomic insertion sites and endogenous late promoters were systematically screened, followed by construction of recombinant PRVs expressing PRRSV GP2, GP3, GP4, GP5, and M individually or as tandem antigen constructs. Recombinant viruses were characterized for antigen expression, replication, and genetic stability. Safety and immunogenicity were initially evaluated in female BALB/c mice, and the leading candidates were further assessed for safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy in 18 Landrace pigs of either sex following challenge with highly pathogenic PRRSV HuN4. Results: The TK locus supported efficient foreign-gene expression, and pUL39 exhibited the highest activity among the tested endogenous late promoters. The recombinant viruses retained replication competence and genetic stability. Among the candidates, rPRV-C-4T induced robust PRRSV- and PRV-specific neutralizing antibody responses and showed no obvious adverse effects during the experimental observation period in pigs. Following HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge, all rPRV-C-4T-immunized pigs survived and exhibited reduced viremia, viral shedding and tissue viral loads, together with markedly alleviated pathological lesions. Conclusions: rPRV-C-4T provided protection against homologous HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge while maintaining PRV-directed immune responses, supporting its potential as a PRV-vectored multivalent vaccine candidate.

title: Decreasing the Non-Fermentable Sugar Concentration in Aspergillus niger by Destroying the alpha-Glucosidase Genes.
authors: Liu, Zhengyu; Mi, Shiwei; Li, Dandan; Zhao, Kexin; Ma, Di; Jiao, Yuhan; Lu, Fuping; Li, Ming
abstract: Aspergillus niger is the main microbial cell factory for industrial citric acid production, but 2-3% of residual sugar typically remains unutilized in the fermentation broth. To reduce carbon loss caused by residual sugars, seven alpha-glucosidase genes potentially involved in non-fermentable sugar formation were investigated. In this study, seven alpha-glucosidase gene-disrupted strains were constructed and were designated as An214233, An119858, An52452, An50927, An50055, An49940, and An40261. Disruption of each gene reduced isomaltose accumulation and increased citric acid production; at the same time, some morphological characteristics of the strain also changed. Among them, the isomaltose content in the fermentation broth of An214233, An50927, An50055, and An40261 decreased by more than 30%, indicating that these genes play important roles in isomaltose formation. However, the reduction in isomaltose content was not directly proportional to the increase in citric acid production. An49940 exhibited the greatest increase in citric acid production despite a relatively moderate reduction of 13.62% in isomaltose content. This strain also exhibited favorable overall performance in total and reducing sugar utilization, together with smaller mycelial pellets and thicker hyphae. These results indicate that citric acid production is influenced not only by non-fermentable sugar formation but also by sugar utilization and mycelial morphology, thereby providing a theoretical basis and potential genetic targets for reducing carbon source loss, improving citric acid production, and decreasing residual sugars in industrial fermentation.

title: Rapid Visual LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12a Detection System for Cytospora Pathogens Associated with Pear Canker Integrating Isothermal Amplification with Programmable Secondary Recognition.
authors: Xie, Pan; Fu, Canpeng; Xu, Lingkai; Ding, Jiaqi; Feng, Beibei; Sha, Shuaishuai
abstract: Pear canker, caused by Cytospora pathogens, is a devastating branch and trunk disease threatening the sustainable development of the fragrant pear industry in Korla, Xinjiang, China. Owing to the pathogen's latent infection capability and the inconspicuous nature of early symptoms, symptom-based diagnosis is inadequate for early warning and precision management. Here, we developed a hybrid LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12a fluorescence detection system targeting Cytospora pyri and its closely related congener C. mali, the dominant Cytospora pathogens associated with pear canker. LAMP primers and Cas12a crRNA recognition sites were designed from conserved sequences of the beta-tubulin (TUB2) gene, enabling rapid isothermal amplification and sequence-specific secondary confirmation. The optimized LAMP module amplifies the target within 30 min at 65  degrees C, and the CRISPR/Cas12a module produces stable fluorescence after approximately 15 min of trans-cleavage at 37  degrees C. The system yields positive signals for both C. pyri and the closely related C. mali, with no cross-reactivity against other Cytospora species or common fruit tree pathogenic fungi, supporting rapid screening of pome fruit canker pathogens. The limit of detection is 1 copy/muL of target template. Validation using Cytospora strains from diverse geographic and host origins demonstrated complete concordance between LAMP gel electrophoresis, CRISPR/Cas12a real-time fluorescence detection, and UV-assisted visual evaluation. Preliminary results from field-collected Korla fragrant pear branch and trunk samples were consistent with conventional PCR, supporting applicability to orchard samples. By integrating rapid isothermal amplification, secondary sequence verification, and simple visual evaluation, this system provides a robust platform for early screening, pathogen surveillance, and precision management of Cytospora canker in Korla fragrant pear orchards.

title: Development of a One-Pot MIRA-CRISPR/Cas12b Fluorescence Biosensing Platform for Rapid Detection of Brucella canis.
authors: Huo, Suxin; Zhu, Yinchu; Ji, Congyun; Fan, Fu; Lin, Ruiping; Ye, Weicheng; Fu, Yuan; Hua, Jionggang; Feng, Gaole; Chen, Liu; Yun, Tao; Zhang, Cun; Wu, Zhuanli; Xu, Xing; Wu, Yue; Ni, Zheng
abstract: Brucellosis is an important zoonotic disease worldwide, and Brucella canis (B. canis) is an emerging concern in companion animal health. Rapid and reliable detection of B. canis in dogs is essential for disease control. Herein, we developed a one-pot MIRA CRISPR/Cas12b fluorescence biosensing platform targeting the conserved omp31 gene. The platform integrates MIRA mediated isothermal amplification with CRISPR/Cas12b-based target recognition and collateral cleavage. After optimization, the assay achieved a detection limit of 5 copies/reaction within 20 min, comparable to qPCR. No cross reactivity was observed with seven common canine pathogens. Among 128 clinical blood samples, the biosensor showed complete agreement with qPCR, achieving 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity. These findings demonstrate that the biosensor provides a rapid, sensitive, and specific approach for B. canis detection, with potential for decentralized veterinary testing through its endpoint visual fluorescence readout and applications in One Health surveillance.

title: Integrated Microfluidic CRISPR-Based Diagnostic Device for Rapid Testing of HPVs.
authors: Wang, Tianci; Li, Lingyun; Wang, Yunxiang; Han, Yongjun; Li, Teng; Yu, Chaoran; Lou, Yufeng; Rong, Zhen; Lin, Kai; Wang, Shengqi
abstract: Screening for high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is a pivotal strategy for the prevention of invasive cervical cancer, particularly in resource-constrained settings. In this study, we developed a CRISPR-based compact automated real-time detection system, termed Ccard, for rapid testing of HPV16, HPV18, and the internal reference gene GAPDH through a streamlined workflow. A simple room-temperature treatment efficiently releases nucleic acids directly from swab samples, bypassing the need for extraction. The mixture was driven through the channels and loaded into the reaction chambers on the microfluidic chip by a vacuum pump. The lyophilized reagents in the reaction zone of the microfluidic chip were redissolved. The system subsequently performs a single-step RPA-CRISPR/Cas13a reaction, with real-time detection enabled by an Internet of Things device. The assay achieved detection within 30 min, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 5 copies/microL for both HPV16 and HPV18. Validation with clinical samples demonstrated high sensitivity (96.8% for HPV16 and 100% for HPV18) and 100% specificity. These results highlight the reliability, precision, and strong potential of the Ccard system for rapid testing of HR-HPVs.

title: Isothermal Strand Displacement Amplification for Chemical Sensing: From Molecular Design to Integrated and Intelligent Platforms.
authors: Lee, Chia-Chun; Hsueh, Wei-Ting; Tseng, Chin-Chung; Fu, Lung-Ming
abstract: Strand displacement amplification (SDA) provides a versatile isothermal framework for chemical and biosensing, coupling polymerase-driven strand displacement with programmable nucleic-acid signal generation. Its analytical scope now extends beyond direct nucleic-acid detection because aptamers, DNAzymes, antibodies, and responsive probes can convert diverse recognition events into amplifiable DNA triggers. This review develops a unified view of SDA from molecular design to practical implementation, with particular emphasis on programmable amplicon generation, recognition-to-DNA transduction, interfacial confinement, cascaded amplification, and CRISPR coupling. The review follows SDA across biomedical, food, and environmental applications, including RNA biomarkers, liquid biopsy, genetic and epigenetic targets, proteins, enzymes, small molecules, and viruses. It also considers how these assays are being transferred into microfluidic, paper-based, lateral-flow, self-powered, regenerative, and intelligent systems. The important distinction is that analytical sensitivity does not necessarily predict practical performance. Extremely low detection limits often depend on cascaded processing beyond SDA itself, whereas real samples expose weaknesses in matrix tolerance, background suppression, reagent stability, fluid control, assay duration, and manufacturing reproducibility. Comparison with commercially established isothermal methods further shows that wider adoption will depend on converting flexible molecular chemistry into robust, standardized, sample-to-answer systems.

title: A Collective CRISPR-Cas12a Biosensing Platform for Effect-Based Screening of Pesticide Residues.
authors: Bo, Xiaoya; Li, Ji; Huang, Chao; Liu, Qun; Qi, Mingyue; Li, Qunxian; Dai, Long; Zhu, Riran; Ding, Shengyong
abstract: The simultaneous screening of multicomponent pesticide residues, rather than a single specific compound, remains a critical yet challenging frontier in safety surveillance, largely due to the inherent one-to-one recognition bottleneck in conventional aptamer- or antibody-based biosensors. Herein, we develop a collective CRISPR-Cas12a biosensing platform for effect-based screening of pesticide residues by integrating effect-based enzymatic recognition with PAM-independent CRISPR signal amplification. Rather than employing a dedicated aptamer or antibody for each pesticide, the proposed strategy exploits the inhibitory effects of diverse pesticide residues on alkaline phosphatase (ALP) as a common biochemical response. ALP activity inhibition serves as a common trigger, converting the presence of diverse toxicants into the controlled generation of Cu(+) as a unified biochemical signal via ALP-mediated ascorbic acid production. To transduce this signal into a robust nucleic acid output, we further engineer a CRISPR-Cas12a system that operates completely independent of PAM sequences through click chemistry-mediated covalent ligation of two hairpin fragments. The complete activator strand activated Cas12a trans-cleavage, thereby circumventing the sequence constraints imposed by PAM recognition. The platform exhibits quantitative responses toward TCE, CPF, and Piri, with limits of detection of 22.1 nM, 19.3 nM, and 12.0 nM, respectively. Furthermore, it successfully reports pesticide contamination in a complex real sample matrix, which provides a simple and flexible strategy for preliminary pesticide screening. Importantly, the platform is not intended to convert the collective fluorescence response into the total concentration of diverse pesticide residues; rather, the output reflects the integrated perturbation of the ALP-mediated biochemical pathway under the defined assay conditions. Overall, this work establishes an effect-based collective sensing paradigm that shifts pesticide screening from compound-specific molecular recognition toward integrated biochemical response, providing a flexible strategy for rapid screening and early warning of multicomponent pesticide contamination.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Cell-Based Therapies in Retinal Disease.
authors: Srivastava, Girish K; Shukla, Priyank; Millas, Sara Crespo; Lokanathan, Yogeswaran
abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.

title: Human-relevant disease models to accelerate the development of nucleic acid-based therapies and other advanced therapeutics.
authors: Colin, Marguerite M; Thaventhiran, James E D; Willis, Anne E
abstract: Advanced therapeutics, including programmable nucleic acid-based therapies (NATs), such as small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), CRISPR-Cas 9 editing systems, modified in vitro transcribed messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), have the potential to transform healthcare. However, while there have been considerable successes, there have also been notable clinical failures in early-stage human trials, which slowed down the progression of these therapeutic platforms. Multiple trials of NATs have been halted or discontinued, or approved products carry black box warnings as unforeseen or underestimated toxicities and poor efficacy have been observed in humans. There are a variety of reasons for failure of NATs, one of which is that many preclinical studies lack disease modelling in a human-relevant manner and, therefore, do not capture disease-specific effects on therapy tolerability and efficacy. This Perspective provides a short overview of why better human disease modelling is required to understand the potential therapeutic liabilities of NATs across modalities.

title: Correction to 'A Rapid, Field-Deployable Diagnostic Platform for Getah Virus Based on RT-RAA and CRISPR EsCas13d'.
hnRNPA2B1 sustains antitumor T cell immunity and enhances cancer immunotherapy through IDR-dependent stabilization of chromatin-regulatory transcripts.
authors: Liu, Shi; Gao, Wenyan; Hu, Menghan; Long, Lingyun; Chen, Hongyan; Zhang, Yun; Cao, Xuetao; Liu, Zhihua
abstract: T cell exhaustion within the tumor microenvironment poses a major barrier to effective cancer immunotherapy, yet the epigenetic mechanisms that preserve functional states of tumor-infiltrating T cells remain incompletely understood. Here, using an in vivo CRISPR screen, we identify heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A2/B1 (hnRNPA2B1) as a regulator of CD8+ T cell fitness. Transcriptomic analyses of cancer patient cohorts reveal that hnRNPA2B1 is preferentially enriched in a proliferative, intermediate exhausted T cell subset associated with favorable clinical outcomes. Genetic ablation of hnRNPA2B1 in CD8+ T cells accelerates terminal exhaustion, impairs antitumor immunity, and diminishes responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. Mechanistically, hnRNPA2B1 forms nuclear puncta and stabilizes RNAs involved in chromatin organization, thereby maintaining chromatin accessibility that restrains exhaustion-associated programs while preserving proliferative and cytotoxic potential. Together, these findings establish hnRNPA2B1 as an RNA-mediated epigenetic regulator sustaining functional exhausted T cell states in tumors.

title: Preclinical modeling of trastuzumab deruxtecan in a mouse model of brain metastatic triple-negative breast cancer identifies two contributors to efficacy.
authors: Khan, Imran; Kumar, Dinesh; Difilippantonio, Simone; Robinson, Christina; Wei, Debbie; Lipkowitz, Stanley; Lake, Ross; Caplen, Natasha J; Fleming, Ronald; Steeg, Patricia S
abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has demonstrated clinical efficacy in advanced HER2-low to -ultralow breast cancer. We employed a mouse model of triple-negative breast cancer in the difficult-to-treat brain metastasis setting to determine T-DXd efficacy and investigate mechanism(s). T-DXd (10 and 3 mg/kg) was compared to an identical ADC except HER2-nonbinding (control) in a hematogenous model of HER2-ultralow brain-tropic triple-negative breast cancer, MDA-MB-231-BR7 (231-BR). The roles of HER2 and the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) were determined by CRISPR-Cas9 deletion and shRNA knockdown, respectively. 231-BR cells exhibited HER2 0+ staining, with occasional membrane expression. T-DXd at 10 mg/kg reduced 231-BR brain metastases by 49% (P=0.002), while a dose reduction showed a 30% (ns) metastasis reduction, each compared to the control-ADC. HER2-specific and -nonspecific ADC uptake into metastases was accompanied by a 23-47% tumor cell Ki-67 decline, and 5-fold increase in tumor apoptosis. A HER2 CRISPR-Cas9 knockout 231-BR formed multiple brain metastases but was insensitive to T-DXd in vivo. 231-BR tumor cells expressed FcRn, potentially enabling nonspecific ADC uptake. Analysis of human tumors showed TNBC tumors expressed FcRn mRNA. T-DXd failed to inhibit brain metastases in two 231-BR FcRn knockdown clones compared to a 231-BR clone transduced with a scrambled shRNA where T-DXd inhibited brain metastases (67% reduction, P=0.01). Despite ultralow HER2 expression, the HER2 binding capacity of T-DXd is a significant contributor to its efficacy. Breast cancers variably express FcRn, suggesting that nonspecific tumor cell uptake of T-DXd via FcRn is also a potential mechanism of T-DXd action.

title: Jasmonate-Induced Metabolic Reprogramming Enhances Fruit Quality, Bioactive Compounds, and Stress Tolerance.
authors: Iqbal, Sabir; Tariq, Komal; Elatafi, Essam; Elhendawy, Basma; Yu, Huan; Liu, Wen; Ali, Shahzad; Aziz, Rana Badar; Nadeem, Muhammad Yousaf; Fang, Jinggui
abstract: Jasmonates (JAs), including jasmonic acid (JA), methyl jasmonate (MeJA), jasmonoyl-isoleucine (JA-Ile), and cis-jasmone, have emerged as central integrators of plant stress adaptation, developmental regulation, and fruit quality formation in horticultural crops. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in JA biosynthesis, metabolic conversion, signal perception, and downstream regulatory networks governing abiotic stress resilience and quality-associated traits. We highlight the coordinated chloroplast-peroxisome biosynthetic pathway leading to the formation of bioactive jasmonates and discuss the molecular basis of JA signaling mediated through the SCF;COI1-JAZ co-receptor complex and key transcriptional regulators, including MYC, MYB, NAC, ERF, WRKY, and bHLH families. Emerging evidence demonstrates that JA signaling orchestrates reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis, antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, secondary metabolism, hormonal crosstalk, and stress-responsive gene expression in response to drought, salinity, temperature extremes, and heavy metal toxicity. Beyond stress adaptation, jasmonates play pivotal roles in regulating fruit ripening, anthocyanin biosynthesis, phenolic accumulation, aroma volatile production, cell wall remodeling, vitamin C metabolism, and postharvest quality maintenance. We also discuss recent progress in multi-omics integration, epigenetic regulation, CRISPR/Cas-based genome editing, systems biology, and precision agriculture approaches that are accelerating understanding and manipulation of JA-mediated pathways in horticultural species. This review provides a mechanistic framework linking JA signaling with metabolic plasticity, stress adaptation, and fruit quality. However, major knowledge gaps remain regarding context-dependent JA responses, hormone crosstalk, metabolic trade-offs, and field-scale validation. Future research should integrate multi-omics, spatial analyses, and standardized field trials to develop precise strategies for improving fruit quality and stress tolerance.

title: In Vivo CRISPR Screen Identifies RPS19 as an Immunotherapy Target in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
authors: He, Lei; Yu, Duo; Xie, Fei; Hou, Kaisheng; Li, Zhaozhao; Dai, Meifang; Yun, Jingyi; Cao, Haiyan; Xiao, Yang; Qiu, Yueyuan; Shi, Gege; Zhang, Wangqian; Wang, Shuning; Hao, Qiang; Zhang, Jieyu; Wang, Zhaowei; Zhang, Yingqi; Zhang, Kuo; Gu, Jintao; Du, Haichen; Li, Meng
abstract: Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy, its efficacy against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains severely limited, highlighting an urgent need for novel targets and strategies to overcome immune evasion. Here, we aimed to identify key regulators of HCC immunity via unbiased functional screening and develop a targeted therapy to remodel the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed an in vivo CRISPR-knockout screen using a 4500-gene sgRNA library in syngeneic HCC mouse models. Single-cell RNA sequencing of human HCC tissues and in vivo macrophage-depletion assays were utilized to dissect cellular populations and validate underlying mechanisms. We identified ribosomal protein S19 (RPS19) as a central mediator of HCC immune evasion, whose deletion in HCC cells mitigates the immunosuppressive TME. Mechanistically, scRNA-seq pinpointed tumor-associated macrophages as the key effector subset, whereby complement C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1) transduces RPS19 signals to trigger macrophage-dependent immune suppression. We further constructed SP94-peptide-modified disulfide-bond-containing nanoparticles (SNP(SS)) for targeted CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. SNP(SS) efficiently homes to HCC cells, releases payloads within the glutathione-rich TME, downregulates RPS19, reverses immune suppression, and robustly suppresses HCC progression in vivo. Collectively, the RPS19-C5aR1-macrophage axis fuels HCC immune escape, and SNP(SS)-based RPS19 gene-editing offers a promising strategy to remodel the TME and boost HCC immunotherapy efficacy.

title: Phosphate-Engineered DNA Reporters Boost CRISPR-Cas12a Trans-Cleavage for Rapid and Sensitive Nucleic Acid Detection.
authors: Yang, Rui; Guo, Chong; Pei, Minjie; Zhang, Jiongyu; Guan, Xin; Zhang, Shuo; Liu, Xingye; Schalper, Kurt T; Avery, Lori; LaSala, Rocco; Banach, David; Liu, Changchun
abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a molecular diagnostics rely on target-activated collateral cleavage of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) reporters to generate fluorescence signals, yet the mechanisms governing reporter substrate processing remain poorly understood. Here we show that Cas12a trans-cleavage involves both endonucleolytic cleavage and exonucleolytic trimming. We further demonstrate that terminal phosphate modification of ssDNA substrates accelerates substrate cleavage activity and modulates trans-cleavage kinetics, thereby enhancing fluorescence output. Guided by this mechanistic insight, we engineered fluorophore-quencher ssDNA reporters bearing terminal phosphate modifications and identified a 3'-phosphate-engineered reporter that enables faster signal generation and higher fluorescence intensity. Incorporation of the engineered reporter into the CRISPR-Cas12a system enabled the development of Phos-CRISPR (Phosphate-engineered DNA reporters boost CRISPR), a rapid, sensitive, and specific nucleic acid detection platform that achieves results within 20 min, approximately threefold faster than conventional CRISPR assays. Applied to herpes simplex virus 1 detection, the Phos-CRISPR combined with recombinase polymerase amplification achieved a limit of detection of 20 aM and accurately identified clinical swab samples. These findings provide a general framework for understanding Cas12a trans-cleavage activity and establish a mechanistically informed strategy for enhancing next-generation CRISPR diagnostics.

title: Microbial serotonin signalling axes in irritable bowel syndrome: integrative molecular crosstalk among enterochromaffin cells, gut microbiota, neuroimmune circuits, and precision therapeutic engineering.
authors: Mehra, Ravinder Kumar; Singh, Bhanu Pratap; Siddiqui, Shakir; Aldawsari, Mohammed F; Kamal, Mohammad Azhar; Anwer, Md Khalid
abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common, often disabling disorder of gut-brain interaction whose molecular basis remains incompletely defined, leaving diagnosis largely symptom-based and treatment largely non-mechanistic. We argue that the serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; hereafter 5-HT, the primary term used throughout, with "serotonin" retained in less technical contexts) signalling axis-positioned at the interface of the gut microbiota, enterochromaffin (EC) cells, enteric neurons, and the mucosal immune system-is a central, unifying integrator of IBS pathophysiology, and that reframing IBS around this axis offers a route toward mechanism-based subtyping and therapy. We first synthesise how microbiota-driven tryptophan metabolism, short-chain fatty acid and secondary bile acid signalling, and epigenetic regulation of tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) shape EC-cell serotonin output, before examining the neuroimmune consequences of dysregulated serotonin secretion-mast cell activation, macrophage polarisation, neurogenic inflammation-and the microbiota-serotonin-gut-brain connectome linking vagal afferent signalling, blood-brain barrier permeability, and central neurotransmitter networks. We then discuss molecular stratification of IBS subtypes through serotonergic endotyping-incorporating SLC6A4 and TPH1 polymorphisms, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics-and critically evaluate next-generation therapeutic strategies, including engineered probiotic chassis, CRISPR-mediated microbial editing, and AI-guided nanomedicine, distinguishing proof-of-concept findings from clinically validated approaches. We conclude that reconceptualising IBS as a disorder of disrupted microbial serotonergic ecosystems, rather than a purely symptom-defined syndrome, offers a coherent and testable framework for biomarker discovery and precision, mechanism-directed therapy, while highlighting the causal-directionality and clinical-translation gaps that must be closed before this framework can be applied at the bedside.
